Cardiac Cycle & Hemodynamics+

The cycle has 4 mechanical phases per beat (left heart): isovolumetric contraction (mitral shuts, aortic still shut, pressure rises with no volume change), ejection (aortic valve opens once LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure; rapid then reduced ejection as the LV repolarizes), isovolumetric relaxation (aortic shuts, mitral still shut, pressure crashes at constant volume), and filling (mitral opens — rapid filling, then diastasis, then the atrial kick).

Heart sounds — origin and meaning
  • S1 — mitral + tricuspid closure, marks the start of isovolumetric contraction. Loudness varies with PR interval (short PR = loud S1, as in mitral stenosis) and mitral leaflet mobility.
  • S2 — aortic + pulmonic closure, marks the end of ejection. Physiologic splitting widens on inspiration (increased venous return delays pulmonic closure) and narrows on expiration — this is normal. Fixed splitting (no respiratory variation) suggests ASD. Paradoxical splitting (narrows on inspiration — the reverse of normal) means aortic closure is delayed, as in LBBB or severe AS.
  • S3 — early diastolic, coincides with rapid filling. Normal in children/young athletes/pregnancy; pathologic in adults, signaling volume overload (HF, MR, VSD).
  • S4 — late diastolic/presystolic, coincides with the atrial kick against a stiff ventricle (HTN, LVH, HOCM, ischemia). Requires organized atrial contraction — absent in atrial fibrillation.
Murmur timing follows the phase
LesionTiming
Mitral/tricuspid regurgitationPansystolic (holosystolic) — valve should be shut the whole time
Aortic/pulmonic stenosisMid-systolic ejection, crescendo-decrescendo
Aortic/pulmonic regurgitationEarly diastolic, decrescendo
Mitral stenosisMid-to-late diastolic rumble, often with opening snap
JVP waveform

a wave (atrial contraction — absent in AFib, cannon a-waves in AV dissociation/complete heart block) → c wave (tricuspid bulging into RA during isovolumetric contraction, often not visible bedside) → x descent (atrial relaxation — blunted/absent in tamponade) → v wave (atrial filling against a closed tricuspid — prominent/giant in TR) → y descent (tricuspid opens, rapid RA emptying — sharp and deep in constrictive pericarditis, "Friedreich's sign").

Key link: every heart sound and murmur is just the cardiac cycle made audible — if you know which phase you're in, you can predict what you should (and shouldn't) hear.
Clinical relevance — where you will actually use this
  • In the OSCE: you will be asked to time a murmur before naming it. Getting timing from the phase, rather than guessing the lesion first, is what examiners are listening for.
  • Triage without imaging: a new pansystolic murmur with a thrill on day 4 post-MI is ventricular septal rupture until proven otherwise (Case 1) — the cycle tells you a systolic leak means a valve or septum that should be closed is not.
  • The AF trap: S4 requires atrial contraction, so it cannot exist in atrial fibrillation. Vignettes use this to test whether you understand the sound or merely memorised it.
The pressure-volume loop — the same cycle, different axes

The PV loop is the Wiggers diagram redrawn with volume on the x-axis and pressure on the y-axis, and it's worth learning because it makes preload/afterload/contractility visually separable in a way the Wiggers diagram doesn't. Going counterclockwise from bottom-right: filling (bottom limb, rightward) → isovolumetric contraction (vertical right side) → ejection (top limb, leftward) → isovolumetric relaxation (vertical left side).

  • Preload = end-diastolic volume — the loop's bottom-right corner. Increasing it widens the loop rightward and raises stroke volume (Frank-Starling).
  • Afterload = the pressure the ventricle must exceed to open the aortic valve — the height at which the loop's right side ends. Raising it reduces stroke volume and raises end-systolic volume.
  • Contractility = the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR), the line touching the loop's top-left corner. This is the only one of the three that's load-independent, which is why it's the true measure of inotropic state — and why ejection fraction, which is load-dependent, can mislead.
Why this matters for exams: "EF is preserved" doesn't mean "contractility is normal" — a hypertensive patient with a small stiff ventricle can have a normal EF with poor stroke volume (this is exactly the paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS problem in Week 11, and the HFpEF problem in Week 3). Reasoning through the loop protects you from equating EF with contractility.
Clinical relevance — where you will actually use this
  • At the bedside: a patient with severe AS who becomes hypotensive is preload- and afterload-dependent. The loop tells you why fluid and phenylephrine help while nitrate and diuresis can kill — the same logic applies in HOCM and RV infarction.
  • Reading an echo report: "EF 55%" in a small hypertensive ventricle can conceal a stroke volume index under 35, which is the trap in paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS (Week 11) and the reason "moderate AS" reports get accepted too readily.
  • Prescribing: every HF drug moves one corner of this loop. Diuretics and nitrates move preload, ACE inhibitors and vasodilators move afterload, inotropes move the ESPVR — knowing which corner explains why chronic inotropes increased mortality while afterload reduction did not.
References
  • Hurst's The Heart — Cardiac Function & Hemodynamics chapters; the standard source for PV loop and cardiac cycle mechanics.
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Mechanisms of Cardiac Contraction and Relaxation; the deepest treatment of the ESPVR/load-independence concept.
  • Objective Cardiology (Mahesh Chandra) — heart sounds and JVP waveform, in the rapid-recall format useful for MCQ drilling.
Cardiac Electrophysiology+

Two distinct action potential types exist, and confusing them is a common source of pharm mistakes later.

Fast response (atrial/ventricular myocyte, Purkinje)

Phase 0 — rapid Na⁺ influx (steep upstroke). Phase 1 — transient outward K⁺ current (small notch). Phase 2 — plateau, Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux (this is what makes cardiac muscle refractory long enough to prevent tetany). Phase 3 — repolarization via K⁺ efflux. Phase 4 — stable resting potential.

Slow response (SA node, AV node)

No fast Na⁺ current — phase 0 is a slower Ca²⁺-driven upstroke. Phase 4 shows spontaneous diastolic depolarization via the "funny current" (If) — this is the basis of automaticity, why the SA node sets the pace, and why nodal tissue is the target of Ca²⁺ channel blockers and beta-blockers (rate control) rather than Na⁺ channel drugs.

Conduction pathway & the PR interval

SA node → internodal tracts → AV node (the only normal electrical connection between atria and ventricles; conducts slowly, on purpose — this delay is the PR interval, and it exists to let the ventricles finish filling before they contract) → Bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje network (fastest conduction in the heart, delivers near-simultaneous ventricular activation).

Refractory periods

Absolute refractory period — no stimulus, however strong, can generate a new action potential (roughly phases 0-2, into early 3). Relative refractory period — a stronger-than-normal stimulus can trigger a response; this is the vulnerable window. A premature beat landing here (the "R on T" phenomenon) can trigger VT/VF, which is exactly why this window matters clinically.

Why the action potential phases predict drug effects

The Vaughan Williams antiarrhythmic classification maps directly onto these phases — learning it this way means you never have to memorize the drug effects separately:

ClassTargetPhase affectedECG consequence
I (a/b/c)Na⁺ channelsPhase 0 upstrokeQRS widening (greatest with Ic: flecainide, propafenone)
IIβ-receptorsPhase 4 in nodal tissue↓HR, PR prolongation
IIIK⁺ channelsPhase 3 repolarizationQT prolongation → Torsades risk (amiodarone, sotalol)
IVCa²⁺ channelsPhase 0 in nodal tissue↓HR, PR prolongation (verapamil, diltiazem)
The reasoning payoff: when a Week 9 question asks why sotalol causes Torsades but flecainide doesn't, you don't need a memorized fact — Class III blocks K⁺ efflux, which prolongs phase 3 repolarization, which is the QT interval, which is the substrate for Torsades. Conversely, Class Ic slows conduction (widening QRS) and is contraindicated in structural heart disease — the CAST trial found excess mortality when flecainide/encainide were used to suppress PVCs after MI, a landmark result worth knowing by name.
Clinical relevance — where you will actually use this
  • Choosing an antiarrhythmic: the first question is always "is there structural heart disease?" Class Ic is off the table after MI or in HFrEF. That single rule, derived from phase 0 conduction slowing across scar, answers most selection questions (Week 9).
  • Ward safety: before adding any QT-prolonging drug, you are mentally checking phase 3 — is the patient already on another Class III agent, a macrolide or an antipsychotic, and is potassium or magnesium low? This is Case 16.
  • Rate control: nodal tissue depends on calcium and phase 4 automaticity, which is why beta-blockers and verapamil/diltiazem work there — and why they are catastrophic in pre-excited AF, where the accessory pathway bypasses the node entirely (Case 4).
The three mechanisms — every arrhythmia is one of these
MechanismBasisExamplesPractical tell
Re-entryTwo pathways with different conduction speed and refractoriness, plus a trigger — a circuit formsAVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, most VT, AF maintenanceStarts and stops abruptly; terminated by cardioversion or by breaking a limb of the circuit (ablation, adenosine)
Enhanced automaticityAbnormally steep phase 4 depolarisationSinus tachycardia, some atrial tachycardias, accelerated idioventricular rhythmWarms up and cools down gradually; not terminated by cardioversion
Triggered activityAfterdepolarisations riding on the preceding action potential — early (EADs, in phase 2/3) or delayed (DADs, calcium overload)EADs → Torsades in long QT. DADs → digoxin toxicity, CPVTPause- or catecholamine-dependent; correcting the trigger abolishes it
Why this classification earns its place: it predicts treatment. Re-entry can be interrupted mechanically or electrically — hence cardioversion and ablation. Automaticity cannot be shocked away, so you treat the driver. Triggered activity is abolished by removing the trigger — which is exactly why magnesium and rate augmentation work in Torsades (EADs are pause-dependent) and why digoxin toxicity needs the drug removed rather than the rhythm shocked.
References
  • Hurst's The Heart — Cardiac Electrophysiology: action potential physiology and the conduction system.
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Genesis of Cardiac Arrhythmias; also the standard source for Vaughan Williams pharmacology.
  • CAST investigators, NEJM 1991 — the trial that established Class Ic contraindication in structural heart disease.
ECG Fundamentals I — Rate, Rhythm, Axis, Intervals+
Rate

Regular rhythm: 300 ÷ number of large boxes between R waves (or 1500 ÷ small boxes). Irregular rhythm: count QRS complexes in a 6-second strip × 10.

Axis — think vectors, not a lookup table

Normal axis: −30° to +90°. Use leads I and aVF as your quadrant finder (both positive = normal axis; I positive/aVF negative = possible LAD, confirm with lead II; I negative/aVF positive = RAD). Left axis deviation: LAFB, inferior MI, sometimes LVH, WPW (depending on pathway location). Right axis deviation: RVH, lateral MI, acute cor pulmonale/PE, WPW.

Don't memorize the table blindly — axis is just "which direction is the net electrical vector pointing." Reasoning from that beats recalling a chart when the combination is unfamiliar.
Intervals
IntervalNormalAbnormal meaning
PR120–200msShort: WPW, LGL. Prolonged: 1st-degree AV block.
QRS<120msWide: bundle branch block, ventricular origin, hyperkalemia, Na-channel-blocking drugs.
QT (corrected)QTc = QT/√RR, <440–460ms roughlyProlonged QTc = Torsades de Pointes risk.
ECG Fundamentals II — Hypertrophy & Ischemia Patterns+
Hypertrophy criteria
ChamberCriteria
LVHSokolow-Lyon: S(V1) + R(V5 or V6) > 35mm. Cornell: R(aVL) + S(V3) > 28mm (men) / >20mm (women).
RVHR > S in V1, plus right axis deviation.
Ischemia → injury → infarct: the evolving pattern

Hyperacute T waves (tall, peaked — often the earliest sign, easy to miss) → ST elevation (transmural injury) → Q wave development (necrosis, though not all infarcts become Q-wave infarcts) → T wave inversion → ST normalization → Q waves often persist permanently as an "old MI" marker.

Territory-to-vessel correlation
TerritoryLeadsUsual vessel
InferiorII, III, aVFRCA (most commonly)
AnteroseptalV1–V4LAD
LateralI, aVL, V5–V6LCx
PosteriorReciprocal ST depression + tall R in V1–V3 (confirm with V7-V9)PDA — from RCA or LCx
ST elevation that isn't infarction

Recognizing mimics prevents both missed MIs and inappropriate reperfusion — and the discriminating features are testable:

MimicDistinguishing features
Acute pericarditisDiffuse ST elevation across territories (not one vascular distribution), PR depression, PR elevation in aVR, no reciprocal changes, concave morphology
Early repolarizationConcave ST elevation with notching/slurring at the J point, usually precordial, stable over time, young patients
LV aneurysmPersistent ST elevation weeks after MI, with well-formed Q waves in the same leads
LBBB / paced rhythmDiscordant ST-T changes are expected; apply Sgarbossa criteria (or modified Smith-Sgarbossa) to detect superimposed infarction
Brugada patternCoved ST elevation confined to V1-V3 with T inversion (see Week 9)
The discriminator to lead with: reciprocal change. True STEMI is a regional electrical event, so elevation in one territory almost always produces depression in the opposite one. Pericarditis is a global inflammatory process, so it elevates everywhere with nothing to reciprocate against.
Clinical relevance — where you will actually use this
  • The activation decision: you are deciding in under a minute whether to activate the cath lab. Reciprocal change is the single most useful discriminator between a true occlusion and a mimic, and it is available on the first ECG.
  • The catastrophic miss: inferior ST elevation in a patient with tearing pain and an inter-arm BP difference is aortic dissection, not STEMI — thrombolysis there is fatal (Case 3). The ECG alone will not save you; the discriminator has to be read alongside the history.
  • The quiet miss: ST depression in V1-V3 dismissed as "subendocardial ischaemia" is posterior STEMI — a reperfusion indication hiding as a non-indication.
References
  • Hurst's The Heart — Electrocardiography chapters; hypertrophy criteria and infarct localization.
  • Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (Thygesen et al., Eur Heart J 2018) — the formal ST-elevation diagnostic thresholds, including age/sex-adjusted V2-V3 cutoffs.
  • Sgarbossa et al., NEJM 1996; Smith et al., Ann Emerg Med 2012 (modified criteria) — diagnosing MI in the presence of LBBB.
Conduction Blocks & Metabolic ECG Patterns+
Bundle branch and fascicular block
BlockRecognitionSignificance
RBBBQRS >120 ms, rsR′ ("M") in V1, slurred S in I and V6Often benign in isolation; consider RV strain, PE, ASD, ischaemia
LBBBQRS >120 ms, broad notched R in V6/I, deep S in V1, no septal QAlmost always structural. New LBBB with ischaemic symptoms is a STEMI equivalent. Also makes ST analysis uninterpretable — use Sgarbossa
LAFBLeft axis deviation, qR in aVL, small q in ICommon; blocks the fascicle activating the superior-lateral wall
LPFBRight axis deviation, rS in I, qR in IIIRare in isolation — if present, suspect significant disease
BifascicularRBBB + LAFB (or + LPFB)Only one fascicle remaining
Trifascicular (loosely used)Bifascicular + 1st-degree AV blockSyncope here raises concern for intermittent complete block — investigate, do not reassure
Why LBBB matters more than RBBB: the left bundle is short, thick and dual-supplied, so blocking it requires substantial disease. RBBB is a thin single structure and can be blocked by relatively trivial insults — hence the very different prognostic weight.
Metabolic, toxic and environmental patterns
CauseECG progression / signature
HyperkalaemiaPeaked narrow-based T waves → PR prolongation and P wave flattening → P loss → QRS widening → sine wave → asystole. A widening QRS is the emergency — give calcium
HypokalaemiaT wave flattening, U waves, ST depression, QT appears long (really QU) — Torsades substrate
Hypocalcaemia / hypercalcaemiaQT lengthens / QT shortens
Digoxin effectDownsloping "reverse tick" ST depression — a therapeutic finding, not toxicity
Digoxin toxicityAlmost any arrhythmia; classically atrial tachycardia with AV block, or bidirectional VT
HypothermiaOsborn (J) waves, bradycardia, prolonged intervals, tremor artefact
Lead misplacementLimb lead reversal gives inverted P and QRS in lead I with normal precordials — check before diagnosing dextrocardia or infarct
Distinguish digoxin effect from digoxin toxicity. The reverse-tick ST depression is expected at therapeutic levels and needs no action. Toxicity is a rhythm diagnosis plus clinical features (nausea, confusion, yellow-green vision) — and the classic rhythm is atrial tachycardia with block.
Coronary Physiology — Supply, Demand & the Vulnerable Zone+

Coronary flow is peculiar among vascular beds and the peculiarity explains most of ischaemic cardiology.

The fundamental oddity: the left ventricle perfuses in DIASTOLE

During systole, intramyocardial pressure exceeds coronary driving pressure and effectively squeezes the vessels shut. So the LV receives most of its flow during diastole — unlike the RV, which perfuses throughout the cycle because its wall pressure is lower.

Three consequences that cascade through the whole subject
  • Tachycardia is profoundly ischaemic. Diastole shortens disproportionately as rate rises, so supply falls at exactly the moment demand climbs. This is why rate control is anti-ischaemic therapy, why beta-blockers help angina, and why a sustained tachyarrhythmia can infarct a normal coronary tree.
  • The subendocardium is the most vulnerable zone — highest wall stress, compressed longest during systole, and furthest from the epicardial vessels. Ischaemia therefore begins subendocardially and spreads outward, which is exactly why infarct LGE on cardiac MRI is subendocardial or transmural (Week 1 imaging) and why ST depression reflects subendocardial ischaemia while ST elevation reflects transmural injury.
  • Aortic diastolic pressure is the coronary driving pressure. Anything that lowers it — severe AR with its wide pulse pressure, or profound vasodilation — impairs coronary perfusion. This is part of why nitrate in severe AS or RV infarct is dangerous.
Oxygen supply and demand — the master relationship
Supply determined byDemand determined by
Diastolic time (heart rate)Heart rate
Aortic diastolic pressureContractility
Coronary vessel patency/toneWall stress (preload, afterload, wall thickness)
Oxygen content (Hb, saturation)—

Note heart rate appears on both sides — it raises demand while cutting supply. That double action is why it is the single most powerful lever in ischaemia.

Autoregulation, steal and collaterals
  • Autoregulation keeps flow constant across a range of perfusion pressures by adjusting arteriolar tone. Distal to a severe stenosis, arterioles are already maximally dilated to maintain resting flow — so coronary flow reserve is exhausted, and any rise in demand produces ischaemia.
  • Coronary steal — a potent arteriolar vasodilator (dipyridamole, adenosine, regadenoson) dilates healthy beds that still have reserve, diverting flow away from the already-maximally-dilated territory beyond a stenosis. This is the mechanism behind vasodilator stress testing, and it is why those agents can provoke genuine ischaemia.
  • Collaterals develop over time in response to chronic ischaemia. They explain why a chronically occluded vessel may cause little infarction while an acute occlusion of the same vessel is devastating — and why a patient with severe stable disease can have a smaller infarct than someone with a mildly stenotic but vulnerable plaque.
The wavefront phenomenon: after coronary occlusion, necrosis begins subendocardially and advances toward the epicardium over hours. That progression is the rationale for time-dependent reperfusion — every minute of delay converts more salvageable myocardium to scar. It is the physiological justification for door-to-balloon targets.
References
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Coronary Blood Flow and Myocardial Ischemia.
  • Reimer & Jennings — the wavefront phenomenon of myocardial necrosis.
Laplace's Law — Why Chamber Geometry Determines Fate+

Wall stress ≈ (pressure × radius) ÷ (2 × wall thickness). Three variables, and almost every structural adaptation in cardiology is an attempt to manage this equation.

SituationWhat happens to wall stressConsequence
Concentric hypertrophy (pressure overload: AS, hypertension)↓ — thickness rises to offset pressureInitially protective; cost is a stiff, non-compliant, ischaemia-prone ventricle
Eccentric dilation (volume overload: MR, AR, DCM)↑ — radius risesHigher stress → more dilation → higher stress: a self-reinforcing spiral
LV aneurysm↑↑ — large radius, thin wallHigh rupture and thrombus risk; persistent ST elevation
Aortic aneurysm↑ with diameterWhy rupture risk rises steeply beyond size thresholds — the basis of surveillance and repair criteria
Clinical relevance
  • Why the dilated ventricle is "doomed" without intervention: dilation raises wall stress, which raises oxygen demand and drives further remodelling. Interrupting that loop is precisely what afterload reduction and neurohormonal blockade achieve — the mechanistic reason GDMT reverses remodelling rather than merely relieving symptoms.
  • Why hypertrophy stops being protective: the thickened wall outgrows its capillary supply and compresses subendocardial vessels, so an adaptation that lowered wall stress ends up causing ischaemia and fibrosis.
  • Why afterload reduction helps regurgitation: lowering afterload reduces the pressure term, favouring forward flow over the regurgitant jet.
Autonomic Physiology & CV Pharm Basics+
Receptor effects

β1 (heart-predominant): ↑HR, ↑contractility, ↑conduction velocity. β2 (vessels/bronchi): vasodilation, bronchodilation. α1 (vessels): vasoconstriction. Vagal (M2, SA/AV node-predominant): ↓HR, ↓AV conduction — ventricular myocardium has minimal direct parasympathetic innervation, which is why vagal maneuvers work on SVTs (nodal-dependent) but not on ventricular arrhythmias.

Drug class mechanisms (concept only — dosing comes later)
  • Beta-blockers — competitive β-antagonists; cardioselective (β1) vs nonselective matters for asthma/COPD patients.
  • ACE inhibitors — block ACE, ↓angiotensin II, ↓aldosterone, and ↑bradykinin (source of the cough/angioedema risk).
  • ARBs — block the AT1 receptor directly; no effect on bradykinin, so no cough — the usual substitute when ACEi causes one.
  • Calcium channel blockers — dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) are vascular-selective, mainly vasodilation; non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) are cardiac-selective, negative chronotropy and inotropy.
  • Diuretics — loop (Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, thick ascending limb) vs thiazide (Na-Cl cotransporter, distal tubule) vs MRA (aldosterone receptor antagonism, also potassium-sparing).
  • Nitrates — NO-mediated cGMP; venodilation (↓preload) predominates at low dose, arterial dilation (↓afterload) adds in at higher doses.
Signature adverse effects — the ones that identify the class in a vignette
ClassSignature effectMechanism
ACE inhibitorDry cough, angioedemaBradykinin accumulation — not histaminergic, so antihistamines often fail
Dihydropyridine CCBAnkle oedema resistant to diureticsPrecapillary arteriolar dilation raises capillary pressure; adding a RAAS blocker relieves it
SpironolactoneGynaecomastiaAndrogen/progesterone receptor affinity — eplerenone is more selective
SGLT2 inhibitorGenital mycotic infection; rare euglycaemic DKAGlycosuria; hold during acute illness, fasting or surgery
AmiodaroneThyroid, pulmonary, hepatic, cornealIodine-rich, very long half-life — needs baseline and periodic monitoring
TicagrelorDyspnoea, ventricular pausesAdenosine reuptake inhibition; usually benign but drives discontinuation
StatinMyalgia → rhabdomyolysisCheck CK; dark urine plus high CK means stop immediately
Two mechanism-derived rules worth carrying forward: aspirin's effect lasts 7-10 days despite a plasma half-life of minutes, because it irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in anucleate platelets. And ivabradine only works in sinus rhythm — it inhibits the funny current in the sinus node, so it does nothing in atrial fibrillation.
Bedside Cardiovascular Examination — OSCE Technique+

The roadmap's other sections cover the physiology of heart sounds and the JVP. This one covers performing and reporting the examination, which is a separate skill assessed in the oral/OSCE component — and the one most candidates practise least. Work through it alongside the Case Bank in Weeks 15-16.

The sequence — never improvise the order

General inspection → hands → face → neck (JVP and carotids) → precordium (inspect, palpate, auscultate) → posterior chest → abdomen → peripheries. Examiners score the system, so a fluent sequence with a missed sign scores better than random findings.

SiteSigns worth naming
HandsClubbing (cyanotic CHD, endocarditis), splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes (tender, immune), Janeway lesions (non-tender, embolic), tar staining, xanthomata, peripheral cyanosis
Face / eyesMalar flush (mitral stenosis), corneal arcus and xanthelasma (lipids), conjunctival pallor, Roth spots, high-arched palate and lens dislocation (Marfan)
NeckJVP height and waveform; carotid character — assess the carotid, not the radial, for upstroke
Pulse character — the diagnostic waveforms
  • Pulsus parvus et tardus — slow-rising, late-peaking: severe aortic stenosis.
  • Collapsing (water-hammer) — wide pulse pressure: aortic regurgitation.
  • Bisferiens — two systolic peaks: mixed AS/AR, or HOCM.
  • Jerky/brisk upstroke — HOCM. This is the discriminator from AS, where obstruction is fixed from the outset rather than dynamic.
  • Pulsus alternans — alternating strong/weak beats: severe LV systolic dysfunction.
  • Radio-radial delay — subclavian stenosis, dissection. Radio-femoral delay — coarctation (Case 17).
Three measurements you must be able to perform, not just describe
  • JVP — patient at 45°, head turned slightly, internal jugular between the sternal heads. Measure vertical height above the sternal angle, add 5 cm for right atrial pressure. Distinguish from carotid: JVP is biphasic, non-palpable, varies with respiration and position, and is occludable.
  • Pulsus paradoxus — inflate above systolic, deflate slowly; note where Korotkoff sounds appear only in expiration, then where they appear throughout. The difference is the paradox; over 10 mmHg is abnormal (Case 19).
  • Abdominojugular reflux — sustained mid-abdominal pressure for 10-15 seconds while the patient breathes normally. A sustained JVP rise suggests raised filling pressures or right ventricular failure. Kussmaul's sign — a paradoxical inspiratory rise in JVP — points to constriction (Case 14).
Palpation before auscultation

Apex beat — normally 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. Displaced and diffuse = volume overload/dilation; heaving and sustained but undisplaced = pressure overload (AS, hypertension); tapping = palpable S1 of mitral stenosis; double impulse = HOCM. Parasternal heave indicates RV pressure overload. Thrills are palpable murmurs and by definition mean at least grade 4 on the Levine scale.

Dynamic manoeuvres — the highest-yield 60 seconds
ManoeuvreEffectLouder
Inspiration↑ venous return to right heartRight-sided murmurs (Carvallo's sign)
Valsalva strain / standing↓ preloadHOCM and mitral valve prolapse (all others soften)
Squatting / leg raise↑ preload and afterloadMost murmurs; HOCM and MVP soften
Handgrip↑ afterloadMR, VSD, AR; AS and HOCM soften
Two manoeuvres separate the two commonest systolic murmur traps. Valsalva distinguishes HOCM (louder) from AS (softer). Inspiration distinguishes tricuspid from mitral regurgitation. If you can only do two things at the bedside, do these.
Reporting it

Lead with a one-line summary, then positives, then relevant negatives, then your interpretation: "On examination, this patient has an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, with a slow-rising carotid pulse, a soft A2 and a sustained undisplaced apex. There is no evidence of decompensation — JVP is normal, chest clear, no oedema. This suggests severe aortic stenosis without heart failure." Ending with an interpretation rather than a list is what distinguishes a strong candidate.

References
  • Hurst's The Heart — The History, Physical Examination, and Cardiac Auscultation.
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System.
  • Levine grading scale for murmur intensity (grade 4 and above = palpable thrill).
Drug Interactions, Toxicity & Reversal+

Placed in Week 1 deliberately: these principles recur in every later week — a statin myopathy in Week 2, a bleeding patient in Week 6, a Torsades arrest in Week 9. Learn the mechanisms once and the specific pairings become derivable rather than memorised.

Three interaction mechanisms generate most exam questions
MechanismKey playersConsequence
CYP3A4 inhibitionAmiodarone, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, verapamil, grapefruit↑ simvastatin/lovastatin (myopathy), ↑ DOAC (bleeding)
CYP3A4 / P-gp inductionRifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort↓ DOAC levels → stroke risk
CYP2C9 inhibitionTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole, amiodarone↑ warfarin effect (S-enantiomer) → INR spike
Regionally important: the rifampicin-DOAC interaction matters greatly in high-tuberculosis-burden settings. A patient with AF on a DOAC starting anti-tuberculous therapy needs the anticoagulation revisited — usually switching to warfarin with INR monitoring. It is easily missed when two teams manage the two problems.
Additive stacks to recognise on sight
  • Hyperkalaemia: ACEi/ARB + MRA + trimethoprim (blocks the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride) ± NSAID. Trimethoprim is the one candidates forget.
  • Bradycardia / AV block: beta-blocker + verapamil or diltiazem + digoxin ± donepezil ± ivabradine.
  • QT prolongation: any two of Class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, ondansetron, methadone — plus hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia.
  • Bleeding: anticoagulant + antiplatelet(s) + NSAID + SSRI, amplified by renal impairment and age.
Reversal agents
DrugReversalNote
WarfarinPCC + IV vitamin KPCC works in minutes; vitamin K sustains it. FFP is slower and volume-heavy
DabigatranIdarucizumabAlso the only DOAC meaningfully dialysable
Apixaban / rivaroxabanAndexanet alfaFactor Xa inhibitors
Unfractionated heparinProtamineOnly partial for LMWH
DigoxinDigoxin-specific FabFor toxicity with arrhythmia or hyperkalaemia
Choosing drugs when the kidneys fail
  • Dabigatran is ~80% renally cleared — the most renally dependent DOAC; contraindicated in severe impairment.
  • Unfractionated heparin is the parenteral agent of choice in significant renal impairment: short half-life, monitorable, reversible.
  • Argatroban is hepatically cleared — useful in renal failure with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
  • Sotalol accumulates and prolongs QT as renal function declines.
  • Apixaban dose reduction needs TWO of three: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 µmol/L. Reducing on one is the commonest prescribing error and under-anticoagulates the patient.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia inverts your instinct. Platelets fall, but the risk is thrombosis, not bleeding. Stop all heparin (LMWH cross-reacts), avoid platelet transfusion, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant — argatroban or fondaparinux. Stopping anticoagulation altogether is the dangerous wrong answer.
References
  • 2023 ESC ACS and 2024 ESC/EACTS AF Guidelines — antithrombotic selection, DOAC dosing and interaction cautions.
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Cardiovascular Drug Therapy chapters.
  • Hurst's The Heart — Pharmacological Options in cardiovascular disease.
Common mistakes
  • Mixing up S3 (early diastolic, volume overload) with S4 (presystolic, stiff/hypertrophied ventricle) — timing relative to S2 is the differentiator, not just "extra sound."
  • Memorizing ECG axis rules as a lookup table instead of understanding the vector concept — falls apart on unusual combinations.
  • Assuming any split S2 is pathologic — physiologic splitting that widens on inspiration and disappears on expiration is normal.
  • Treating right axis deviation as one diagnosis — RVH, lateral MI, and WPW all produce it; context decides which.
  • Forgetting that S4 requires organized atrial contraction — it cannot occur in atrial fibrillation, a favorite exam trap.
  • Reaching for a vagal maneuver on a wide-complex/ventricular arrhythmia — it works on nodal-dependent SVTs, not ventricular tissue.
Week 2CAD & Acute Coronary Syndrome Survey
+
📚 Deep-dive guides🗂️ Flashcards
Atherosclerosis & Plaque Biology+

Sequence: endothelial dysfunction → LDL infiltration and oxidation in the intima → monocyte recruitment, differentiation into macrophages, foam cell formation → fatty streak → smooth muscle migration and collagen deposition forms a fibrous cap over a lipid core.

Stable vs vulnerable plaque

A stable plaque has a thick fibrous cap and small lipid core — flow-limiting if severe, producing predictable exertional angina. A vulnerable plaque has a thin cap, large lipid core, and active macrophage inflammation (matrix metalloproteinases thinning the cap from within). Rupture or erosion here exposes thrombogenic material and triggers acute thrombosis.

Key point: most MIs arise from plaques that were only mildly-to-moderately stenotic beforehand — vulnerability, not tightness of the stenosis, is what predicts rupture.
ACS Spectrum — What Separates Each Entity+
EntityClinicalBiomarkerECG
Stable anginaExertional, predictable, relieved by rest/nitratesNormalNormal or old changes
Unstable anginaNew-onset, crescendo, or rest anginaNormal (this is what separates it from NSTEMI)May show transient ST/T changes
NSTEMISame picture as UAElevated troponinNo persistent ST elevation
STEMIOngoing ischemic chest painElevatedPersistent ST elevation or new LBBB
ECG Localization in ACS+

Same territory map as Week 1, applied clinically: check reciprocal changes to confirm true infarct pattern (ST depression opposite the elevated leads supports true STEMI over benign ST elevation mimics like pericarditis or early repolarization).

Two leads that get missed
  • Posterior MI — no standard posterior leads on a routine 12-lead. Suspect it when V1–V3 show ST depression + tall R waves (a mirror image of what posterior leads V7-V9 would show as elevation). Confirm with V7-V9 if suspected.
  • RV infarct — suspect in any inferior STEMI. Get right-sided leads (V4R); ST elevation there confirms RV involvement, which changes management (avoid preload reducers).
Cardiac Biomarkers+
MarkerRisesPeaksNormalizes
Troponin I/T3–4h12–24h7–14 days
CK-MB3–6h12–24h48–72h

High-sensitivity troponin assays detect injury earlier but at the cost of more non-ACS positives. CK-MB's shorter normalization window is precisely why it's still useful for detecting reinfarction within days of an index event — troponin would already be elevated from the first event and wouldn't reliably show a second rise.

Non-ACS causes of troponin elevation

Pulmonary embolism, sepsis, renal failure (reduced clearance), myocarditis, sustained tachyarrhythmia, acute stroke, strenuous endurance exercise. Elevated troponin means myocardial injury has occurred — it does not by itself mean coronary plaque rupture.

The MI type classification — why it exists

The Fourth Universal Definition separates myocardial injury (troponin above the 99th percentile) from myocardial infarction (injury plus clinical evidence of ischemia). Within MI:

TypeMechanismManagement implication
Type 1Atherothrombotic — plaque rupture/erosion with thrombusThe classic ACS pathway; antithrombotic therapy and revascularization
Type 2Supply-demand mismatch without acute plaque event (sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, severe anemia, hypotension, hypertensive crisis)Treat the precipitant. Reflexive DAPT and cath may cause harm without benefit
Type 3Sudden cardiac death with ischemic features before biomarkers obtainable—
Type 4a / 4b / 5PCI-related / stent thrombosis / CABG-relatedProcedure-specific thresholds apply
High-yield distinction: Type 1 vs Type 2 is one of the most clinically important calls in acute cardiology and appears constantly in vignettes. The tell is usually in the stem — a septic, tachycardic, or profoundly anemic patient with chest discomfort and a modest troponin rise is far more likely Type 2. Anticoagulating them aggressively while ignoring the sepsis is the trap.
🆕 Lipids — 2025 ESC/EAS Focused Update of the 2019 Dyslipidaemia Guidelines (evidence through March 2025). Two things changed that matter for this roadmap:
  • Risk estimation now uses SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP (the older-persons algorithm) to predict 10-year fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events — replacing the fatal-events-only SCORE. SCORE2-Diabetes exists for type 2 diabetes.
  • The update adds explicit guidance for ACS, cancer and HIV populations, and pushes toward earlier and more decisive treatment intensification rather than sequential slow escalation.
The very-high-risk target itself is unchanged — ≥50% LDL-C reduction from baseline AND <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) — so answers built on that target remain correct. What changed is how you get there and how risk is calculated.
References
  • Thygesen K, et al. Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018), Eur Heart J — the authoritative source for MI types and the injury-vs-infarction distinction.
  • 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720-3826.
  • 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes.
  • Hurst's The Heart — Atherosclerosis and Acute Coronary Syndromes chapters.
Initial ACS Management Framework+

General approach: oxygen only if hypoxic (not routine with normal saturation), dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + a P2Y12 inhibitor), parenteral anticoagulation (heparin/LMWH/fondaparinux), anti-ischemic therapy (nitrates, beta-blockers if no contraindication), and high-intensity statin.

Contraindications worth knowing cold
  • Nitrates — avoid in RV infarct, hypotension, or recent PDE5 inhibitor use (severe, refractory hypotension risk).
  • Beta-blockers — avoid in acute decompensated HF, cardiogenic shock, or severe bradycardia/high-grade AV block.
Common mistakes
  • Treating any troponin elevation as MI — PE, sepsis, renal failure, and myocarditis all raise it without coronary occlusion.
  • Missing posterior MI — ST depression in V1-V3 is a reciprocal change, not "just ischemia"; think posterior leads.
  • Giving nitrates freely in inferior MI without checking for RV involvement — RV infarct is preload-dependent and nitrates can cause severe hypotension.
  • Assuming the tightest-looking stenosis on angiography is always the culprit — vulnerable plaques can rupture from a modest baseline stenosis.
  • Using troponin alone to rule out reinfarction days after an index MI — it's still elevated from the first event; CK-MB's faster normalization is more useful here.
Week 3Heart Failure & Arrhythmia Survey
+
📚 Deep-dive guides🗂️ Flashcards
HFrEF vs HFpEF+
HFrEFHFpEF
EF≤40%≥50% (41–49% = HFmrEF, mildly reduced)
DefectSystolic — impaired contractilityDiastolic — impaired relaxation/compliance
RemodelingEccentric hypertrophy, chamber dilationConcentric hypertrophy, stiff ventricle
Typical driverIschemic injury, dilated cardiomyopathyLong-standing HTN, diabetes, obesity, aging

In HFrEF, the Frank-Starling curve shifts down and to the right — the ventricle needs a higher filling pressure to generate the same stroke volume. Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, sympathetic tone, natriuretic peptides) is compensatory acutely but maladaptive chronically — this is the entire rationale behind the four pillars: each one interrupts a piece of that maladaptive activation.

The neurohormonal cascade, and why each pillar exists

Reduced cardiac output → baroreceptor unloading → sympathetic activation and renal hypoperfusion → renin release → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, afterload rise, direct myocyte hypertrophy and fibrosis) → aldosterone (sodium/water retention, myocardial and vascular fibrosis). Meanwhile, ventricular stretch releases natriuretic peptides (BNP/ANP) — a counter-regulatory system promoting natriuresis and vasodilation, but one that gets overwhelmed.

  • ACEi/ARB interrupt angiotensin II generation or action → less afterload, less fibrosis.
  • ARNI adds neprilysin inhibition → augments the failing counter-regulatory natriuretic peptide arm rather than only blocking the harmful arm. This is why ARNI outperformed enalapril in PARADIGM-HF.
  • Beta-blockers interrupt chronic sympathetic toxicity — which is why they must be started when stable, since the acute effect is negative inotropy.
  • MRA blocks aldosterone's fibrotic effect, not just its sodium retention (RALES, EMPHASIS-HF).
  • SGLT2 inhibitors — mechanism is still incompletely explained, but benefit appears independent of glycemic control (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced), plausibly via natriuresis, improved myocardial energetics, and reduced cardiac fibrosis.
The unifying idea worth carrying into orals: HFrEF therapy is not primarily about making the heart pump harder — historically, drugs that did that (chronic inotropes) increased mortality. The four pillars work by blocking maladaptive neurohormonal remodeling. If you can articulate that, you're reasoning at the level examiners are listening for.
Clinical relevance — where you will actually use this
  • Defending your prescription: when a colleague wants to stop an ACE inhibitor for a modest creatinine rise, this framework is your argument — you are protecting a mortality benefit, not a blood pressure number (Case 7).
  • Explaining to patients: "these drugs stop your heart getting worse" is mechanistically true and more persuasive than "they help your heart pump."
  • Knowing when it does NOT apply: in cardiac amyloidosis the four pillars are poorly tolerated and often withdrawn (Case 5). Understanding why GDMT works is what lets you recognise the disease where it does not.
References
  • 2021 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3599-3726, with the 2023 Focused Update.
  • 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure, Circulation 2022.
  • Landmark trials: PARADIGM-HF (ARNI), RALES/EMPHASIS-HF (MRA), DAPA-HF & EMPEROR-Reduced (SGLT2i), MERIT-HF/CIBIS-II/COPERNICUS (beta-blockers).
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Pathophysiology of Heart Failure; the fullest account of the neurohormonal model.
Staging — Two Different Axes+

NYHA I-IV is functional and symptom-based — it can improve or worsen with treatment (a patient can move from NYHA III back to II).

ACC/AHA Stage A→D is structural and progressive — Stage A (at risk, no structural disease yet, e.g. HTN/diabetes alone) → B (structural disease, asymptomatic) → C (structural disease + symptoms) → D (refractory, end-stage). This axis does not move backward; a patient can improve symptomatically within a stage but doesn't get "destaged."

These two systems are tested together deliberately — a vignette will often expect you to assign both, and they don't always move in parallel.
Arrhythmia Overview (Survey Level)+
Bradyarrhythmias

Sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus syndrome) and AV blocks — 1st degree (prolonged PR, every beat conducts), 2nd degree Mobitz I/Wenckebach (progressively lengthening PR until a beat drops — usually benign, vagally mediated), 2nd degree Mobitz II (constant PR then a sudden dropped beat, no warning — often infranodal disease, higher risk of progressing to complete block), 3rd degree/complete (no relationship between P waves and QRS — atria and ventricles beat independently).

Supraventricular tachycardias

Atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia — deep dive comes in Week 8.

Ventricular arrhythmias

PVCs, monomorphic VT, polymorphic VT (including Torsades), VF — deep dive comes in Week 9.

The HF "Four Pillars" — Mechanism Only+
  • ACEi/ARB/ARNI — ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) combines neprilysin inhibition (raises natriuretic peptide levels, promoting natriuresis/vasodilation) with AT1 receptor blockade.
  • Beta-blockers — only the evidence-based ones count for HFrEF mortality benefit: carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (not tartrate), bisoprolol.
  • MRA — spironolactone or eplerenone, blocks aldosterone's fibrotic and sodium-retaining effects.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors — the newer fourth pillar (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin); benefit in HFrEF is independent of diabetes status.
Common mistakes
  • Assuming all HF means reduced EF — HFpEF is roughly half of HF cases and follows a different treatment logic.
  • Starting beta-blockers during acute decompensation — they're initiated once the patient is euvolemic and stable, not during the crisis.
  • Not separating Mobitz I (usually benign/vagal) from Mobitz II (often needs a pacemaker) — same "2nd degree block" label, very different urgency.
  • Treating NYHA class and ACC/AHA stage as interchangeable — one is symptom-based and reversible, the other structural and one-directional.
  • Using metoprolol tartrate interchangeably with succinate for HFrEF — only the succinate (extended-release) formulation has the mortality-benefit evidence.
Week 4HTN, Valvular, Cardiomyopathy, Congenital + Diagnostic Test
+
📚 Deep-dive guides🗂️ Flashcards❓ Diagnostic MCQ run
Hypertension+

ACC/AHA 2017 thresholds: Normal <120/80, Elevated 120-129/<80, Stage 1 130-139/80-89, Stage 2 ≥140/90. ESC/PERKI classifications run slightly differently (Optimal/Normal/High-normal/Grade 1-3) — know that the exact numeric cutpoints can diverge between systems, so check which guideline a question is anchored to.

Secondary causes worth being able to list cold

Renal (renal artery stenosis, CKD), endocrine (primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome, thyroid disease), coarctation of the aorta, obstructive sleep apnea, drug-induced (NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, decongestants).

Urgency vs emergency

Hypertensive urgency — severe BP elevation, no acute end-organ damage. Hypertensive emergency — severe BP elevation with acute end-organ damage: encephalopathy, aortic dissection, papilledema, acute decompensated HF, ACS, or acute kidney injury. The number alone never makes the diagnosis — the end-organ picture does.

Valvular Disease Overview+

Stenosis = pressure overload on the chamber proximal to the valve, driving concentric hypertrophy. Regurgitation = volume overload, driving eccentric hypertrophy/dilation. Murmur timing follows the same logic covered in Week 1 — stenotic lesions murmur during the phase blood is being forced through a narrow orifice; regurgitant lesions murmur whenever the valve should be shut but isn't.

Cardiomyopathy Classification+
TypeDefectCommon causes
DilatedSystolic dysfunction, ventricular dilationIschemic, idiopathic, genetic, viral myocarditis, alcohol, peripartum, tachycardia-induced
HypertrophicDiastolic dysfunction ± outflow obstructionSarcomere protein mutations (genetic); classically asymmetric septal hypertrophy
RestrictiveDiastolic dysfunction, stiff myocardium, near-normal EF/wall thicknessAmyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, radiation
Congenital Heart Disease Survey+

Left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA) are acyanotic at onset — they volume-overload the pulmonary circulation. Over years, chronic overcirculation drives pulmonary vascular remodeling and pulmonary hypertension.

Eisenmenger syndrome — the endpoint of a long-standing untreated L→R shunt: pulmonary vascular resistance eventually exceeds systemic resistance, and the shunt reverses to right-to-left, producing cyanosis. This is a late complication, not the starting point.

Primary right-to-left shunts (e.g. Tetralogy of Fallot) are cyanotic from birth or early infancy — a structurally different situation from Eisenmenger's acquired reversal.

References for Week 4
  • 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension, Eur Heart J 2024 — the current European standard (note it diverges from ESH 2023; see Week 10).
  • 2017 ACC/AHA Hypertension Guideline — the source of the 130/80 Stage 1 threshold still used in many question banks.
  • 2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease (see Week 11 for detail).
  • 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503-3626.
  • 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645.
  • PERKI hypertension consensus — check your Guidelines module for the current Indonesian thresholds.
End of week: run the full 200-Q MCQ bank untimed, no prep. This becomes your priority map for Phases 2 and 3 — don't skip it.
Common mistakes
  • Diagnosing hypertensive emergency by BP number alone — it's defined by end-organ damage, not a threshold.
  • Forgetting HOCM murmur behaves oppositely to most others — louder with Valsalva/standing, softer with squatting.
  • Assuming all congenital shunts are right-to-left — most start left-to-right; Eisenmenger is the late reversal, not the default.
  • Applying identical numeric BP thresholds across ACC/AHA, ESC, and PERKI without checking which guideline the question is using.
  • Confusing Tetralogy of Fallot (cyanotic from the start) with Eisenmenger physiology (cyanotic only after years of an untreated left-to-right shunt) — both end in R-to-L shunting, but the mechanism and timeline differ completely.
