Week 5ACS Deep Dive I — STEMI
+
📚 Guide (full depth)🗂️ Spaced flashcards❓ Topic-locked MCQs
STEMI Diagnosis & Reperfusion Strategy+

Diagnostic threshold: ST elevation ≥1mm in 2 contiguous limb leads, ≥2mm in 2 contiguous precordial leads (age/sex-adjusted in V2-V3), or new LBBB with an ischemic clinical picture.

Choosing the reperfusion strategy

Primary PCI is preferred whenever it can be delivered within the guideline window — door-to-balloon ≤90 min at a PCI-capable center, ≤120 min if transfer is needed. If that window can't be met, fibrinolysis is the fallback (door-to-needle ≤30 min), followed by transfer for rescue or routine early PCI.

Fibrin-specific agents (tenecteplase, alteplase) are preferred over streptokinase. Rescue PCI is indicated if lysis fails — persistent ST elevation or hemodynamic/electrical instability within ~90 minutes of the lytic.

Total ischemic time is what saves myocardium — the specific strategy matters less than how fast reperfusion happens by whichever route is actually achievable.
🆕 Recent update: the 2023 ESC and 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines both retired the separate STEMI/NSTEMI documents and now manage ACS as one spectrum in a single guideline — think in terms of risk tier and time-to-angiography rather than a strict STEMI-vs-NSTEMI dichotomy. Two specific STEMI changes worth knowing: complete revascularization (treating significant non-culprit lesions during the index procedure or within 45 days) is now Class I — culprit-only PCI is no longer the default outside cardiogenic shock. And P2Y12 pretreatment before angiography, once routine, is now only Class IIb ("may be considered") for primary PCI.
Mechanical Complications — Why Timing Is the Exam Clue+

Three complications cluster in the same window — days 3-5 post-MI — because that's when necrotic myocardium is at its softest and most friable, before fibrous scar has had time to form. Recognizing that timing window is often the fastest way to answer a vignette.

ComplicationTypical timingPresentation
Free wall rupture1-4 days (can be early)Sudden hemodynamic collapse/PEA, tamponade physiology — often fatal before intervention is possible
Papillary muscle rupture3-5 daysAcute severe MR, flash pulmonary edema, new murmur
Ventricular septal rupture3-5 daysNew harsh holosystolic murmur + step-up in O₂ saturation from RA to RV on right heart cath

Why the posteromedial papillary muscle ruptures more often: it has a single blood supply (from the PDA), while the anterolateral papillary muscle has dual supply (LAD + a diagonal/obtuse marginal branch) — redundancy that protects it.

True aneurysm (thinned but intact myocardial wall, often with persistent ST elevation weeks later) carries thrombus/arrhythmia risk but low rupture risk. Pseudoaneurysm (a contained rupture, walled off only by pericardium/thrombus) carries high rupture risk and generally needs surgical repair — don't conflate the two just because both show a bulge on imaging.

Cardiogenic Shock Management+

Defined by SBP<90 with hypoperfusion signs, elevated filling pressures, and low cardiac index — usually from a large infarct territory (>40% of LV) or one of the mechanical complications above.

The SCAI shock stages (A through E) are now the standard vocabulary and worth knowing by letter: A At risk (no shock), B Beginning (hypotension/tachycardia, no hypoperfusion), C Classic (hypoperfusion requiring intervention), D Deteriorating (failing to respond to initial escalation), E Extremis (circulatory collapse, often refractory arrest). Staging matters because outcomes and appropriate escalation differ sharply across them, and interviewers increasingly expect the terminology.

Revascularization is the priority intervention — early PCI improves survival in cardiogenic shock (this is the single most important management step, more than any pharmacologic support). Norepinephrine is generally favored over dopamine as first-line vasopressor per contemporary evidence. Mechanical circulatory support (Impella, ECMO) can bridge unstable patients; IABP is used less now — a major trial (IABP-SHOCK II) failed to show a mortality benefit from routine IABP use.

Nuance on culprit-only vs complete revascularization: the Week 5 update notes complete revascularization is now Class I in STEMI generally — but cardiogenic shock is the explicit exception. The CULPRIT-SHOCK trial found culprit-lesion-only PCI produced better 30-day outcomes than immediate multivessel PCI in shock. Knowing both the general rule and its exception is exactly the kind of distinction that separates strong candidates.
References
  • 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720-3826 — reperfusion strategy, timing targets, complete revascularization.
  • 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS Guideline.
  • CULPRIT-SHOCK (NEJM 2017) — culprit-only PCI in cardiogenic shock; IABP-SHOCK II (NEJM 2012) — routine IABP.
  • Baran DA, et al. SCAI clinical expert consensus on the classification of cardiogenic shock, 2019 (updated 2022).
  • Hurst's The Heart — ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction and its Complications.
Common mistakes
  • Waiting on troponin to "confirm" STEMI before reperfusion — STEMI is a clinical + ECG diagnosis; don't delay.
  • Missing RV infarct in inferior STEMI — get right-sided leads (V4R) before assuming it's a simple inferior MI.
  • Overlooking fibrinolytic contraindications (recent stroke, active bleeding) under time pressure.
  • Expecting mechanical complications immediately post-MI — they cluster in the days 3-5 window when necrotic myocardium is most friable, not in the first few hours.
  • Forgetting the posteromedial papillary muscle's single blood supply makes it far more vulnerable to rupture than the dual-supplied anterolateral muscle.
  • Defaulting to IABP as first-line mechanical support in cardiogenic shock — the evidence doesn't support a routine mortality benefit; revascularization is what actually saves lives here.
  • Sticking with culprit-only PCI as the default outside cardiogenic shock — current guidance now favors complete revascularization of significant non-culprit lesions, either at the index procedure or within 45 days.
Week 6ACS Deep Dive II — NSTEMI/UA + Guideline Comparison
+
📚 Guide (full depth)❓ Topic-locked MCQs📋 Guidelines module (PERKI/ESC/AHA)
Risk Stratification — TIMI vs GRACE+

TIMI score (7 points — age≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, known CAD ≥50% stenosis, aspirin use in the past 7 days, severe angina ≥2 episodes/24h, ST deviation ≥0.5mm, elevated biomarkers) predicts 14-day risk of death/MI/urgent revascularization. It's simple and fast at the bedside.

GRACE score (age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest at admission, ST deviation, elevated biomarkers) is more complex but better calibrated for in-hospital and 6-month mortality — it's the score guidelines lean on for deciding how fast to go to the cath lab.

They answer different questions: TIMI is a quick early-decision tool, GRACE is the more accurate mortality predictor that drives invasive timing.
Invasive vs Conservative Strategy Timing+

The 2023 ESC guideline simplified this to a 3-tier system — drop the older 4-tier (very high/high/intermediate/low) framework if that's what you learned before.

Risk categoryTriggerTiming
Very high riskHemodynamic instability/cardiogenic shock, refractory angina, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complication, acute HF from ongoing ischemia, recurrent dynamic ECG changesImmediate (emergency, ASAP)
High riskConfirmed NSTEMI diagnosis (troponin rise), dynamic ST/T changes, or high GRACE scoreEarly (<24h)
Non-high riskNone of the aboveSelective/ischemia-guided — no routine early invasive angiography
🆕 Recent update: the <24h "early invasive" recommendation for high-risk patients was actually downgraded in 2023 — from Class I (2020 guideline) to Class IIa. The trial evidence behind early angiography turned out to mainly reduce future revascularizations rather than mortality or stroke, so it's now a slightly softer recommendation than older material may suggest.
Antiplatelet & Anticoagulant Selection+

Ticagrelor or prasugrel are generally preferred over clopidogrel in ACS — more potent, faster onset. Prasugrel is contraindicated with a history of stroke/TIA, and needs dose caution in patients >75y or <60kg. Clopidogrel remains the choice when bleeding risk is high or the patient is already on anticoagulation (triple-therapy scenarios).

Standard DAPT duration is 12 months post-ACS — shortened if bleeding risk is high, or considered for extension beyond 12 months if ischemic risk remains high and bleeding risk is low. It's a risk-balance decision, not a fixed rule. More precisely, per the current ESC de-escalation ladder:

  • Event-free at 3-6 months, not high ischemic risk → switch to single antiplatelet (preferably P2Y12 monotherapy)
  • High bleeding risk → aspirin or P2Y12 monotherapy after just 1 month of DAPT can be considered
  • Never de-escalate in the first 30 days post-ACS regardless of bleeding risk — confirmed by the STOPDAPT-3 trial
  • Beyond 12 months, aspirin monotherapy remains the default long-term choice
🆕 Recent update — and a genuine ESC vs ACC/AHA disagreement. Read this carefully, because a single-answer version of it is wrong.
  • DAPT itself is not in question. Aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor for a default of at least 12 months after ACS (absent high bleeding risk) is Class I in both guidelines. Ticagrelor or prasugrel are preferred over clopidogrel for PCI-managed ACS.
  • What is contested is PRETREATMENT — loading the P2Y12 before coronary anatomy is known.
    ESC 2023 de-escalated routine upfront loading to Class IIb, and specifically advises against routine pretreatment in NSTE-ACS when an early invasive strategy is planned and anatomy is unknown. The evidence base is ATLANTIC, the SWEDEHEART registry and supporting meta-analyses, which found no mortality or event benefit from loading before angiography.
    ACC/AHA 2025 retains a Class I recommendation for P2Y12 loading, and frames the delay question differently: starting an oral P2Y12 inhibitor before transfer to the cath lab is Class IIb if an expected delay exceeds 24 hours.
  • They also differ on de-escalation. ESC permits P2Y12 monotherapy from 1 month after PCI; ACC/AHA is more conservative, favouring 12 months of DAPT with de-escalation to monotherapy considered at 3-6 months in low ischaemic risk, and ticagrelor monotherapy from ≥1 month where bleeding risk dominates.
How to answer this: aspirin immediately, always. For the P2Y12 timing, name the split rather than picking one — "ESC says defer until anatomy is known in NSTE-ACS going early invasive; ACC/AHA still loads upfront." If the question forces a single answer and names no guideline, default to PERKI, which has tracked ESC more closely.
Guideline Concordance — PERKI vs ESC 2023 vs ACC/AHA 2025+

The core ACS skeleton — DAPT, anticoagulation, risk-stratified invasive timing, revascularization for high-risk features — is concordant across all three. Where they tend to diverge is in the specifics: exact score cutoffs for invasive timing, P2Y12 preference ordering, and DAPT duration defaults for different risk profiles. (The American side is now the 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes — it replaced the older separate 2013 STEMI and 2014 NSTEMI documents, mirroring ESC's move to a unified ACS framework.)

Exam rule: PERKI's specific recommendation wins whenever a question doesn't explicitly name another guideline. Treat this section as the reasoning framework — your existing SKA Confluence comparison in the Guidelines module is the authoritative source for the exact current cutpoints, so cross-check the precise numbers there before exam day.
References
  • 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720-3826 — the 3-tier invasive timing framework and the Class III pretreatment recommendation.
  • 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes.
  • PERKI Pedoman Tatalaksana Sindrom Koroner Akut Ed. 5 — the Indonesian reference; your SKA Confluence document maps this against ESC/AHA module by module.
  • STOPDAPT-3, MASTER DAPT, TWILIGHT — the de-escalation and short-DAPT evidence base.
  • Fox KAA et al. (GRACE) and Antman EM et al. (TIMI) — the original derivation papers for each risk score.
Bedside Scores & the Non-Atherothrombotic ACS Syndromes+
Three scores that do different jobs
ScoreSettingWhat it answers
HEARTUndifferentiated chest pain in the EDHistory, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin — can this patient be safely discharged?
GRACEConfirmed ACSMortality risk — drives invasive timing
TIMIConfirmed ACSQuick composite risk at the bedside
Killip classACS at presentationI no failure · II crackles/S3 · III pulmonary oedema · IV cardiogenic shock. Strong independent mortality predictor and a GRACE input
HEART answers "can this person go home"; GRACE answers "how fast must this person reach the cath lab". Using one for the other's job is a common error.
When the coronaries are open — the MINOCA differential
  • SCAD (spontaneous coronary artery dissection) — disproportionately affects younger women, and is associated with peripartum status and fibromuscular dysplasia. Crucially, management is usually conservative: stenting risks extending the dissection, so it is reserved for ongoing ischaemia or instability. Reflexive stenting is the error.
  • Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal / variant angina) — rest pain, often nocturnal or early morning, with transient ST elevation that resolves. Treat with calcium channel blockers and nitrates; beta-blockers can worsen it by leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed. Smoking is the dominant risk factor.
  • Takotsubo — regional wall motion abnormality extending beyond a single coronary territory, classically apical ballooning, usually after emotional or physical stress; typically reversible over weeks.
  • Myocarditis, PE, and Type 2 supply-demand mismatch complete the differential.
Two reflexes to suppress: stenting a SCAD, and giving a beta-blocker as first-line in vasospastic angina. Both are the standard ACS reflex applied to a non-atherothrombotic mechanism.
Dressler's syndrome

Immune-mediated pericarditis weeks after infarction (distinct from early peri-infarct pericarditis in the first days). Presents with pleuritic pain, fever, raised inflammatory markers and often an effusion. Treat with aspirin plus colchicine — and note that NSAIDs other than aspirin and corticosteroids are generally avoided post-MI, as they may impair infarct healing.

Antithrombotic Pharmacology — Agent-Level Detail+
AgentMechanismDecisive feature
AspirinIrreversible COX-1 acetylationEffect lasts the 7-10 day platelet lifespan despite a plasma half-life of minutes — stop 5-7 days pre-surgery
ClopidogrelProdrug, CYP2C19-activatedLoss-of-function alleles are more prevalent in East/Southeast Asian populations → reduced platelet inhibition
TicagrelorDirect, reversibleDyspnoea and ventricular pauses; twice-daily; needs low-dose aspirin
PrasugrelProdrug, more reliable activationAbsolute contraindication with prior stroke/TIA; caution >75y or <60 kg
CangrelorIV, direct, ultra-short actingBridging when oral agents impractical
Population-specific point worth carrying into a viva: CYP2C19 loss-of-function allele frequency is substantially higher in East and Southeast Asian populations than in European ones. That is a real argument for preferring a direct-acting P2Y12 inhibitor where bleeding risk permits — and it shows you are reasoning about your own population rather than reciting trial data from elsewhere.
Choosing the P2Y12 agent by scenario
  • PCI-managed ACS, standard bleeding risk → ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel.
  • After fibrinolysis → clopidogrel, the only agent with supporting evidence in that setting.
  • Requires concurrent oral anticoagulation → clopidogrel; avoid ticagrelor and prasugrel.
  • Prior stroke or TIA → never prasugrel.
  • High bleeding risk → clopidogrel, shortened DAPT, radial access, PPI cover.
Never de-escalate within the first 30 days post-ACS regardless of bleeding risk — thrombotic hazard is highest then, confirmed by STOPDAPT-3. After that, the ladder is triple therapy (kept short) → anticoagulant plus clopidogrel → anticoagulant alone beyond 12 months.
References
  • 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines — antithrombotic selection and de-escalation.
  • PLATO (ticagrelor), TRITON-TIMI 38 (prasugrel), CLARITY-TIMI 28 and COMMIT (clopidogrel with fibrinolysis).
  • AUGUSTUS, PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI — anticoagulant plus antiplatelet combinations after PCI.
Common mistakes
  • Using TIMI and GRACE interchangeably — TIMI guides strategy decisions, GRACE better predicts mortality; they're not the same tool.
  • Defaulting to the Western guideline answer — on a PERKI-affiliated exam, PERKI's version wins when it diverges.
  • Continuing triple therapy indefinitely without reassessing bleeding risk.
  • Choosing prasugrel for a patient with a prior stroke/TIA — this is an absolute contraindication, not a relative caution.
  • Treating DAPT duration as a rigid fixed 12 months in every case — it flexes with bleeding vs ischemic risk.
  • Loading a P2Y12 inhibitor at first contact for NSTE-ACS with unknown anatomy before an early invasive strategy — routine pretreatment here is now actively discouraged (Class III), a reversal of older practice.
Week 7Heart Failure Deep Dive
+
📚 Guide (full depth)🗂️ Spaced flashcards❓ Topic-locked MCQs🩺 Case sim #1
HFrEF GDMT — Sequencing & Titration+

Modern practice favors early, simultaneous, low-dose initiation of all four pillars rather than the older approach of maxing out one drug before starting the next — each class shows benefit even at starting doses, and delay itself costs mortality benefit. A beta-blocker, SGLT2 inhibitor, and MRA can often start together if hemodynamically tolerated, with ARNI/ACEi/ARB added as blood pressure allows.

The goal is target dose, or maximally tolerated dose — not just "some dose." Monitor renal function/potassium for ACEi/ARB/ARNI/MRA (hyperkalemia risk) and watch for symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension with beta-blockers.

Washout matters: switching from an ACE inhibitor to an ARNI requires a ≥36-hour gap — giving them concurrently sharply raises angioedema risk.
🆕 Recent update: the 2023 ESC focused update gives SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) a Class I recommendation across the entire EF spectrum — HFrEF, HFmrEF, and HFpEF — not just reduced EF. It also gives a Class I recommendation to an intensive strategy of starting and rapidly up-titrating GDMT before discharge, with close follow-up visits through the first 6 weeks after a HF hospitalization — that early window is now explicitly where the guideline wants titration to happen, not spread passively over months.
Acute Decompensated HF Management+

Classify by the bedside "wet/dry, warm/cold" framework:

ProfileMeaningApproach
Wet-warmCongested, adequately perfused (most common)Diuretics ± vasodilators
Wet-coldCongested + hypoperfused (cardiogenic shock)Inotropes ± vasopressors, consider mechanical support
Dry-coldHypoperfused without congestionCareful fluid/inotrope balance, avoid aggressive diuresis

IV loop diuretics are first-line for congestion; if diuretic resistance develops, adding a thiazide provides synergistic "sequential nephron blockade." Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) are reserved for low-output/hypoperfusion states — not routine therapy for congestion alone.

Device Therapy — ICD & CRT+

ICD (primary prevention): EF≤35% despite ≥3 months of optimized GDMT, NYHA II-III, life expectancy >1 year. Wait at least 40 days post-MI before assessing — early EF often recovers, and trials of very early post-MI ICD placement (DINAMIT, IRIS) failed to show a mortality benefit.

CRT: EF≤35%, NYHA II-IV on GDMT, with the strongest indication being LBBB and QRS≥150ms — it resynchronizes dyssynchronous ventricular contraction.

Iron Deficiency in Heart Failure+

Iron deficiency is common in HF and worth screening for independent of anemia (ferritin <100 ng/mL, or 100-299 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%, is the usual definition). In symptomatic HFrEF/HFmrEF with iron deficiency, IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose) is recommended to improve symptoms and quality of life, and should be considered to reduce HF hospitalization risk.

Oral iron doesn't work here — absorption is unreliable in the HF/inflammatory state, which is why the guideline-supported route is specifically IV.
Cardiorenal Syndrome+

Bidirectional heart-kidney dysfunction, classified into 5 types by direction and acuity: Type 1 (acute HF → AKI), Type 2 (chronic HF → progressive CKD), Type 3 (AKI → acute cardiac dysfunction), Type 4 (CKD → chronic cardiac dysfunction), Type 5 (a systemic condition driving both).

Nuance worth knowing: a rising creatinine during diuresis doesn't automatically mean stop the diuretic — it can reflect hemoconcentration from effective decongestion rather than true renal injury. Look at the whole clinical trajectory, not the creatinine number alone.
Managing the barriers to GDMT

The two things that most often derail titration are hyperkalemia and renal function decline — and the reflex to simply stop the drug is usually the wrong move, because withdrawing an ACEi/ARB/MRA removes proven mortality benefit.

  • Hyperkalemia — before stopping the RAAS blocker, review dietary potassium, stop potassium supplements and other contributors (NSAIDs, trimethoprim), and consider a potassium binder (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) specifically to enable continued RAAS inhibition. Guidelines now support this "enabling" use.
  • Renal decline — a modest, stable creatinine rise (commonly cited as up to ~30% and plateauing) after RAAS blockade initiation is expected hemodynamic adaptation, not injury, and is not a reason to discontinue.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors produce a characteristic early eGFR "dip" that recovers — this is anticipated and does not warrant stopping the drug.
References
  • 2021 ESC HF Guidelines + 2023 Focused Update, Eur Heart J — SGLT2i across the EF spectrum, IV iron, and the intensive post-discharge titration recommendation.
  • 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Heart Failure Guideline, Circulation 2022;145:e895-e1032.
  • STRONG-HF (Lancet 2022) — the trial behind rapid up-titration and close follow-up after HF hospitalization.
  • AFFIRM-AHF and IRONMAN — IV iron in HF with iron deficiency.
  • DINAMIT and IRIS — the trials establishing the 40-day post-MI ICD waiting period.
  • Hurst's The Heart — Heart Failure chapters; Braunwald's for cardiorenal physiology.
Common mistakes
  • Under-dosing GDMT out of fear of hypotension — the mortality benefit is dose-dependent, not just "on vs off."
  • Reaching for inotropes first-line in a normotensive decompensated patient — diuretics/vasodilators come first.
  • Forgetting the ICD primary-prevention waiting window — typically 40 days post-MI and 3 months of optimized GDMT before reassessing EF.
  • Sequencing all four GDMT drugs slowly, one at a time — modern practice favors earlier simultaneous low-dose initiation since delay itself costs benefit.
  • Starting an ARNI within 36 hours of stopping an ACE inhibitor — the washout period exists specifically to avoid angioedema.
  • Stopping diuretics reflexively the moment creatinine rises during decongestion — this can be hemoconcentration from effective treatment, not renal injury.
  • Reserving SGLT2 inhibitors for HFrEF only — current guidance extends the Class I recommendation across HFmrEF and HFpEF too.
  • Giving oral iron for iron deficiency in HF — absorption is unreliable in this setting; IV iron is the guideline-supported route.
Week 8Arrhythmias Deep Dive I — Bradyarrhythmias & SVTs
+
📚 Guide (full depth)🗂️ Spaced flashcards❓ Topic-locked MCQs🩺 Case sim #2
AV Block Types & Pacemaker Indications+
BlockPatternLevelPacemaker?
1st degreeProlonged PR, every beat conductsUsually AV nodalGenerally not needed
2nd degree Mobitz IProgressively lengthening PR, then a dropped beatAV nodal, vagally responsiveOnly if symptomatic
2nd degree Mobitz IIConstant PR, sudden dropped beat, no warningInfranodal/His-PurkinjeGenerally indicated, even if asymptomatic
3rd degree/completeNo relationship between P waves and QRSAny levelIndicated (unless a clearly reversible cause)
Mobitz II carries a higher risk of sudden progression to complete block — that's why it gets a pacemaker even without symptoms, unlike Mobitz I.
Atrial Fibrillation — Scoring, Rate/Rhythm, Anticoagulation+

CHA₂DS₂-VASc (the version most textbooks and question banks still use): CHF (1), HTN (1), Age≥75 (2), Diabetes (1), prior Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), Sex category female (1). A score of ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women generally warrants anticoagulation.

Rate control: a lenient target (<110bpm) is acceptable in asymptomatic patients with preserved EF; stricter control is used if symptomatic or EF is reduced.

Anticoagulation: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for most patients — the exception is valvular AFib (mechanical valve, or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis), where warfarin remains standard.

🆕 Recent update — 2024 ESC/EACTS AFib guideline (a full update, not just a focused one):
  • The score is now written CHA₂DS₂-VA — the sex category point has been removed entirely, so scoring and thresholds shift slightly from the version above. Know both forms; a question may use either.
  • Catheter ablation is now first-line therapy (Class I) for suitable patients with paroxysmal AF — not just a fallback after antiarrhythmic drugs fail. This is a real reversal from older teaching.
  • Early rhythm control (started within 12 months of diagnosis) is Class IIa for selected patients at thromboembolic risk or with CKD/LVH, to reduce cardiovascular death and hospitalization.
  • The safety window for cardioversion without prior anticoagulation/TEE screening was shortened from 48 hours to 24 hours from AF onset.
  • Rhythm control strategy does not change the anticoagulation decision — that still runs off the thromboembolic risk score regardless of whether the patient is in sinus rhythm.
🆕 Also new — 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS (US) guideline: AFib is now staged as a progressive disease: At risk → Pre-AF → AF (3A paroxysmal / 3B persistent / 3C long-standing persistent / 3D post-ablation) → Permanent. This replaces the old idea of paroxysmal/persistent/permanent as independent buckets.
AVNRT vs AVRT, and the WPW Danger in AFib+

AVNRT — reentry within the AV node itself, using dual (fast/slow) nodal pathways. The most common regular narrow-complex SVT; P waves are often buried in the QRS or appear as a pseudo-R' in V1.

AVRT — reentry uses an accessory pathway plus the AV node. Orthodromic AVRT conducts antegrade through the AV node (narrow QRS). Antidromic AVRT conducts antegrade through the accessory pathway (wide QRS) — and can be mistaken for VT.

The WPW + AFib trap: if AFib occurs in a patient with an accessory pathway, AV-nodal-blocking drugs (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers) block the normal pathway — forcing all conduction down the accessory pathway, which can conduct extremely fast and degenerate into VF. Treat AFib+WPW with procainamide, ibutilide, or DC cardioversion if unstable — never an AV nodal blocker.

Recognizing pre-excited AF on the ECG: an irregularly irregular, wide-complex, very rapid tachycardia with beat-to-beat QRS morphology variation. The irregularity distinguishes it from monomorphic VT; the width and rate distinguish it from ordinary AF with aberrancy. Rates can exceed 250 bpm, and the shortest pre-excited RR interval is the marker of pathway refractoriness — shorter means higher VF risk.

References
  • 2024 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation, Eur Heart J 2024 — CHA₂DS₂-VA, first-line ablation, 24h cardioversion window.
  • 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation, Circulation 2024;149:e1-e156 — the AF staging framework.
  • 2019 ESC Guidelines for the management of supraventricular tachycardia — AVNRT/AVRT and pre-excitation management.
  • 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy — AV block pacemaker indications.
  • EAST-AFNET 4 (NEJM 2020) — early rhythm control; CABANA and EARLY-AF — ablation evidence.
Common mistakes
  • Giving AV nodal blockers (verapamil, adenosine, beta-blockers) in AFib with WPW — can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway and precipitate VF.
  • Anchoring anticoagulation decisions on AFib duration instead of CHA₂DS₂-VASc score.
  • Applying one universal rate-control target regardless of symptoms or LV function.
  • Treating all 2nd-degree AV block the same for pacemaker decisions — Mobitz II generally needs one even without symptoms, unlike Mobitz I.
  • Missing that antidromic AVRT (wide QRS) can look like VT — the mechanism, not just QRS width, is what distinguishes them.
  • Defaulting to warfarin for AFib anticoagulation — DOACs are now preferred except in valvular AFib.
  • Treating catheter ablation as a last resort after drugs fail — for suitable paroxysmal AF patients, it's now a first-line Class I option.
  • Assuming restoring sinus rhythm removes the need for anticoagulation — the anticoagulation decision runs independently off thromboembolic risk score, not rhythm status.
Week 9Arrhythmias Deep Dive II — Ventricular Arrhythmias & ECG Mastery
+
📚 Guide (full depth)🗂️ Spaced flashcards❓ Topic-locked MCQs🩺 Case sim #3
VT vs SVT with Aberrancy+

For any wide-complex tachycardia: assume VT until proven otherwise, especially if the patient is unstable or has known structural heart disease/prior MI. Features favoring VT: AV dissociation, fusion beats, capture beats, extreme axis deviation, QRS >160ms, and precordial concordance (all leads positive or all negative).

The Brugada criteria are a stepwise algorithm (absence of an RS complex in the precordial leads, R-to-S interval, AV dissociation, specific V1/V6 morphology) used to formally differentiate VT from SVT with aberrancy — but under time pressure, hemodynamic instability alone should push you toward treating it as VT.

🆕 Recent update: the 2022 ESC VA/SCD guideline expands catheter ablation earlier into the pathway — it's increasingly used in select patients (no structural heart disease, or only mild EF reduction, with hemodynamically tolerated VT) rather than being reserved strictly for drug-refractory cases. ICD risk stratification is also explicitly moving beyond LVEF alone, incorporating newer risk markers (e.g. late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI, genetic risk calculators for laminopathies and long QT syndrome) alongside the established HCM risk calculator.
Long QT & Torsades de Pointes+

Congenital long QT (Romano-Ward, Jervell-Lange-Nielsen) vs acquired (class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolide/fluoroquinolone antibiotics, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia).

Torsades de Pointes is polymorphic VT with the QRS axis appearing to twist around the baseline — classically triggered by a PVC landing on a prolonged T wave ("R on T") in the setting of a long QT.

Management: IV magnesium first-line regardless of measured magnesium level, correct electrolytes, stop the offending drug. Torsades is often pause-dependent — a preceding bradycardia/pause sets up the triggering PVC — so overdrive pacing or isoproterenol can help in that specific pattern. Defibrillate if it degenerates to VF/pulseless.
Advanced ECG Patterns — Brugada, Wellens', de Winter+
PatternECG findingSignificance
Brugada patternCoved ST elevation V1-V3 with T inversion (Type 1)Sodium channelopathy (SCN5A); risk of sudden death from polymorphic VT/VF
Wellens' syndromeBiphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2-V3, patient often pain-freeCritical proximal LAD stenosis — high risk for anterior MI if not intervened
de Winter patternUpsloping ST depression + tall symmetric T waves in precordial leadsSTEMI-equivalent — acute proximal LAD occlusion

When the pattern isn't spontaneously present but Brugada is suspected (family history of Brugada/sudden arrhythmic death syndrome, or a resuscitated cardiac arrest without structural heart disease), current guidance supports provocative drug testing with ajmaline or flecainide to unmask a Type 1 pattern.

References
  • 2022 ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126.
  • 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for Management of Patients With Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death.
  • Brugada P & Brugada J, JACC 1991 (the syndrome); Brugada P et al., Circulation 1991 (the VT differentiation algorithm) — note these are two different contributions sharing a name.
  • de Zwaan C et al., Am Heart J 1982 (Wellens'); de Winter RJ et al., NEJM 2008 (de Winter pattern).
  • Hurst's The Heart — Ventricular Arrhythmias and Sudden Cardiac Death.
Cardiac Arrest, Post-ROSC Care & VT Storm+

Peri-arrest management sits here because it is where the Week 9 arrhythmia knowledge is actually applied under time pressure — and it is examined both as MCQ and as an oral scenario.

The branch point that governs everything

In any tachyarrhythmia, the first question is haemodynamic stability, not rhythm diagnosis. Unstable — hypotension, altered consciousness, ischaemic chest pain, or acute heart failure — means synchronised DC cardioversion, regardless of whether you have settled the VT-versus-SVT question. Stable buys you time for a 12-lead and a drug decision.

RhythmShockable?Key drug
VF / pulseless VTYes — defibrillate immediatelyAdrenaline after the 3rd shock; amiodarone after the 3rd shock
PEA / asystoleNoAdrenaline as soon as possible, then every 3-5 min

Reversible causes — the 4 Hs and 4 Ts: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary). In a cardiology context, tamponade, coronary thrombosis and hyperkalaemia are the ones most often actionable.

CPR quality is the intervention that most changes survival

Depth 5-6 cm, rate 100-120/min, full recoil, minimise interruptions (aim for chest compression fraction above 80%), change compressor every 2 minutes, and avoid over-ventilation — which raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return.

Post-ROSC — the golden hour
  • Avoid hyperoxia and hypoxia — titrate to a normal oxygen saturation target rather than giving maximal FiO₂.
  • Avoid hypocapnia — over-ventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction.
  • Maintain adequate perfusion pressure — treat hypotension, which worsens brain injury.
  • Targeted temperature management and active avoidance of fever.
  • Treat the cause — 12-lead ECG immediately. ST elevation after arrest mandates immediate angiography. Without ST elevation, in a haemodynamically stable patient, routine immediate angiography has not shown benefit (COACT, TOMAHAWK) and can be deferred — a genuine change from older reflexive practice.
  • Defer neuroprognostication — multimodal, and not before 72 hours off sedation.
VT storm

Defined as three or more separate episodes of sustained VT, VF or appropriate ICD therapies within 24 hours. Management runs on four parallel tracks:

  • Suppress the trigger — correct electrolytes, treat ischaemia, review proarrhythmic drugs.
  • Reduce sympathetic drive — this is the counterintuitive one: beta-blockade (often IV) is central, and sedation helps. Refractory cases may need stellate ganglion blockade or cardiac sympathetic denervation.
  • Antiarrhythmic therapy — amiodarone is usual; lidocaine has a role particularly in ischaemic VT.
  • Catheter ablation — increasingly used early rather than as a last resort, and mechanical support may be needed to tolerate mapping.
Reprogram the ICD, don't just accept the shocks. Repeated shocks in VT storm increase sympathetic drive and perpetuate the arrhythmia — a self-sustaining loop. Anti-tachycardia pacing and adjusted detection thresholds can break it, and sedation is therapeutic rather than merely humane.
References
  • 2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death — VT storm and post-arrest care.
  • European Resuscitation Council / AHA Advanced Life Support guidelines.
  • COACT (NEJM 2019) and TOMAHAWK (NEJM 2021) — timing of angiography after arrest without ST elevation.
Antiarrhythmic Selection — Matching Drug to Substrate+

The single question that governs antiarrhythmic choice is: is there structural heart disease? Get that right and most selection questions answer themselves.

SubstrateAcceptableAvoid
Structurally normal heartFlecainide, propafenone ("pill in pocket"), sotalol, dronedarone—
Coronary disease / prior MIAmiodarone, sotalol (with QT/renal caution)Class Ic (flecainide, propafenone) — CAST excess mortality
HFrEFAmiodaroneClass Ic; dronedarone (increased mortality in decompensated HF); sotalol; verapamil/diltiazem
Pre-excited AF (WPW)Procainamide, ibutilide, DC cardioversionAll AV nodal blockers — adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin
Derive, don't memorise: Class Ic slows phase 0 conduction, which is proarrhythmic across scarred myocardium — hence the structural-disease contraindication. Class III blocks phase 3 repolarisation, which is the QT interval — hence Torsades risk, and hence why sotalol becomes dangerous as renal function declines and the drug accumulates.
Agent-specific limits worth knowing
  • Amiodarone — the safest antiarrhythmic in structural disease, but multi-organ toxicity (thyroid, lung, liver, cornea, skin) demands baseline and periodic monitoring. It also raises digoxin and warfarin levels and inhibits CYP3A4, capping simvastatin dose.
  • Sotalol — renally cleared; accumulation prolongs QT. Check renal function and QTc before and during therapy.
  • Dronedarone — contraindicated in permanent AF and in decompensated heart failure (ANDROMEDA, PALLAS showed harm).
  • Adenosine — half-life of seconds; avoid in severe asthma; ineffective and hazardous in pre-excited AF.
  • Digoxin — narrow therapeutic index, potentiated by hypokalaemia, and levels raised by amiodarone, verapamil and quinidine.
In Torsades, avoid amiodarone. It is a Class III agent and prolongs the QT further. Give IV magnesium regardless of level, correct potassium, stop offending drugs, and if the arrhythmia is pause-dependent, increase the rate with overdrive pacing or isoprenaline.
References
  • 2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death.
  • CAST (Class Ic in structural disease); PALLAS and ANDROMEDA (dronedarone harm).
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Antiarrhythmic Drugs; Vaughan Williams framework.
Common mistakes
  • Calling an unstable wide-complex tachycardia "probably SVT with aberrancy" — assume VT until proven otherwise when the patient is unstable.
  • Skipping the medication list before invasive workup — drug-induced QT prolongation is a reversible cause that's easy to miss.
  • Confusing the Brugada ECG pattern (a diagnosis) with Brugada criteria (a method for diagnosing VT) — same name, unrelated concepts.
  • Missing that Torsades is often pause-dependent — a preceding bradycardia sets up the triggering PVC landing on the vulnerable T wave.
  • Treating Wellens' syndrome as reassuring because the patient is pain-free — it signals critical proximal LAD stenosis and impending anterior MI.
  • Not recognizing de Winter pattern as a STEMI-equivalent — the absence of frank ST elevation doesn't mean it's safe to defer catheterization.
  • Reserving catheter ablation strictly for drug-refractory VT — for select patients without significant structural disease, it's now considered earlier in the pathway.
  • Basing every primary-prevention ICD decision on LVEF alone — newer risk markers (imaging, genetic calculators) increasingly factor into the decision alongside EF.
Week 10Hypertension & Guidelines Deep Dive
+
📚 Guide (full depth)❓ Topic-locked MCQs📋 Guidelines module🩺 Case sim #4
Resistant HTN & Secondary Workup+
🆕 Major recent update — ESC 2024 Hypertension Guideline (a new, standalone guideline, distinct from the 2023 ESH update): the old 7-category BP classification is gone. It's now 3 categories: Non-elevated, Elevated BP (120-139/70-89 mmHg — a brand-new category), and Hypertension (still ≥140/90 mmHg — the diagnostic threshold itself didn't move). What did move is the treatment target: most patients are now treated to a first-instance SBP goal of 120-129 mmHg, replacing the older two-step approach of treating to <140/90 first and only later considering <130/80. Renal denervation is newly included as a treatment option for resistant/uncontrolled hypertension in both the ESC 2024 and ESH 2023 documents.
🆕 And a second one — the 2025 ACC/AHA multisociety High Blood Pressure Guideline (August 2025) replaced the 2017 document. If your source material cites "2017 ACC/AHA," it is now a guideline cycle behind. Key changes:
  • The PREVENT risk calculator replaces the older pooled cohort equations. It integrates cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic health into a single 10-year risk estimate, and now drives the decision to start drug therapy.
  • Risk-based initiation thresholds: in adults without clinical cardiovascular disease but with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or an estimated 10-year risk of ≥7.5%, antihypertensive drug therapy is recommended at an average BP of ≥130/80 mmHg.
  • New content on the link between elevated BP and cognitive decline and dementia.
  • New pregnancy recommendations, including treating chronic hypertension in pregnancy at ≥140/90 mmHg.
The exam-relevant contrast: ESC 2024 restructured the classification (3 categories) and set an aggressive first-instance SBP target of 120-129. ACC/AHA 2025 kept its diagnostic thresholds broadly stable but rebuilt the risk model driving who gets treated. Two different routes to more intensive treatment — know which one a question is testing.

Resistant HTN: BP above goal despite 3 optimally-dosed agents (including a diuretic), or controlled BP requiring ≥4 drugs. First step is always confirming it's true resistance — rule out white-coat effect with home/ambulatory monitoring, check adherence, and screen for interfering substances (NSAIDs, decongestants, oral contraceptives, licorice).

Secondary causes and their clues
  • Primary aldosteronism — hypokalemia + resistant HTN; screen with aldosterone-renin ratio.
  • Renal artery stenosis — young patient (fibromuscular dysplasia) or older with atherosclerosis, flash pulmonary edema, renal bruit.
  • Pheochromocytoma — paroxysmal headache, palpitations, diaphoresis.
  • OSA — obesity, suggestive symptoms; screen with a sleep study.
Hypertensive Emergency — Organ-Specific Targets+

The BP target and the drug sequence both change depending on which organ is at risk — using one universal approach is the single most common trap here.

ScenarioApproach
Aortic dissectionMost aggressive target: SBP 100-120 within 20 min, HR<60. Beta-blocker first (esmolol/labetalol) before any vasodilator — vasodilating without rate control first causes reflex tachycardia that increases aortic wall shear stress.
Ischemic strokePermissive hypertension — generally treat only if >220/120 (not a thrombolysis candidate) or >185/110 (thrombolysis candidate). Aggressive lowering can worsen penumbral perfusion.
Hemorrhagic strokeMore aggressive than ischemic stroke, but still moderate — roughly SBP ~140 per major trial evidence.
Acute pulmonary edemaNitrates + diuretics, reduce afterload.
Pheochromocytoma crisisAlpha-blockade before beta-blockade — giving a beta-blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening the crisis.
Target Organ Damage & the Resistant HTN Drug Sequence+

Hypertension is not treated to a number for its own sake — it is treated to prevent end-organ injury. Documenting that injury reclassifies risk and often changes drug choice, so the assessment is not optional.

OrganWhat to look forWhy it changes management
HeartLVH on ECG (Sokolow-Lyon, Cornell) or echo; diastolic dysfunction; left atrial enlargementLVH is an independent risk marker and regresses with treatment — RAAS blockade is preferred
KidneyeGFR, and albuminuria (ACR) — the earliest and most sensitive markerProteinuria makes ACEi/ARB effectively mandatory
BrainPrior stroke/TIA, cognitive impairment, white matter changeAlters BP targets and lowering speed in the acute phase
EyeHypertensive retinopathy — haemorrhages, exudates or papilloedema define an emergencyFundoscopy is a bedside test that can convert "urgency" to "emergency"
VesselsABI, carotid plaque, pulse wave velocityPolyvascular disease roughly doubles event risk
Nocturnal dipping on ambulatory monitoring is worth knowing: BP normally falls 10-20% overnight. Non-dippers and reverse dippers carry higher cardiovascular risk, and a non-dipping pattern should prompt a search for obstructive sleep apnoea or chronic kidney disease.
The resistant hypertension sequence

Confirm true resistance first — ambulatory or home monitoring to exclude white coat effect, adherence check, and review of interfering substances (NSAIDs, decongestants, oral contraceptives, liquorice, steroids). Pseudo-resistance is more common than true resistance.

  • Foundation: ACEi or ARB + calcium channel blocker + thiazide-like diuretic, each at optimal dose.
  • Fourth-line agent: spironolactone. PATHWAY-2 showed it clearly superior to doxazosin or bisoprolol as the added fourth drug — consistent with sodium retention driving much true resistance. This is a named, testable trial answer.
  • Alternatives if spironolactone is not tolerated: amiloride, doxazosin, or a beta-blocker.
  • Renal denervation is now included as an option for selected patients at experienced centres.
The "triple whammy" — ACEi or ARB + diuretic + NSAID. The NSAID blocks the prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation the kidney relies on when RAAS is blocked and volume is depleted. This combination is a leading cause of avoidable acute kidney injury, and it is a prescribing trap rather than a physiology curiosity.
Indonesian CV Epidemiology & Prevention Context+

Every other section of this roadmap draws on international guidelines. This one covers the local epidemiology and access constraints — which is exactly the ground an Indonesian interview panel is likely to test, and where reciting European data alone reads poorly.

Riskesdas 2018 — the national picture
Risk factorBurdenThe exam-relevant point
Hypertension34.1% of adults ≥18y; only ~11.8% controlledThe gap is awareness and control, not diagnosis criteria — most are unaware
Dyslipidaemia28.0% with total cholesterol >200 mg/dLMinority on treatment
Diabetes10.9% (up from 5.7% in 2007); ~70% undiagnosedNear-doubling in 11 years; Indonesia is among the top 10 countries globally
SmokingVery high male prevalence, early initiationDominated by kreteks — see below

The underlying story is an epidemiological transition: declining infectious disease burden alongside steeply rising non-communicable disease. Being able to state that framing, rather than just quoting numbers, is what makes the answer sound like a clinician's rather than a statistic recital.

Access constraints that change what "guideline-directed" means locally

Guidelines assume drug availability. In practice, at Faskes Tingkat I under BPJS, simvastatin 10-40 mg and atorvastatin 10-40 mg (FORNAS) are widely available, while high-potency statins such as rosuvastatin, and non-statin agents such as ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors, are rarely accessible at primary care level.

How to use this in an oral: when asked how you would reach an LDL-C below 55 mg/dL, the strongest answer names the target, then acknowledges the access reality and how you would work within it — maximise available statin potency, ensure adherence, escalate through referral pathways where indicated. That demonstrates you can practise guideline-informed medicine in the system you actually work in, which is a more mature answer than reciting the target alone.
Kreteks — why Indonesian smoking cessation is a distinct problem
  • Kreteks (clove cigarettes, roughly 60-70% tobacco with 30-40% ground clove) account for the large majority of Indonesian cigarette sales.
  • Eugenol from cloves acts as a topical anaesthetic, reducing throat irritation and thereby facilitating deeper and more frequent inhalation — so toxin deposition per cigarette is higher, and biomarker levels exceed those of conventional cigarettes.
  • Clove pyrolysis adds reactive aldehydes and phenols to the exposure.
  • Initiation is often before age 16, so nicotine dependence is established early and cultural identity around smoking is strong — cessation messaging has to address that, not just deliver risk information.
Brief cessation intervention — the 5 A's

Ask about tobacco use at every visit → Advise to quit, clearly and personally → Assess willingness to attempt → Assist with pharmacotherapy and support → Arrange follow-up. Pair this with the stages-of-change model (precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance): matching your intervention to the patient's stage is what makes it effective, and saying so signals you understand behaviour change rather than just instructing.

Worth quoting: smoking cessation delivers the largest relative risk reduction of any single secondary prevention measure after myocardial infarction — larger than most drugs — and benefit begins within weeks. That framing is more persuasive to a patient, and to an examiner, than a list of harms.
References
  • Riskesdas 2018 (Riset Kesehatan Dasar) — national health survey data.
  • FORNAS / BPJS formulary — for current availability at each Faskes tier; verify locally, as formularies are revised.
  • 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease prevention in clinical practice; PERKI prevention consensus.
  • Prochaska & DiClemente stages of change; the 5 A's brief intervention framework.
PERKI HTN Specifics vs International Guidelines+

HTN classification and first-line drug logic track closely between PERKI, ESC/ESH, and ACC/AHA, but exact numeric thresholds per stage and first-line/combination-therapy defaults can differ, partly reflecting regional drug availability and population risk data. Even the European societies aren't fully aligned right now — ESH 2023 kept the older 7-category system and a two-step target, while ESC 2024 moved to the 3-category system with the more aggressive 120-129 first-instance target described above.

Treat the shared conceptual core here as reliable, but don't assume PERKI has already adopted the ESC 2024 numeric targets — cross-check your Guidelines module for PERKI's exact current thresholds before exam day, since this is exactly the kind of specific number that shifts between guideline cycles and adoption isn't necessarily simultaneous.
References
  • 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension, Eur Heart J 2024 — the 3-category classification and 120-129 SBP target.
  • 2023 ESH Guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension, J Hypertens 2023 — note this retains the older classification, so ESC and ESH currently differ.
  • 2017 ACC/AHA Hypertension Guideline, Hypertension 2018;71:e13-e115.
  • AHA 2024 Scientific Statement on acute BP management in hospitalized patients — already processed in your Guidelines module.
  • SPRINT (NEJM 2015) — the intensive BP-lowering evidence underpinning lower targets; INTERACT3/ATACH-2 for hemorrhagic stroke BP targets.
  • PERKI hypertension consensus — the Indonesian reference.
Common mistakes
  • Using one BP-lowering speed for every hypertensive emergency — aortic dissection needs rapid lowering plus heart-rate control first; ischemic stroke tolerates permissive hypertension.
  • Missing pheochromocytoma when symptoms are paroxysmal rather than constant.
  • Screening every hypertensive patient for secondary causes instead of targeting young-onset, resistant, or suddenly-worsening cases.
  • Giving a vasodilator before rate control in aortic dissection — reflex tachycardia from vasodilation alone can propagate the dissection.
  • Aggressively lowering BP in acute ischemic stroke outside the specific thresholds — permissive hypertension protects penumbral perfusion in most cases.
  • Starting a beta-blocker before alpha-blockade in suspected pheochromocytoma crisis — unopposed alpha-vasoconstriction can precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis.
  • Citing the old 7-category BP classification or a passive <140/90-then-<130/80 treatment approach as current — the 2024 ESC guideline replaced both with a 3-category system and a first-instance 120-129 SBP target for most patients.

Weeks 11-14 · The topics Phases 1-2 left thin, plus retrieval-practice on everything. MCQs go mixed/random from here on — oral practice starts.

Cross-checked against current releases: ESC/EACTS 2025 Valvular Heart Disease, ESC 2023 Cardiomyopathies (the first-ever comprehensive CMP guideline), ESC 2025 Myocarditis & Pericarditis, ESC 2023 Infective Endocarditis, ESC 2025 Cardiovascular Disease and Pregnancy, ESC 2024 Peripheral Arterial & Aortic Diseases, and ESC/ERS 2022 Pulmonary Hypertension. This phase carries the heaviest concentration of recent changes in the whole roadmap — several of these guidelines are brand new or were fully rewritten, so older textbooks are most likely to be stale here. Changes flagged inline as 🆕 Recent update.
Week 11Valvular Heart Disease Deep Dive
+
📚 Guide (full depth)❓ Mixed MCQs🩺 Case sim #5🎙️ Oral practice begins
Aortic Stenosis — Grading & Intervention Timing+
Severity grading
ParameterSevere AS
Aortic valve area<1.0 cm² (or <0.6 cm²/m² indexed)
Mean gradient≥40 mmHg
Peak velocity≥4.0 m/s
The low-flow, low-gradient trap

A patient can have severe AS by valve area but a mean gradient under 40 — because gradient depends on flow. Two flavors:

  • Classical LF-LG — reduced EF (<50%), low stroke volume index (<35 mL/m²). Use dobutamine stress echo to distinguish true severe AS (gradient rises with augmented flow, valve area stays small) from pseudo-severe AS (valve area increases with flow — the valve was never truly that tight).
  • Paradoxical LF-LG — preserved EF but low stroke volume from a small, stiff, hypertrophied LV. Easy to under-call as "moderate." Calcium scoring on CT helps confirm.
🆕 Major recent update — 2025 ESC/EACTS VHD guideline: two changes here matter a lot.
  • The watchful-waiting era is ending. Intervention now extends to asymptomatic patients with severe high-gradient AS and preserved LVEF, provided procedural risk is low — a real departure from the old "wait for symptoms or EF drop" teaching.
  • The TAVI age cut-off dropped from 75 to 70. TAVI is now recommended for anatomically suitable patients ≥70 years with a tricuspid valve; SAVR remains standard in those <70 at low surgical risk. Non-transfemoral TAVI was upgraded for patients unsuitable for both surgery and transfemoral access.
Decision-making is framed as a Heart Team judgment combining age, procedural risk, anatomical suitability, life expectancy, and lifetime management — not a single risk score.
🆕 Three further 2025 VHD changes worth knowing (28 new recommendations in total):
  • TAVI may now be considered for severe AORTIC REGURGITATION in symptomatic patients judged ineligible for surgery by the Heart Team. This is new territory — TAVI was historically an aortic stenosis therapy, and AR was considered unsuitable because there is often no calcium to anchor the valve.
  • Explicit sex-specific considerations. The guideline flags that women are referred less often and later, and that flow-limitation cut-offs differ by sex — a recognised source of undertreatment. The RHEIA trial supported TAVI over surgery in women.
  • Reducing undertreatment is a stated theme, alongside directing complex patients to experienced centres.
Mitral Disease — Primary vs Secondary MR, Rheumatic MS+

Primary (degenerative) MR — the valve apparatus itself is diseased (prolapse, flail leaflet, chordal rupture, rheumatic). Treatment is mechanical: repair is preferred over replacement when feasible.

Secondary (functional) MR — the valve leaflets are structurally normal; the problem is ventricular or atrial geometry pulling them apart. Treatment starts with optimizing GDMT for the underlying HF, since fixing the ventricle can improve the regurgitation.

Rheumatic mitral stenosis — still highly relevant in Indonesia and other high-RHD-burden settings, so expect it to be tested more heavily than Western board material might suggest. Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy is the intervention of choice when valve morphology is favorable (assessed by Wilkins score) and there's no significant MR or left atrial thrombus.

🆕 Recent update: the 2025 guideline draws a sharper line between atrial and ventricular secondary MR — they carry different prognosis and different management, so "secondary MR" is no longer one bucket. Criteria for intervening in asymptomatic primary MR were refined, and transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) has large-scale data confirming its role in high-surgical-risk patients.
Rheumatic Heart Disease — The Local Priority+

Western board material under-weights this. In Indonesia and comparable settings it is a leading cause of valve disease in young adults, and an exam panel is entitled to expect real depth.

The natural history in one line

Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → acute rheumatic fever (molecular mimicry, antibodies cross-reacting with cardiac tissue) → recurrent episodes causing cumulative valve damage → chronic rheumatic heart disease presenting decades later.

Pattern of valve involvement

Mitral is affected most often (roughly two-thirds involve mitral alone), then aortic; tricuspid less commonly and usually alongside left-sided disease; pulmonary rarely. Acute carditis causes regurgitation from leaflet inflammation and annular dilation; chronic disease causes commissural fusion and stenosis. That is why a teenager presents with MR and the same patient presents with MS in their thirties.

The most important intervention is not surgical. Secondary prophylaxis with long-acting benzathine penicillin every 3-4 weeks prevents recurrence, and recurrence is what drives cumulative damage. Duration is severity-stratified — longest with established carditis and residual valve disease. A candidate who leads with prophylaxis rather than valve intervention is thinking about the disease correctly.
Echocardiographic screening for subclinical disease

The World Heart Federation criteria define definite and borderline RHD on echo in individuals without a history of acute rheumatic fever, enabling population screening in endemic regions. This matters because subclinical disease detected early can be brought into a prophylaxis programme before valve damage becomes irreversible.

Practical barriers worth naming in a viva
  • Painful intramuscular injections every few weeks over years — adherence is the central challenge, not drug efficacy.
  • Penicillin supply continuity and cold chain.
  • Late presentation, since early disease is asymptomatic.
  • Access to surgery and to anticoagulation monitoring after mechanical valve replacement — which is a genuine argument for balloon commissurotomy or bioprosthesis in selected patients where INR monitoring is unreliable.
Acute Valve Emergencies — Where Chronic Rules Invert+

Acute severe regurgitation behaves nothing like its chronic counterpart, because the receiving chamber has had no time to dilate and become compliant. The same lesion is a slow outpatient problem when chronic and a surgical emergency when acute.

Chronic severe AR / MRAcute severe AR / MR
ChamberDilated, compliant — accommodates volumeNormal size, non-compliant — pressure spikes
Pulse pressure (AR)Wide, collapsing pulseNarrow — the classic signs are ABSENT
MurmurLoud, longSoft and short — pressures equalise rapidly
PresentationYears of compensationFlash pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock
ManagementElective, criteria-drivenEmergency surgery
The trap is that acute severe lesions have QUIETER signs than chronic ones. A soft murmur and a narrow pulse pressure in a crashing patient argue for acute severe regurgitation, not against it. Candidates who grade severity by murmur loudness get this exactly backwards.
Causes and specific management
  • Acute AR — aortic dissection (Case 3), infective endocarditis, trauma. Consider dissection first, since it changes everything. Avoid intra-aortic balloon pump — diastolic augmentation worsens the regurgitation. Beta-blockade must be used cautiously: these patients depend on tachycardia to shorten diastole and limit regurgitant time.
  • Acute MR — papillary muscle rupture post-MI (Case 1), chordal rupture in myxomatous disease, endocarditis. Afterload reduction and mechanical support bridge to urgent surgery.
Two quantitative tools worth naming
  • Gorlin formula — derives valve area from flow and gradient. Its practical importance is that it makes the flow-dependence of gradient explicit, which is the whole basis of the low-flow low-gradient AS problem.
  • Carpentier classification of mitral regurgitation mechanism: Type I normal leaflet motion (annular dilation, perforation), Type II excessive motion (prolapse, flail — typically primary MR), Type IIIa restricted in systole and diastole (rheumatic), Type IIIb restricted in systole (ischaemic/functional). It matters because it predicts repairability — Type II is the most repairable.
Prosthetic Valves & Anticoagulation+
Valve typeAnticoagulationDurability
MechanicalLifelong warfarin — DOACs are contraindicatedVery durable; the tradeoff is lifelong anticoagulation
BioprostheticShort-term only in most cases; long-term antiplateletStructural degeneration over ~10-15 years

INR target runs higher for mitral than aortic mechanical valves (mitral position is more thrombogenic — lower flow velocity, larger surface area). Roughly 2.5-3.5 for mitral vs 2.0-3.0 for a modern bileaflet aortic valve, adjusted upward for additional risk factors.

Absolute rule: DOACs must never be used for mechanical prosthetic valves — the RE-ALIGN trial was stopped early for excess thromboembolism and bleeding with dabigatran. This is a favorite exam question.
Two extras that show up in harder vignettes
  • Heyde syndrome — the triad of severe AS, acquired von Willebrand syndrome (high shear across the stenotic valve cleaves large vWF multimers), and GI bleeding from angiodysplasia. The reason it matters: valve replacement often resolves the bleeding, so an elderly patient with AS and recurrent unexplained GI bleeding is a valve problem, not just a GI one.
  • Prosthetic valve thrombosis vs pannus — both cause obstruction and raised gradients. Thrombosis is usually more acute, associated with subtherapeutic anticoagulation, and may respond to fibrinolysis or need surgery; pannus is chronic fibrous ingrowth requiring surgery. CT and fluoroscopy help distinguish them.
AS natural history — the classic survival figures: once symptoms appear in severe AS, average survival without intervention is roughly 5 years after angina, 3 years after syncope, and 2 years after heart failure onset. These numbers are old but still quoted and still tested, and they explain why symptom onset historically triggered intervention — and why the 2025 shift toward earlier asymptomatic intervention is such a meaningful change.
References
  • 2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease, Eur Heart J 2025 — TAVI ≥70, asymptomatic severe AS intervention, atrial vs ventricular SMR.
  • 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease, Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227.
  • DEDICATE-DZHK6, PARTNER 3, Evolut Low Risk — the low-risk TAVI evidence behind the age-threshold change.
  • RE-ALIGN (NEJM 2013) — dabigatran in mechanical valves, stopped early for harm.
  • COAPT and MITRA-FR — the divergent secondary MR TEER trials; understanding why they differed (proportionate vs disproportionate MR) is a strong viva answer.
  • Ross J & Braunwald E, Circulation 1968 — the original AS natural history data.
Common mistakes
  • Grading AS severity by gradient alone — low-flow low-gradient severe AS gets missed without accounting for flow state.
  • Waiting for symptoms in severe AS with EF under 50% — intervention is indicated even asymptomatic in that scenario.
  • Using the same INR target for mitral and aortic mechanical valves — mitral position needs a higher target.
  • Still quoting 75 as the TAVI age threshold — the 2025 guideline lowered it to 70, and older question banks will have the stale number.
  • Applying "watchful waiting" to every asymptomatic severe AS patient — current guidance supports early intervention when procedural risk is low.
  • Prescribing a DOAC for a mechanical valve — this is contraindicated, not merely second-line.
  • Jumping straight to intervention for secondary MR before optimizing GDMT — the ventricle is the primary problem in ventricular SMR.
Week 12Cardiomyopathies & Pericardial Disease
+
📚 Guide (full depth)❓ Mixed MCQs🩺 Case sim #6🎙️ Oral practice
The New Cardiomyopathy Classification+
🆕 Major recent update — 2023 ESC Cardiomyopathies guideline: this is the first comprehensive international guideline covering all cardiomyopathies (previously only HCM had its own). Most of its 158 recommendations are new, and it introduced a phenotype-first classification with five categories:
  • Hypertrophic (HCM)
  • Dilated (DCM)
  • Non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC) — a brand-new category that won't appear in older textbooks at all
  • Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC)
  • Restrictive
Critically, the guideline stresses these phenotypes are not diagnoses in themselves — they're the first step toward an etiological diagnosis, which is frequently genetic. Cardiac MRI and genetic testing are now central to the diagnostic pathway rather than optional add-ons.
HCM — Obstruction & Sudden Death Risk+

The obstruction physiology: LVOT obstruction worsens with anything that reduces preload or afterload, or increases contractility. This is why the HOCM murmur behaves backwards from most others — louder with Valsalva and standing (↓preload), softer with squatting and handgrip (↑preload/afterload).

Management logic follows directly: beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine CCBs (negative inotropes, longer filling time) help. Aggressive diuresis, vasodilators, and inotropes worsen obstruction and can precipitate collapse. Septal reduction therapy (myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) is for refractory symptomatic obstruction.

SCD risk stratification: validated risk calculators (HCM Risk-SCD for adults, HCM Risk-Kids for children) are now the recommended first step in deciding on a primary-prevention ICD — not a gestalt judgment or a simple risk-factor tally.

🆕 Recent update: mavacamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor, should be considered for HCM patients with LVOT obstruction who remain symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy. This is an entirely new drug class targeting the underlying sarcomere hypercontractility — it won't be in older texts.
Restrictive Cardiomyopathy vs Constrictive Pericarditis+

Both present with right-heart failure, preserved EF, and elevated filling pressures — and exam writers love the differentiation because the treatments diverge completely (constriction is potentially curable by pericardiectomy; restriction is not).

FeatureConstrictive pericarditisRestrictive cardiomyopathy
ProblemRigid pericardium confining the heartStiff myocardium itself
Respiratory variation in mitral inflowMarked (enhanced ventricular interdependence)Minimal
Septal bouncePresentAbsent
Tissue Doppler e′Normal or increased ("annulus reversus")Reduced
Pericardium on CT/MRIOften thickened/calcifiedNormal
TreatmentPericardiectomyTreat the underlying infiltrative cause
Counterintuitive pearl: in constriction, tissue Doppler e′ is often preserved or high despite severe diastolic dysfunction — because the myocardium itself is healthy; only the pericardium is the problem. In restriction, the myocardium is diseased, so e′ falls. This single finding often cracks the case.

Always ask what's causing a restrictive picture — cardiac amyloidosis is the one not to miss, since transthyretin amyloidosis now has disease-modifying therapy available.

Cardiac amyloidosis — the red flags

Suspect it when LV wall thickening on echo is accompanied by findings that don't fit ordinary hypertensive LVH:

  • Discordance between wall thickness and ECG voltage — thick walls with low or normal QRS voltage (infiltration adds mass without adding functioning myocytes). This is the single most characteristic clue.
  • Apical sparing on strain echocardiography (the "cherry on top" bull's-eye pattern).
  • Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (often years earlier), spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture — extracardiac ATTR clues.
  • Intolerance of standard HF drugs — beta-blockers and ACEi are often poorly tolerated because these patients are preload-dependent with a fixed stroke volume.

Diagnostic pathway: exclude a monoclonal protein (serum/urine immunofixation and free light chains) to rule out AL amyloidosis, then bone scintigraphy (99mTc-DPD/PYP/HMDP) — strong cardiac uptake with a negative monoclonal screen can establish ATTR non-invasively, avoiding biopsy. Genetic testing then separates hereditary from wild-type ATTR. Tafamidis is the established disease-modifying therapy (ATTR-ACT).

Order matters: never interpret a positive bone scan as ATTR without first excluding a monoclonal gammopathy — AL amyloidosis can also show uptake, and AL is a haematological emergency with a completely different treatment pathway and far worse untreated prognosis.
References
  • 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503-3626 — the five-phenotype classification, NDLVC, HCM Risk-SCD.
  • 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis, Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952-4041 — replaces the 2015 pericarditis guideline; updated Lake Louise criteria.
  • 2024 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
  • EXPLORER-HCM and VALOR-HCM — the mavacamten trials.
  • ATTR-ACT (NEJM 2018) — tafamidis in transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. Gillmore JD et al., Circulation 2016 — the non-biopsy diagnostic algorithm.
  • ICAP and CORP/CORP-2 — the colchicine trials establishing its role in acute and recurrent pericarditis.
  • Braunwald's Heart Disease — Cardiomyopathies and Pericardial Disease chapters.
Pericarditis & Tamponade+

Acute pericarditis — diagnosis needs at least 2 of 4: pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, pericardial friction rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and new/worsening pericardial effusion. First-line treatment is NSAID/aspirin plus colchicine — colchicine substantially reduces recurrence and isn't optional. Corticosteroids are generally avoided early because they increase recurrence risk.

Cardiac tamponade — Beck's triad (hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP drop >10 mmHg from exaggerated ventricular interdependence in a fixed pericardial space), and electrical alternans. Management is pericardiocentesis; avoid aggressive diuresis or vasodilation, which drop the preload the compromised heart depends on.

🆕 Recent update — 2025 ESC Myocarditis & Pericarditis guideline: this fully replaces the 2015 pericarditis guideline and covers myocarditis for the first time, under a unified "inflammatory myocardial and pericardial syndromes" (IMPS) framework with presentation-driven diagnostic pathways. Practical points: CMR diagnosis uses the updated Lake Louise criteria; endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for high-risk myocarditis with hemodynamic instability or intermediate-risk cases not responding to therapy; and physical activity should be restricted to sedentary levels until symptoms resolve, clinical remission is achieved, and inflammatory markers normalize.
Common mistakes
  • Treating constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy as the same entity — similar presentation, but imaging and hemodynamics distinguish them, and management differs completely.
  • Not connecting pulsus paradoxus to tamponade physiology when it shows up in a vignette.
  • Using diuretics/inotropes aggressively in HOCM with outflow obstruction — this can worsen the obstruction.
  • Using only the old three-way dilated/hypertrophic/restrictive classification — the current framework has five phenotypes and includes NDLVC, which older textbooks don't mention.
  • Expecting reduced tissue Doppler e′ in constriction — it's typically normal or high there, which is exactly what separates it from restriction.
  • Omitting colchicine from first-line acute pericarditis therapy, or reaching for corticosteroids early — steroids raise recurrence risk.
  • Deciding on a primary-prevention ICD in HCM without running a validated risk calculator (HCM Risk-SCD) first.
Week 13Congenital Heart Disease & Special Populations
+
📚 Guide (full depth)❓ Mixed MCQs🎙️ Oral practice
Shunt Lesions — ASD, VSD, PDA+
LesionSignature findingClosure logic
ASDFixed split S2 (no respiratory variation); RV volume overloadClose for significant shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5) or RV enlargement, if PVR is still acceptable
VSDHarsh holosystolic murmur — smaller defects are often louder (more turbulence)Close for significant shunt, LV volume overload, or recurrent endocarditis
PDAContinuous "machinery" murmur, wide pulse pressureClose for significant shunt or LV volume overload
The hard stop: once Eisenmenger physiology has developed — pulmonary vascular resistance exceeding systemic, with shunt reversal and cyanosis — closing the defect is contraindicated. The shunt has become the RV's escape valve; closing it removes the pop-off and precipitates acute RV failure. This is a classic exam discriminator.
Coarctation & Tetralogy of Fallot+

Coarctation of the aorta — upper-limb hypertension with reduced/delayed femoral pulses (radio-femoral delay), rib notching on chest X-ray from collateral intercostal vessels. Strongly associated with bicuspid aortic valve and with Turner syndrome. It's a genuinely important secondary cause of hypertension in a young patient, so it links back to Week 10.

Tetralogy of Fallot — the four components: VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow tract obstruction, RV hypertrophy. Severity of cyanosis tracks the degree of RVOT obstruction, not the VSD size. "Tet spells" (hypercyanotic episodes) are managed by increasing systemic vascular resistance and preload — squatting or the knee-chest position does exactly this, which is why children instinctively adopt it.

Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy+

Normal physiology to know first: plasma volume and cardiac output rise ~40-50%, systemic vascular resistance falls, and heart rate increases. This is why stenotic lesions (especially mitral stenosis) decompensate in pregnancy — a fixed orifice can't accommodate the increased flow — while regurgitant lesions are often better tolerated, since falling afterload reduces the regurgitant fraction.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy — new systolic dysfunction in late pregnancy or the months following delivery, with no other identifiable cause. Genetic testing is now recommended for these patients.

Contraindicated drugs: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI, MRAs (fetotoxic), and warfarin (teratogenic, particularly in the first trimester, though it may still be used in specific mechanical-valve situations after careful risk discussion). Beta-blockers are generally acceptable, with labetalol and metoprolol preferred; atenolol is avoided for fetal growth restriction.

🆕 Recent update — 2025 ESC Cardiovascular Disease and Pregnancy guideline (replacing 2018):
  • Risk stratification now uses mWHO 2.0 — a refined, expanded version of the modified WHO classification incorporating CARPREG II evidence.
  • A formal Pregnancy Heart Team is now recommended for women classified mWHO 2.0 class II-III or higher, with a dedicated chapter on its structure.
  • A notable philosophical shift: the guideline moves away from simply advising high-risk women to avoid pregnancy, toward personalized multidisciplinary counselling and shared decision-making. If a question frames the answer as blanket "advise against pregnancy," that's now out of step with current guidance.
  • Genetic testing is recommended for women with aortic disease and for peripartum cardiomyopathy; pregnancy should be postponed at least 1 year after cardiac transplantation; fetal echo is offered routinely at 18-22 weeks when a parent has congenital heart disease.
Infective Endocarditis+

Modified Duke criteria logic: definite IE requires 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major = typical organisms in persistently positive blood cultures, plus imaging evidence of endocardial involvement. Minor = predisposing condition, fever, vascular phenomena (septic emboli, Janeway lesions), immunologic phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis), and supporting microbiological evidence not meeting major criteria.

Surgical indications — heart failure from valve destruction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteremia despite appropriate antibiotics), and prevention of embolism (large mobile vegetations, especially after an embolic event).

🆕 Recent update — 2023 ESC IE guideline & 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria: the diagnostic criteria were revised in two parallel efforts — the ESC's own 2023 version and the Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria. Both add sensitivity over the 2000 modified Duke criteria, largely by expanding the list of typical microorganisms (some counted as typical only when intracardiac prosthetic material is present) and incorporating advanced imaging such as 18F-FDG PET/CT and cardiac CT. Duke-ISCVID has generally preserved specificity better in validation studies. On prophylaxis, the 2023 ESC guideline simplified the regimen and reaffirmed the narrow scope: antibiotic prophylaxis is for high-risk patients undergoing oral-dental procedures only, with general hygiene measures (including oral hygiene) emphasized for intermediate- and high-risk patients. Prophylaxis before dental procedures is specifically not warranted to prevent cardiac device-related IE.

High-risk categories (the ones who do get prophylaxis): prosthetic valves or prosthetic material used for valve repair, previous infective endocarditis, and specified untreated/palliated congenital heart disease. Everything else, including most native valve disease, does not.

References for Week 13
  • 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease and pregnancy, Eur Heart J 2025;46:4462- — mWHO 2.0, Pregnancy Heart Team, shift away from blanket pregnancy avoidance.
  • 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948-4042.
  • Fowler VG et al., Clin Infect Dis 2023 — the Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria.
  • 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645.
  • CARPREG II (Silversides CK et al., JACC 2018) — the risk-prediction evidence feeding mWHO 2.0; ROPAC registry data.
  • Hurst's The Heart — Congenital Heart Disease in Adults; Pregnancy and Heart Disease.
