Complex Congenital Lesions & the Adult Survivor+

More adults now live with congenital heart disease than children, so the exam-relevant question is increasingly about the repaired adult rather than the neonatal diagnosis.

Shunt quantification

Qp:Qs is the ratio of pulmonary to systemic blood flow. Around 1.0 is normal; ≥1.5 indicates a haemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt and is the usual threshold for considering closure, provided pulmonary vascular resistance remains acceptable.

LesionCore anatomyThe adult problem
Tetralogy of Fallot (repaired)VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH — all from a single anterocephalad deviation of the outlet septumPulmonary regurgitation after RVOT repair → progressive RV dilation, exercise intolerance, VT and sudden death. Timing of pulmonary valve replacement is the key long-term decision
D-TGA after arterial switchVentriculo-arterial discordance; requires mixing to surviveCoronary ostial problems, neo-aortic root dilation and regurgitation, branch pulmonary stenosis
D-TGA after atrial switch (Mustard/Senning)Historical repair — blood redirected at atrial levelThe morphological RV remains the systemic ventricle → systemic ventricular failure, baffle obstruction or leak, atrial arrhythmias, sinus node dysfunction
ccTGA (L-TGA)Double discordance — "corrected" physiologicallyAgain the RV supports the systemic circulation; plus high rates of complete heart block
Fontan circulationSystemic venous return routed directly to the pulmonary arteries — no subpulmonary ventricleFlow is passive and dependent on venous pressure and low PVR. Complications: arrhythmia, thrombosis, protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, Fontan-associated liver disease
AVSDCommon AV junction; strong Down syndrome associationCharacteristic ECG: superior/left axis deviation — a pathognomonic pairing worth remembering
The Fontan patient is preload-dependent with no pump driving pulmonary flow. Dehydration, positive pressure ventilation, tachyarrhythmia and rising pulmonary vascular resistance are all poorly tolerated. Treat hypovolaemia and loss of sinus rhythm as urgent problems rather than incidental ones.
Genetic associations worth knowing

Down syndrome → AVSD, VSD. Turner syndrome → bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation. Noonan syndrome → pulmonary stenosis, HCM. 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) → conotruncal anomalies including tetralogy and truncus. Williams syndrome → supravalvular aortic stenosis. Marfan → aortic root dilation, mitral valve prolapse.

Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy+

A distinct syndrome from chronic hypertension, and one where the cardiovascular and obstetric decisions are inseparable.

EntityDefinition
Chronic hypertensionPresent before pregnancy or before 20 weeks
Gestational hypertensionNew after 20 weeks, without proteinuria or organ dysfunction
Pre-eclampsiaNew hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, neurological, haematological) or uteroplacental dysfunction
EclampsiaPre-eclampsia with seizures
HELLPHaemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — a severe variant

Pathophysiology in one line: defective trophoblastic invasion leaves the spiral arteries inadequately remodelled, causing placental ischaemia and release of anti-angiogenic factors that produce systemic endothelial dysfunction. That endothelial injury — not the blood pressure itself — is what damages the maternal organs.

Management essentials
  • Antihypertensives: labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa; hydralazine for acute severe hypertension. ACEi, ARB and MRA are contraindicated.
  • Magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and for treating eclampsia — superior to phenytoin and diazepam. Monitor for toxicity: loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, reduced urine output. Calcium gluconate is the antidote.
  • Delivery of the placenta is the only definitive treatment — timing balances maternal risk against fetal maturity.
  • Aspirin prophylaxis from early pregnancy reduces pre-eclampsia risk in high-risk women.
Why a cardiologist must know this
  • Pre-eclampsia is an independent long-term risk factor for later hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, stroke and heart failure — so an obstetric history is a cardiovascular risk factor, and asking about it is part of a proper risk assessment in a woman.
  • Peripartum cardiomyopathy and pre-eclampsia can coexist and present with overlapping breathlessness and oedema.
  • Magnesium toxicity presents with bradycardia and conduction changes — cardiology may be asked to interpret them.
Cardiovascular Pharmacology in Pregnancy & Lactation+
Generally acceptableAvoid / contraindicated
HypertensionLabetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa, hydralazineACEi, ARB, ARNI, MRA (fetotoxic); atenolol (fetal growth restriction)
Anticoagulation (VTE)LMWH — does not cross the placentaDOACs (inadequate data, placental transfer); warfarin (teratogenic, esp. 1st trimester)
ArrhythmiaBeta-blockers, adenosine, digoxin; DC cardioversion is safeAmiodarone (fetal thyroid) except when no alternative
Heart failureLoop diuretics if congested, beta-blockers, hydralazine + nitrateACEi/ARB/ARNI/MRA, SGLT2 inhibitors
LipidsDefer treatmentStatins — generally stopped in pregnancy
The mechanical valve dilemma is the hardest prescribing decision in this area. Warfarin gives the best maternal valve protection but is teratogenic, with risk concentrated in the first trimester and dose-dependent. LMWH is fetally safer but carries higher maternal valve thrombosis risk and needs anti-Xa monitoring. There is no risk-free option — the answer is an individualised Pregnancy Heart Team decision with explicit counselling, and saying that is stronger than naming one drug.
Lactation

Labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa have acceptable lactation data. Enalapril and captopril are sometimes used with specialist input. ARBs lack adequate data, and spironolactone raises antiandrogenic concerns. Warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding — it does not enter milk in clinically significant amounts, which surprises many candidates.

Why the physiology drives the pharmacology here

Pregnancy raises plasma volume, cardiac output and heart rate while lowering systemic vascular resistance. That means stenotic lesions decompensate (a fixed orifice cannot accommodate the flow) while regurgitant lesions often improve (falling afterload reduces regurgitant fraction). It also means rate control is the key therapeutic lever in mitral stenosis with new AF — lengthening diastole restores filling time.

References
  • 2025 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease and pregnancy — mWHO 2.0, Pregnancy Heart Team, drug safety tables.
  • ROPAC registry — outcome data underpinning current risk stratification.
Common mistakes
  • Over-applying endocarditis prophylaxis to all valve disease — current guidance restricts it to specific high-risk conditions.
  • Forgetting ACEi/ARB and warfarin are contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • Misweighting Duke major vs minor criteria when working through a case vignette.
  • Recommending shunt closure once Eisenmenger physiology has developed — this is contraindicated and can precipitate RV failure.
  • Defaulting to "advise against pregnancy" for high-risk cardiac patients — the 2025 guideline explicitly moves toward personalized counselling and shared decision-making instead.
  • Assuming regurgitant lesions are the dangerous ones in pregnancy — it's the stenotic lesions that decompensate, since a fixed orifice can't handle the increased cardiac output.
  • Using only the 2000 modified Duke criteria — both the ESC 2023 and Duke-ISCVID 2023 revisions expanded the microbiology and imaging criteria.
Week 14Vascular/Aortic Disease + Full Integration Review
+
📚 Guide (full depth)❓ Full mixed MCQs🎙️ Oral practice
Peripheral Arterial Disease & Acute Limb Ischemia+
ABI interpretation
ABIMeaning
>1.40Non-compressible — calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD). Abnormal, but not from stenosis; use toe-brachial index instead
1.00–1.40Normal
0.91–0.99Borderline
≤0.90Diagnostic of PAD

Acute limb ischemia — the 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia. The last two (paresthesia and paralysis) are the ones that signal a threatened limb requiring urgent revascularization — pain and pallor alone don't carry the same urgency.

🆕 Recent update — 2024 ESC Peripheral Arterial & Aortic Diseases guideline: this merged the old separate 2017 PAD and 2014 aortic guidelines into one document ("PAAD"). Key practical points: ABI is the recommended first-line screening test with ≤0.9 diagnostic for PAD; lipid targets in atherosclerotic PAAD are aggressive — ≥50% LDL-C reduction from baseline with a goal <55 mg/dL (<1.4 mmol/L); and AAA screening by duplex ultrasound is recommended in men ≥65 with a smoking history and in all men ≥75. The guideline also emphasizes evaluating the whole arterial circulation, since polyvascular disease affects roughly 1 in 4-6 atherosclerotic patients and nearly doubles cardiovascular event risk.
Aortic Dissection+
StanfordAnatomyManagement
Type AInvolves the ascending aorta (regardless of origin)Emergency surgery — risk of tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary occlusion, and rupture into the pericardium
Type BDescending only, distal to the left subclavianMedical first — aggressive BP/HR control; intervention (usually TEVAR) reserved for complications: malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension

The reason Type A is a surgical emergency comes directly from anatomy — the ascending aorta sits inside the pericardial reflection, so rupture there means tamponade, and proximal extension can shear the aortic valve or coronary ostia.

Links back to Week 10: BP control in dissection is beta-blocker first, then vasodilator. Target SBP 100-120 and HR <60. Vasodilating before rate control produces reflex tachycardia that raises aortic wall shear stress and can propagate the dissection.
Pulmonary Hypertension+
🆕 Major recent update — 2022 ESC/ERS PH guideline changed the definition itself: pulmonary hypertension is now mPAP >20 mmHg at rest (lowered from the long-standing ≥25). Pre-capillary PH additionally requires PVR >2 Wood units (lowered from >3) with PAWP ≤15 mmHg. If your source material still says "mPAP ≥25 and PVR >3," it predates this change. Note the guideline explicitly cautions that these new thresholds don't yet translate into treatment recommendations for the newly-captured mild range — the efficacy of PAH therapy at mPAP 21-24 or PVR 2-3 WU remains unproven.
The 5 groups
GroupCategoryTreatment principle
1Pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, drug/toxin, connective tissue disease, congenital shunts)PAH-specific therapy — this is the group those drugs are for
2PH due to left heart diseaseTreat the left heart; PAH drugs can be harmful
3PH due to lung disease/hypoxiaTreat the lung disease, oxygen
4Chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH)Pulmonary endarterectomy — potentially curable, don't miss it
5Unclear/multifactorialCause-directed

Diagnosis follows a 3-step pathway: suspicion by a first-line clinician → detection by echocardiography → confirmation by right heart catheterization at a PH centre. Right heart catheterization remains the gold standard — echo estimates probability, it doesn't make the diagnosis.

Integration Review+

Re-attack whatever the Week 4 diagnostic and your subsequent MCQ work have flagged as still weak. This is also the point to start deliberately connecting domains rather than studying them in isolation — the questions that separate candidates are usually cross-domain: an AFib patient with mitral stenosis (anticoagulation choice changes), a dissection presenting as inferior STEMI (reperfusion would be catastrophic), a HFpEF patient whose real diagnosis is cardiac amyloidosis.

References for Week 14
  • 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538-3700 — merges the 2017 PAD and 2014 aortic guidelines.
  • 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618-3731 — the mPAP >20 / PVR >2 WU redefinition.
  • 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease, Circulation 2022;146:e334-e482.
  • IRAD (International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection) — the observational data underlying Type A/B management.
  • 2019 ESC Guidelines on acute pulmonary embolism — relevant to the Week 14 PH differential and to case work.
  • Hurst's The Heart — Diseases of the Aorta; Peripheral Arterial Disease; Pulmonary Hypertension.
Common mistakes
  • Applying surgical management to all Type A dissections but forgetting Type B is medical-first unless complicated.
  • Only flagging ABI below 0.9 as abnormal — above 1.4 (non-compressible, calcified vessels) is also abnormal, just for a different reason.
  • Treating all pulmonary hypertension with PAH-specific therapy — that class can be harmful in Group 2/3 disease.
  • Still using mPAP ≥25 mmHg and PVR >3 WU as the PH definition — both thresholds were lowered in 2022 (to >20 and >2 respectively).
  • Diagnosing PH on echocardiography alone — echo establishes probability; right heart catheterization is the confirmatory gold standard.
  • Missing CTEPH (Group 4) in the workup — it's the one form that's potentially curable with pulmonary endarterectomy.
  • Treating pain and pallor as sufficient markers of a threatened limb — paresthesia and paralysis are the findings that mandate urgent revascularization.
04

Exam Simulation & Taper

Weeks 15-17 · Convert knowledge into performance. No new content after Week 16.

A different kind of phase: Phases 1-3 built knowledge. This one builds retrieval under pressure — a separate skill that doesn't come free with knowing the material. Most candidates who underperform relative to their preparation lose points here, not in content gaps: mistimed pacing, second-guessing correct answers, or freezing in the interview. Treat these three weeks as skills training, not more studying.
Week 15Full Mock Exam I + Oral Case Drills
+
❓ Timed mock (100-150Q)🎙️ Oral drills, 2-3 cases/day
Running the Mock Properly+

The point of a mock isn't the score — it's exposing failure modes you can still fix. That only works if the conditions are real: single sitting, timed, phone away, no lookups, no pausing to check something you're unsure about. A mock taken comfortably teaches you almost nothing.

Pacing discipline

Calculate your per-question budget before starting (total minutes ÷ total questions) and set checkpoints — at 25% of the time you should be at 25% of the questions. Check at each quarter, not constantly.

The rule that saves the most points: if you're stuck past roughly twice your per-question budget, flag it, put down your best current answer, and move on. An unanswered question at the end is worth zero; a flagged guess is worth its probability. Time spent on a single hard question is stolen from three easy ones you haven't reached yet.

Answer-changing: the evidence on this is more nuanced than the folk wisdom "always trust your first instinct." Changes made because you spotted new information or caught a misread are usually improvements. Changes made from pure anxiety — no new reasoning, just discomfort — usually aren't. The test is whether you can articulate a specific reason for the change.
The Error Log — Where the Real Gains Are+

Reviewing a mock takes longer than sitting it, and that's correct. For every wrong answer, classify the error type — because the fix differs completely by type:

Error typeWhat it meansFix
Knowledge gapYou didn't know the factAdd to flashcards; revisit the guide section
Reasoning errorYou knew the facts but applied them wronglyMost valuable to fix — re-derive the logic, don't just memorize the answer
MisreadMissed a key qualifier ("most likely," "next best step," "except")A reading-discipline problem, not a knowledge one
Guideline currencyYou gave the older guideline's answerCross-check the 🆕 flags in Phases 2-3
TimingRushed or unreachedPacing drill, not content review

For every wrong answer, also work out why each distractor was wrong. Distractor logic repeats across question banks — the same wrong-but-tempting reasoning gets reused. Understanding why "give a beta-blocker" is wrong in one vignette often gets you three future questions.

Also review the questions you got right but guessed on. These are indistinguishable from knowledge in your score but are pure luck — and they'll regress to the mean on exam day. Mark them during the mock so you can find them afterward.
Oral Exam Structure — How to Answer Out Loud+

Interviewers are assessing your reasoning process, not just your conclusion. A structured answer signals clinical maturity even when your final answer isn't perfect; a correct answer delivered as a disorganized list of facts doesn't.

A reusable spine for any case
  • Summarize — one sentence restating the case in your own words. Buys thinking time and confirms you understood it.
  • Commit to a leading diagnosis with the specific features that support it.
  • Differential — two or three alternatives, and crucially what would distinguish them.
  • Immediate priorities — what you'd do in the first minutes (stabilization, monitoring, key investigations).
  • Definitive management, with the guideline basis where you know it.
  • Complications/follow-up you'd watch for.

Practice out loud — actually speaking, not rehearsing silently. Silent recall and verbal fluency are different skills, and the gap between them only shows up under pressure. Recording yourself is uncomfortable and unusually effective; you'll hear the hedging and circling that you don't notice while speaking.

Say "I don't know" cleanly when you don't. Bluffing is far more damaging than a gap — examiners detect it easily and it undermines everything else you said. The strong version: "I'm not certain of the specific threshold, but the principle is X, and I'd verify the exact figure before acting." That demonstrates both honesty and safe practice.
Common mistakes
  • Reviewing only the correct answer — distractor logic repeats across similar questions, so understanding why the wrong options are wrong is where the real learning is.
  • Rehearsing oral answers silently — interview performance is a different skill from silent recall; you have to practice speaking it.
  • Taking mocks untimed or with interruptions — this trains nothing about exam-day conditions and inflates your sense of readiness.
  • Treating the mock score as the output — the error log is the output; the score is just a byproduct.
  • Ignoring lucky guesses that happened to be right — they inflate your score and hide real gaps.
  • Over-dwelling on one hard question — time taken there is stolen from easier questions you haven't reached.
  • Bluffing through an oral answer instead of naming the gap — examiners spot it, and it costs more credibility than the gap itself.
Week 16Full Mock Exam II + Guideline Cross-Check
+
❓ Timed mock, weak-domain focus📋 Guidelines cross-check🎙️ Oral drills with pushback
Mock II — Targeting, Not Repeating+

Mock II should be weighted toward whatever Mock I's error log exposed. Compare the two error logs directly — the useful question isn't "did my score improve" but "did the error types shift?"

  • Knowledge-gap errors falling → your content work is landing.
  • Reasoning errors persisting → you're memorizing answers rather than rebuilding the logic. Go back and re-derive from mechanism.
  • Timing errors persisting → this is now the priority; no amount of content review fixes pacing.
  • Misreads persisting → build the habit of underlining the question stem's actual ask ("next best step" vs "most likely diagnosis") before looking at options.

Also do a targeted pass over the 🆕 flagged items across Phases 2 and 3. These are disproportionately likely to appear because guideline changes are what distinguishes a current candidate from one working off old material — and they're exactly where your instinct will pull toward the outdated answer.

Guideline Discrepancy Drilling+

Build a short list of the specific points where PERKI, ESC, and ACC/AHA actually diverge — using your SKA Confluence document as the authoritative source. For each one, be able to state: what each body recommends, and which answer you'd give if the question doesn't specify.

Default rule: on a PERKI-affiliated exam, PERKI's recommendation wins when the question doesn't name a guideline. Where PERKI is silent, ESC is generally the closer reference point for Indonesian practice than ACC/AHA.

Also be ready for the meta-question: some interviewers deliberately ask about a point of disagreement to see whether you know that guidelines can disagree. Answering "ESC says X while ACC/AHA says Y, and here's the evidence tension behind the difference" is a stronger answer than confidently asserting one as universal truth.

Oral Drills Under Pushback+

Interviewers commonly challenge an answer — sometimes because it's wrong, but often to test whether you can defend sound reasoning under pressure. Both possibilities need a response, and the same opening move handles both: listen to the specific objection before responding.

Three response patterns worth rehearsing
  • You're right and the challenge is a probe. Restate the reasoning with the evidence behind it, calmly. Don't escalate volume or repeat the same sentence louder — add the why.
  • The challenge revealed a genuine error. Acknowledge it directly and correct course: "That's a fair point — I hadn't weighted the renal function there, which changes my choice to X." Fast, non-defensive correction reads as clinical maturity, not weakness.
  • The challenge is ambiguous. Ask for the clarification: "Are you asking about the acute setting specifically?" This is legitimate and shows precision.

Have someone play the interviewer if you can — a colleague also sitting the exam is ideal, since you can trade. If not, record yourself answering, then re-listen and argue against your own answer out loud.

The failure mode to train out: abandoning a correct answer the instant someone questions it. Caving under pushback with no new information suggests you never had reasoning behind the answer, only recall. This costs more than being wrong with good logic.
Common mistakes
  • Defaulting to the international guideline answer on a question that doesn't specify — default to PERKI unless told otherwise.
  • Freezing when an interviewer challenges your answer — practice staying calm and explaining your reasoning rather than just re-reciting it louder.
  • Abandoning a correct answer purely because it was questioned — this signals recall without reasoning.
  • Comparing Mock I and Mock II by score only, ignoring whether the error types changed.
  • Treating persistent timing errors as a content problem — more studying won't fix pacing.
  • Asserting one guideline as universal truth when the question is probing whether you know they disagree.
Week 17Final Taper
+
🗂️ Flashcard maintenance only❓ One short mock, early week
Why Taper Instead of Cram+

Cramming in the final week feels productive and generally isn't. Consolidation of what you've already learned happens largely during sleep, so late-night cramming trades a proven mechanism (memory consolidation) for an unproven one (last-minute encoding), while raising anxiety that degrades retrieval on the day.

The goal this week is arriving rested and confident, not maximally crammed. A candidate who knows 90% and is calm outperforms one who knows 93% and is exhausted — because retrieval under pressure is where the marks are actually won or lost, and fatigue attacks retrieval hardest.

If you find a genuine gap this week, note it and do a brief targeted review — don't spiral into re-studying an entire domain. Finding gaps at this stage is normal and not a signal that your preparation failed.
Day-by-Day Structure+
DayFocus
Day 1-2One short timed mock (50-75Q) to keep the pacing rhythm warm. Review errors, but briefly — this is calibration, not a new learning cycle.
Day 3-4Skim the 🆕 guideline-update flags and your personal high-yield list. Daily flashcards, due cards only. One or two oral cases out loud to stay verbally fluent.
Day 5Light review only. Stop testing. Confirm exam logistics — venue, travel time, required documents, ID, start time.
Day 6Flashcards only, short session. Do something genuinely restorative. Sleep at your normal time, not early — trying to sleep unusually early usually backfires.
Exam dayEat properly. Arrive early. No last-minute review of new material in the waiting area — it only surfaces things you don't know and spikes anxiety right before you need calm.
The Final Review List+

Rather than skimming everything, concentrate the last passes on categories that carry disproportionate weight:

  • The 🆕 guideline changes — highest yield per minute, since these are exactly where an otherwise-prepared candidate gives the outdated answer.
  • Absolute contraindications — AV nodal blockers in WPW+AFib, DOACs with mechanical valves, shunt closure in Eisenmenger, beta-blockade before alpha-blockade in pheochromocytoma, ACEi/ARB in pregnancy. These are binary, high-confidence marks.
  • Time-critical decisions — reperfusion windows, invasive strategy timing, post-MI complication timelines.
  • Your own persistent error patterns from the error logs — the specific things you personally keep getting wrong.

Deliberately don't spend this week on rare conditions or fine details you've never reliably retained. The marginal return is low and the anxiety cost is real.

Common mistakes
  • Cramming new material the night before — it raises anxiety and disrupts sleep without meaningfully improving recall.
  • Stopping flashcards entirely in the final week — light maintenance is still needed to prevent decay right before the exam.
  • Taking a full-length mock in the last 48 hours — a poor score at that point damages confidence with no time left to act on it.
  • Reviewing notes in the waiting area — it surfaces gaps at the worst possible moment.
  • Trying to sleep unusually early the night before, which typically produces frustrated lying awake; keep your normal schedule.
  • Spending the final week on rare conditions instead of the highest-yield categories and your own known error patterns.
Soft timeline note: if your actual exam date lands earlier than 4 months, compress Phase 3 first (lower-yield fill-in) — never Phase 2 (high-yield core) or Phase 4 (exam simulation).
🩺

OSCE & Viva Case Bank

Twenty multi-stage cases for Weeks 15-16 · Each evolves across stages with new data that should change your answer. Model answers and examiner probes included.

How to use these: read only the stem, then say your answer out loud before opening the model answer. The cases are deliberately built with traps — each one contains at least one intervention that seems reasonable and would harm the patient. Getting caught is the point; that's cheaper here than on exam day. Work one case per session, and revisit any case where you fell into the trap a week later.
Case 1 · High complexityInferior STEMI with Escalating Complications
+
Presentation

A 58-year-old man presents to a district hospital with 3 hours of crushing chest pain, nausea, and diaphoresis. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and smokes. The nearest PCI-capable centre is a 3-hour transfer.

BP 88/56HR 48RR 22SpO₂ 96% RAJVP elevatedLungs clear

ECG: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with ST elevation greater in III than II. Reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. Sinus bradycardia with intermittent dropped beats.

Stage 1

The referring doctor has already given aspirin, ticagrelor, and sublingual nitrate — and reports the patient became "much more hypotensive" immediately after the nitrate. What is your assessment, and what do you do now?

Model answer+
Assessment. This is an inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction. Three features point there: hypotension with an elevated JVP but clear lungs (right-sided failure without left-sided congestion), ST elevation greater in III than II with reciprocal depression in aVL (favouring RCA as culprit, proximal enough to involve the RV branch), and the profound hypotensive response to nitrate — the signature of a preload-dependent ventricle.
  • Confirm: right-sided leads immediately. ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic of RV involvement.
  • Stop all preload reducers — no further nitrates, no morphine-driven venodilation, no diuretics.
  • Fluid challenge — cautious boluses of crystalloid. The RV needs filling pressure to deliver preload to the LV. Reassess after each bolus; over-filling can cause septal shift and worsen LV output.
  • Bradycardia: atropine for symptomatic bradycardia; this is likely vagally mediated/AV nodal (the AV node is RCA-supplied in most people) and often responds. Prepare for transcutaneous pacing.
  • Reperfusion: transfer is 3 hours, so PCI within 120 minutes is not achievable. Give fibrinolysis now (door-to-needle ≤30 min) after checking contraindications, then transfer for routine early or rescue PCI. Do not delay lysis waiting for transfer.
Examiner probes
  • "Why is ST elevation in III > II useful?" — It favours RCA over left circumflex as the culprit, because the RCA-supplied inferior territory sits more rightward; LCx occlusion typically gives II ≥ III. Combined with reciprocal depression in aVL, RCA is likely, and RV involvement becomes a live concern.
  • "He's on ticagrelor already and you're about to lyse. Problem?" — Yes, worth flagging. Ticagrelor/prasugrel are not the recommended P2Y12 agents alongside fibrinolysis; clopidogrel is the agent with the supporting evidence base in that setting. This is a real-world pre-hospital error to recognize, and you'd manage the bleeding risk accordingly rather than pretend it didn't happen.
  • "How much fluid?" — There's no fixed number. Titrate to response, reassessing perfusion and lung fields after each bolus. If hypotension persists despite adequate filling, add an inotrope (dobutamine) rather than continuing to volume-load.
Stage 2

Lysis is given; ST segments resolve by 60%. He is transferred and undergoes angiography showing a proximal RCA culprit lesion, successfully stented, plus a 70% mid-LAD lesion and a 60% obtuse marginal lesion. He stabilises.

What do you do about the non-culprit lesions?

Model answer+
He is now haemodynamically stable, so the current guidance applies: complete revascularization is Class I — the significant non-culprit lesions should be treated, either during the index procedure or in a staged fashion within 45 days. Culprit-only PCI is no longer the default for a stable STEMI patient.

Lesion significance can be confirmed physiologically (FFR/iFR) or angiographically for clearly severe lesions. The decision should factor in renal function, contrast load already given, and lesion complexity.

Examiner probe
  • "Would your answer change if he were still in cardiogenic shock?" — Yes, and this is the key distinction. In cardiogenic shock, CULPRIT-SHOCK showed culprit-lesion-only PCI produced better 30-day outcomes than immediate multivessel PCI. So the general Class I complete-revascularization rule has an explicit shock exception. Knowing both the rule and its exception is what a strong answer looks like here.
Stage 3

On day 4, he becomes acutely dyspnoeic and hypotensive. A new harsh holosystolic murmur is audible at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill.

BP 82/50HR 118RR 30SpO₂ 89%Bilateral crackles

What has happened, how do you confirm it, and how do you manage it?

Model answer+
Day 4 with a new murmur and haemodynamic collapse means a mechanical complication — this is the days 3-5 window when necrotic myocardium is most friable. The differential is essentially two entities:
Ventricular septal rupturePapillary muscle rupture
MurmurHarsh, LLSB, thrill often presentOften soft or absent (rapid pressure equalisation), apex/axilla
EchoSeptal defect with left-to-right colour jetFlail leaflet, severe eccentric MR
Right heart cathOxygen step-up RA→RVNo step-up; giant v waves in PCWP tracing
Pulmonary oedemaPresent but often less fulminantTypically flash pulmonary oedema

The thrill and LLSB location favour VSR. Confirm with urgent transthoracic ± transoesophageal echo with colour Doppler; an oxygen step-up on right heart catheterisation is confirmatory if available.

Management:
  • Urgent surgical consultation — this is a surgical emergency. Medical management alone carries very high mortality.
  • Afterload reduction (vasodilator, or mechanical support) reduces the left-to-right shunt if blood pressure permits — but he is hypotensive, so mechanical circulatory support (IABP or Impella) is the more appropriate bridge here than aggressive pharmacological vasodilation.
  • Avoid inotropes as the primary strategy — increasing contractility can increase the shunt fraction.
Examiner probes
  • "Which papillary muscle would you expect to rupture, and why?" — The posteromedial, because it has a single blood supply from the PDA, whereas the anterolateral has dual supply (LAD plus a diagonal or obtuse marginal). Given this is an RCA/inferior infarct, the posteromedial muscle is in the infarct territory.
  • "He had successful lysis and PCI. Does that make mechanical complication less likely?" — Successful reperfusion reduces but does not eliminate the risk, and importantly, delayed or failed reperfusion is the bigger risk factor. His initial 3-hour delay plus lysis-then-transfer means he had meaningful ischaemic time. Never let a good angiographic result stop you considering this diagnosis at day 3-5.
  • "Timing of surgery — immediate or wait to stabilise?" — This is genuinely contested and a good answer acknowledges that. Early surgery faces friable tissue that holds sutures poorly; delayed surgery risks death while waiting. Contemporary practice favours early repair in unstable patients, using mechanical support to bridge, with the decision made by a multidisciplinary team.
What separates a strong answer
  • Recognising RV infarct from the nitrate response rather than waiting for V4R — clinical reasoning, not protocol-following.
  • Choosing lysis decisively rather than defaulting to "transfer for PCI" because PCI is "better."
  • Knowing complete revascularization is now Class I and that shock is the exception.
  • Using day 4 timing as a diagnostic instrument, not just a background detail.
Case 2 · High complexityPregnant Woman with Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis
+
Presentation

A 27-year-old woman, G2P1, at 30 weeks' gestation, presents with 5 days of progressive dyspnoea, now at rest, with orthopnoea and a dry cough. She had rheumatic fever in childhood and has not had cardiac follow-up. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated.

BP 104/68HR 142 irregularRR 30SpO₂ 90% RAAfebrile

Exam: irregularly irregular pulse, loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, bibasal crackles. ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate 142.

Stage 1

Explain the physiology of what has happened, and outline your immediate management.

Model answer+
Physiology — three insults compounding. She has previously undiagnosed rheumatic mitral stenosis. Pregnancy raises plasma volume and cardiac output by 40-50% and increases heart rate; a fixed stenotic orifice cannot accommodate that increased flow, so left atrial pressure rises. Third trimester is the peak haemodynamic load, which is why she is presenting now. Then new-onset AF delivers two further hits: loss of the atrial kick (which contributes disproportionately to filling across a stenotic valve) and, more importantly, tachycardia shortens diastole — and diastole is precisely when the LV fills through the narrowed valve. The result is acute pulmonary oedema.

The single most important therapeutic lever here is rate control, because lengthening diastole directly restores filling time.

Immediate management:
  • Rate control with a beta-blocker — this is first-line and mechanistically the right answer. Metoprolol or labetalol; avoid atenolol (fetal growth restriction).
  • Oxygen, sit upright, cautious IV loop diuretic for pulmonary congestion — cautious because excessive preload reduction in MS can drop cardiac output.
  • Anticoagulation — AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis is valvular AF. DOACs are contraindicated; she needs heparin (LMWH or UFH) in this acute setting.
  • If she becomes haemodynamically unstable, synchronised DC cardioversion is safe in pregnancy and should not be withheld — fetal monitoring during the procedure, but this is not a contraindication.
  • Activate a multidisciplinary Pregnancy Heart Team: cardiology, obstetrics, anaesthesia, neonatology.
Examiner probes
  • "Why does her first uncomplicated pregnancy not reassure you?" — MS is progressive, and the haemodynamic burden of pregnancy is a stress test she may have narrowly passed before. Valve area may also have declined in the interval. Prior tolerance predicts nothing.
  • "Why not a DOAC — she's young with good renal function?" — Two independent reasons, and citing both is stronger: DOACs are contraindicated in valvular AF (moderate-severe mitral stenosis), and they are also contraindicated in pregnancy. Either alone rules them out.
  • "She asks whether the diuretic will harm the baby." — Loop diuretics are used when clinically indicated for pulmonary congestion; the risk of untreated maternal pulmonary oedema outweighs the theoretical concerns. The honest framing is that we use the minimum effective dose with fetal monitoring, and that maternal stability is what protects the fetus.
Stage 2

She stabilises on beta-blockade and diuresis. Echo shows mitral valve area 0.9 cm², mean gradient 14 mmHg, moderate pulmonary hypertension, no significant mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus, and a pliable non-calcified valve with minimal subvalvular disease (favourable Wilkins score).

She remains NYHA III on optimal medical therapy at 31 weeks. What are her options?

Model answer+
This is severe mitral stenosis (valve area <1.0 cm²) with refractory symptoms despite medical therapy — an indication for intervention, and pregnancy does not remove that indication.
  • Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC) is the procedure of choice. Her anatomy is ideal: favourable Wilkins score, pliable non-calcified valve, no significant MR, and no LA thrombus — the four things that must be true.
  • It can be performed during pregnancy, preferably after the first trimester and ideally beyond 20 weeks, with abdominal shielding and minimised fluoroscopy time. Echo guidance reduces radiation further.
  • Surgical commissurotomy or valve replacement carries substantially higher fetal loss rates (cardiopulmonary bypass is poorly tolerated by the fetus) and is reserved for cases where PMBC is not feasible.
  • Continue rate control and anticoagulation throughout.
Examiner probes
  • "What would make you say no to PMBC?" — Left atrial thrombus, moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation, heavy calcification or severe subvalvular disease (unfavourable Wilkins score), or bicommissural calcification. Each has a mechanistic reason: thrombus risks embolisation, existing MR will worsen dramatically with commissurotomy.
  • "How would you classify her risk formally?" — Severe mitral stenosis falls in the highest mWHO 2.0 categories. Under the 2025 ESC pregnancy guideline, that mandates a Pregnancy Heart Team and care at an expert centre. Note the guideline has moved away from simply advising against pregnancy in high-risk women toward personalised counselling — so the framing is risk management and shared decision-making, not prohibition.
  • "Delivery plan?" — Vaginal delivery with a short assisted second stage is generally preferred if she is stable, with regional anaesthesia carefully titrated to avoid abrupt vasodilation and preload drop. Caesarean is reserved for obstetric indications or persistent haemodynamic instability. Note the immediate postpartum period is a high-risk window — autotransfusion from the contracting uterus abruptly increases preload, which a stenotic valve handles poorly.
What separates a strong answer
  • Naming tachycardia shortening diastole as the core mechanism — not just "AF caused decompensation."
  • Recognising valvular AF and giving both reasons DOACs are out.
  • Knowing DC cardioversion is safe in pregnancy — many candidates hesitate here.
  • Flagging the postpartum autotransfusion window as the period of greatest danger.
  • Framing the pregnancy conversation as shared decision-making per the 2025 guideline rather than "she should not have become pregnant."
Case 3 · Very high complexityChest Pain with Inferior ST Elevation — The Trap
+
Presentation

A 61-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension presents with severe chest pain of sudden onset 40 minutes ago, described as "tearing" and radiating to his back between the shoulder blades. He is agitated and diaphoretic.

BP right arm 178/96BP left arm 142/80HR 104RR 24SpO₂ 97%

ECG: ST elevation 2mm in II, III, aVF. Exam: early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge; pulse deficit noted in the left radial artery.

Stage 1

The emergency physician is preparing thrombolysis, as transfer time exceeds 120 minutes. What do you say?

Model answer+
Stop. Do not thrombolyse. This is very likely a Stanford Type A aortic dissection presenting with inferior ST elevation from retrograde extension occluding the right coronary ostium. Thrombolysis here would be catastrophic — it converts a contained dissection into uncontrolled haemorrhage and tamponade.

The features that should stop you, and they were all in the stem:

  • Tearing pain radiating to the interscapular region, maximal at onset — ischaemic pain typically builds rather than peaking instantly.
  • Inter-arm blood pressure differential (>20 mmHg) and a pulse deficit — branch vessel involvement.
  • New early diastolic murmur — aortic regurgitation from disruption of the valve commissures by proximal extension.
  • The combination of hypertension plus these findings in a patient with "STEMI" should always trigger the dissection question.
What to do instead:
  • Urgent imaging: CT angiography of the aorta (or transoesophageal echo if too unstable to move). Do not delay for troponin.
  • Blood pressure and heart rate control, in the correct order — beta-blocker first (IV esmolol or labetalol) to target HR <60, then a vasodilator to target SBP 100-120. Giving a vasodilator first causes reflex tachycardia, which raises aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) and can propagate the dissection.
  • Adequate analgesia — pain drives the sympathetic surge.
  • Immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral if Type A is confirmed. Type A is a surgical emergency; mortality rises roughly 1-2% per hour untreated.
  • Withhold antiplatelets and anticoagulation pending imaging.
Examiner probes
  • "Why inferior leads specifically?" — The dissection flap most commonly compromises the right coronary ostium, because of the geometry of the aortic root and the typical location of the intimal tear in the ascending aorta. So a dissection masquerading as STEMI is usually an inferior pattern — which makes any inferior STEMI with atypical features worth a second look.
  • "He's already had aspirin from the ambulance. Does that change anything?" — It doesn't change the diagnosis or the need for surgery, but flag it to the surgical team as a bleeding-risk factor. Don't give further antiplatelets or heparin.
  • "What if the CT shows Type B instead?" — Then management is medical first: aggressive BP and HR control, and intervention (usually TEVAR) only for complications — malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, or refractory pain/hypertension. The inferior ST elevation would then need another explanation, and you'd reconsider concurrent ACS.
  • "His BP drops to 80/50 and JVP rises during workup." — Suspect cardiac tamponade from rupture into the pericardium — a Type A complication. This is an indication for immediate surgery, not pericardiocentesis, which can accelerate bleeding by relieving the tamponade that is partially containing it.
What separates a strong answer
  • Refusing thrombolysis and being able to name the specific stem features that justified refusing — not just pattern-matching to "tearing pain."
  • Getting the beta-blocker-before-vasodilator sequence right, with the dP/dt reasoning.
  • Knowing that pericardiocentesis in Type A tamponade can worsen the situation.
  • Being willing to override a colleague already committed to a plan — examiners are watching for whether you assert a safety concern clearly.
Case 4 · High complexityWide-Complex Tachycardia in a Young Adult
+
Presentation

A 24-year-old man is brought in with palpitations and lightheadedness that began 30 minutes ago during exercise. No known cardiac history, but he reports occasional past episodes of "racing heart" that stopped on their own.

BP 92/58HR ~230Alert but paleSpO₂ 95%

ECG: very rapid, irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia with varying QRS morphology and width beat to beat. Rate ranges roughly 180-260.

Stage 1

A colleague is drawing up verapamil, saying it looks like SVT. What is the rhythm, and what do you do?

Model answer+
Stop the verapamil. This is pre-excited atrial fibrillation — AF conducting antegrade down an accessory pathway (WPW). The triad that identifies it: irregularly irregular + wide + very fast with beat-to-beat QRS variation. That combination is essentially diagnostic.

Why it matters so much: AV nodal blocking agents — verapamil, diltiazem, adenosine, beta-blockers, and digoxin — block the normal conduction route, removing competition and forcing conduction preferentially down the accessory pathway. The pathway may have a very short refractory period, allowing 1:1 conduction of atrial rates over 300, which can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Giving verapamil here can kill him.

Correct management:
  • Unstable (hypotension, altered mental state, ischaemia, heart failure) → synchronised DC cardioversion. His BP is 92/58 with lightheadedness — I would have the defibrillator at the bedside and a low threshold for cardioverting.
  • Stable → procainamide is the classical agent of choice (slows accessory pathway conduction); ibutilide is an alternative. Amiodarone is more contentious in pre-excited AF than older teaching suggested — it has AV nodal blocking properties and case reports of haemodynamic deterioration, so it is not the safe default it was once taught to be.
  • Correct electrolytes; avoid anything that increases sympathetic drive.
Examiner probes
  • "How do you distinguish this from polymorphic VT?" — Both are irregular and wide. Polymorphic VT (including Torsades) typically shows a twisting axis around the baseline, usually arises with a preceding long QT or ischaemic substrate, and is usually less sustained. Pre-excited AF shows the chaotic irregularity of AF with variable degrees of pre-excitation, and there's often a history of prior palpitations or a delta wave on an old ECG. Practically, both may need cardioversion, so the immediate action converges — but the drug choice diverges completely.
  • "Where does the danger actually come from?" — The shortest pre-excited RR interval during AF is the key marker. Under roughly 250 ms indicates a short accessory pathway refractory period and a high risk of degenerating to VF.
  • "What happens after he's converted?" — Obtain a 12-lead in sinus rhythm looking for the delta wave, short PR, and QRS slurring confirming WPW. Then refer for electrophysiology study and catheter ablation of the accessory pathway, which is curative. Given he has had a haemodynamically significant pre-excited AF episode, this is a strong indication, not an optional one.
  • "He asks if he can keep playing football." — Restrict competitive/strenuous activity until the pathway is ablated and he's confirmed free of pre-excitation. A symptomatic pathway with rapid conduction that has already produced pre-excited AF carries real sudden death risk.
What separates a strong answer
  • Identifying the rhythm from the irregular + wide + fast triad rather than defaulting to "wide = VT."
  • Naming the full list of contraindicated drugs, including digoxin and adenosine — not just verapamil.
  • Not treating amiodarone as automatically safe here.
  • Escalating to definitive therapy (ablation) rather than stopping at acute termination.
Case 5 · Very high complexityBreathless Elderly Man — Diagnostic Reasoning Marathon
+
Presentation

A 74-year-old man presents with 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and ankle swelling. Treated as "heart failure" by his GP with escalating furosemide, plus ramipril and bisoprolol — but he has felt worse on the beta-blocker and became hypotensive on the ACE inhibitor. Past history: bilateral carpal tunnel release 4 years ago, lumbar spinal stenosis.

BP 96/62HR 72JVP raisedAscitesPitting oedema to thighs

Echo: LV wall thickness 16 mm, LVEF 48%, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling pattern, small pericardial effusion. ECG: low QRS voltage in limb leads, pseudo-infarct Q waves in V1-V3.

Stage 1

What is the unifying diagnosis, and which single feature makes you most confident?

Model answer+
Cardiac amyloidosis, most likely transthyretin (ATTR) given his age, sex, and the extracardiac history.

The single most powerful clue is the discordance between wall thickness and ECG voltage. A 16 mm wall with low limb-lead voltage is physiologically contradictory for ordinary hypertensive LVH — hypertrophy adds myocytes and therefore voltage. Infiltration adds mass without adding functioning electrical tissue, so the walls thicken while voltage falls. That single mismatch should redirect the entire workup.

Supporting features, all present:
  • Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome years earlier — amyloid deposition in the flexor retinaculum often precedes cardiac presentation by 5-10 years. Lumbar spinal stenosis is the same phenomenon.
  • Drug intolerance — poor tolerance of beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors is characteristic. These patients have a stiff ventricle with a relatively fixed stroke volume, so cardiac output is heart-rate dependent; slowing them with a beta-blocker reduces output. They are also preload-dependent and vasodilator-sensitive.
  • Restrictive filling, biatrial enlargement, pseudo-infarct pattern, pericardial effusion — all consistent.
  • Note his EF is 48% — this is an HFmrEF/HFpEF-range EF with severe symptoms, another hint that a standard HFrEF framework doesn't fit.
Examiner probe
  • "What else could give this picture?" — Constrictive pericarditis is the main differential (Week 12): also right-heart failure with preserved EF. Distinguishers: constriction shows marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow, septal bounce, pericardial thickening/calcification, and — counterintuitively — normal or increased tissue Doppler e′ ("annulus reversus") because the myocardium itself is healthy. Amyloid reduces e′. Other infiltrative causes: sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, Fabry disease (which can also present with LVH and has specific therapy).
Stage 2

How do you confirm it, and in what order?

Model answer+
The order is the answer here.
  • Step 1 — exclude a monoclonal protein first. Serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis plus serum free light chain assay. This screens for AL amyloidosis.
  • Step 2 — bone scintigraphy (99mTc-DPD, PYP, or HMDP). Grade 2-3 cardiac uptake in the absence of a monoclonal protein establishes ATTR cardiac amyloidosis non-invasively — no biopsy required. This non-invasive pathway is a genuinely important advance.
  • Step 3 — genotyping to distinguish hereditary (variant) ATTR from wild-type, which has implications for family screening and prognosis.
  • Cardiac MRI is supportive (diffuse subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal T1/ECV) but is not required if the scintigraphy pathway is definitive.
  • Endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for equivocal cases or when AL is suspected and tissue is needed.
Examiner probes
  • "Why is the order non-negotiable?" — Because AL amyloidosis can also produce cardiac uptake on bone scintigraphy. Calling a positive scan "ATTR" without excluding a monoclonal protein risks misdiagnosing AL — which is a haematological emergency requiring urgent plasma-cell-directed therapy and carries a far worse untreated prognosis. This is the single most dangerous shortcut in the amyloid workup.
  • "His free light chains are mildly abnormal and he's 74 with CKD." — Careful — mildly abnormal light chains are common in elderly CKD (reduced clearance) and with MGUS, which is itself common at this age. An abnormal screen doesn't confirm AL; it means you cannot use the non-invasive ATTR pathway and need haematology input, possibly tissue.
Stage 3

ATTR wild-type cardiac amyloidosis is confirmed. He is still congested. He also develops atrial fibrillation with a rate of 88.

How do you manage him now?

Model answer+
  • Disease-modifying therapy — tafamidis, a TTR stabiliser, reduces mortality and hospitalisation in ATTR cardiomyopathy (ATTR-ACT). Refer to a specialist amyloidosis centre; access and funding vary by setting.
  • Diuretics are the mainstay of symptom control — loop diuretic, often with an MRA. The therapeutic window is narrow: too little leaves him congested, too much drops his preload-dependent output.
  • Withdraw or minimise the beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor. This is counterintuitive if you're pattern-matching to "heart failure = four pillars," but standard GDMT is often poorly tolerated and not evidence-based in amyloid cardiomyopathy. His clinical deterioration on both drugs was informative, not incidental.
  • Anticoagulation for the AF — and importantly, patients with cardiac amyloidosis and AF have a high thromboembolic risk that is not well captured by CHA₂DS₂-VASc alone; anticoagulation is generally recommended regardless of a low score. Also be aware intracardiac thrombus can be present even in sinus rhythm.
  • Avoid digoxin if possible — it binds to amyloid fibrils, raising toxicity risk. Use cautiously with monitoring if genuinely needed.
  • Rate 88 in AF is acceptable; aggressive rate control risks compromising his heart-rate-dependent output.
  • Discuss prognosis and advance care planning; screen family members if genotype were variant (not needed for wild-type).
What separates a strong answer
  • Using the voltage/wall-thickness discordance as the pivot, rather than listing amyloid as one of many possibilities.
  • Reading the drug intolerance as diagnostic information rather than an adherence problem.
  • Getting the workup order right and being able to say why reversing it is dangerous.
  • Being willing to stop guideline-standard HF drugs — this demonstrates you understand that GDMT is disease-specific, not universal.
  • Knowing the anticoagulation threshold differs from ordinary AF.
Case 6 · Viva styleSyncope in an Elderly Woman — Layered Decision-Making
+
Presentation

A 76-year-old woman presents after collapsing while climbing stairs. She recovered within a minute without confusion. She admits to 6 months of exertional dyspnoea and two prior near-faints, which she had not reported. She also has iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 9.2) under investigation for intermittent dark stools.

BP 118/86HR 78Narrow pulse pressureSlow-rising carotid

Exam: harsh late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids; soft/absent A2. Echo: aortic valve area 0.8 cm², mean gradient 28 mmHg, LVEF 40%, stroke volume index 28 mL/m².

Stage 1

The echo report says "moderate aortic stenosis — mean gradient below the severe threshold." Do you accept that?

Model answer+
No. This is classical low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis, and the report has been misled by the gradient.

The reasoning: valve area is 0.8 cm² (severe range), but mean gradient is only 28 mmHg. Gradient is flow-dependent — it is generated by the ventricle pushing blood through the orifice. With LVEF 40% and stroke volume index 28 mL/m² (low-flow is <35), the ventricle simply cannot generate a high gradient across even a critically narrow valve. The low gradient reflects a weak pump, not a mild lesion.

Next step: dobutamine stress echocardiography (low-dose), to distinguish:
  • True severe AS — with augmented flow, the gradient rises (mean >40) while valve area stays small (<1.0). The valve was always severe.
  • Pseudo-severe AS — valve area increases with flow (the weak ventricle was simply not opening a moderately diseased valve fully), and gradient stays low. The primary problem is the myocardium.
  • Absence of contractile/flow reserve — no meaningful augmentation. This carries a worse prognosis and makes interpretation harder; aortic valve calcium scoring on CT is then the tiebreaker.
Examiner probes
  • "What are the physical signs supporting severity?" — Narrow pulse pressure, slow-rising, late-peaking carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus), a late-peaking murmur (peak timing tracks severity better than loudness), and a soft or absent A2 (the calcified valve can't close crisply). Note that murmur intensity can paradoxically fall in very severe AS with a failing ventricle — another reason not to grade by loudness.
  • "She had syncope on exertion. Significance?" — Syncope is one of the three cardinal symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnoea) and marks a decisive prognostic change. Historically, untreated severe symptomatic AS carried roughly 5-year survival after angina, 3 years after syncope, and 2 years after heart failure. Symptomatic severe AS is an intervention indication.
Stage 2

Dobutamine stress echo confirms true severe AS with contractile reserve. Coronary angiography shows no significant coronary disease. She is otherwise independent, mildly frail, with an estimated life expectancy well beyond 5 years. CT shows a tricuspid aortic valve with suitable transfemoral access.

TAVI or SAVR? Justify your answer.

Model answer+
TAVI, via transfemoral access.

Under the 2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, TAVI is recommended for anatomically suitable patients aged ≥70 with a tricuspid aortic valve, while SAVR remains standard for those under 70 at low surgical risk. She is 76 with a tricuspid valve and suitable transfemoral anatomy, so she sits clearly in the TAVI recommendation.

Flag the guideline change explicitly — the age threshold was lowered from 75 to 70 in 2025. If you learned 75, or your question bank uses it, that's now outdated. Her mild frailty further supports the less invasive option.

The decision should be made by the Heart Team, integrating age, procedural risk, anatomy, estimated life expectancy, and lifetime management — including whether she may need a future valve-in-valve procedure.

Examiner probes
  • "What if she were 62 with the same anatomy and low surgical risk?" — Then SAVR would be the standard recommendation. The reasoning is lifetime management: a younger patient will likely outlive a bioprosthesis, and starting with surgical replacement preserves the option of a later valve-in-valve TAVI — whereas starting with TAVI can constrain future options.
  • "What if the valve were bicuspid?" — Bicuspid anatomy is more complex (asymmetric calcification, associated aortopathy) and the evidence base is thinner. TAVI is discussed on anatomical suitability with comprehensive Heart Team evaluation rather than being a straightforward recommendation.
Stage 3

Return to her anaemia and dark stools. Is this relevant, or a coincidental finding to hand to the gastroenterologists?

Model answer+
Highly relevant — this is likely Heyde syndrome. The triad is severe aortic stenosis, acquired von Willebrand syndrome, and gastrointestinal bleeding from angiodysplasia.

Mechanism: high shear stress as blood is forced through the stenotic orifice unfolds and cleaves the largest, most haemostatically active von Willebrand factor multimers (via ADAMTS13). Losing those multimers produces a functional bleeding tendency, which manifests where fragile angiodysplastic vessels exist — typically the GI tract.

Why it matters clinically: the bleeding often resolves after valve replacement, because correcting the shear restores the vWF multimers. So this is not a separate GI problem to be handed off — it's a manifestation of her valve disease, and it strengthens rather than delays the case for intervention.

  • Still investigate the GI tract appropriately, and correct the iron deficiency — anaemia worsens her symptoms and is itself a surgical/procedural risk factor.
  • Don't let "she needs a colonoscopy first" indefinitely postpone treating symptomatic severe AS with syncope.
What separates a strong answer
  • Rejecting the echo report's conclusion and explaining why gradient is flow-dependent — this is the highest-value reasoning in the case.
  • Knowing the dobutamine stress echo has three possible outcomes, not two, and what to do when there's no contractile reserve.
  • Citing the 2025 TAVI age change and flagging that older sources say 75.
  • Articulating lifetime management as the reason age drives the TAVI/SAVR choice.
  • Connecting the anaemia to the valve rather than compartmentalising it — this kind of cross-system synthesis is exactly what viva examiners reward.
Case 7 · High complexityDecompensated Heart Failure with Cardiorenal Conflict
+
Presentation

A 64-year-old man with ischaemic HFrEF (EF 28%) is admitted with 10 days of worsening orthopnoea and weight gain of 6 kg. His medications are ramipril 10 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg and furosemide 40 mg daily. He has type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 3.

BP 104/64HR 92RR 26SpO₂ 91% RAJVP 8 cmSacral + leg oedema

Bloods: creatinine 168 µmol/L (baseline 132), K⁺ 5.3 mmol/L, NT-proBNP markedly elevated, Hb 10.2 g/dL, ferritin 62 ng/mL, TSAT 14%.

Stage 1

The admitting team proposes stopping ramipril and spironolactone because of the rising creatinine and potassium, and holding the beta-blocker. How do you respond?

Model answer+
I would push back on stopping the RAAS agents reflexively, but I agree with reassessing the beta-blocker in context.
  • He is congested, not hypoperfused. Warm peripheries, adequate BP and good mentation put him in the "wet and warm" profile. The priority is decongestion — escalate to IV loop diuretic at at least 2.5 times his home oral dose, not to withdraw disease-modifying therapy.
  • The creatinine rise may be the treatment working, not failing. A modest rise during effective decongestion often reflects haemoconcentration rather than injury. What matters is the clinical trajectory — symptoms, weight, JVP — not the number alone.
  • Potassium 5.3 does not mandate stopping an MRA. Review dietary potassium, stop any supplements, and check for contributors such as NSAIDs or trimethoprim. If it persists, a potassium binder should be used specifically to enable continued RAAS blockade rather than accepting withdrawal of proven mortality benefit.
  • Beta-blocker: continue if he is not hypoperfused, though dose reduction is reasonable if congestion is severe. Abrupt withdrawal is associated with worse outcomes. Never initiate during acute decompensation — but he is already established.
  • Also treat the iron deficiency. Ferritin 62 with TSAT 14% meets criteria independent of anaemia, and IV iron improves symptoms and reduces HF hospitalisation. Oral iron is not effective here.
Examiner probes
  • "How much creatinine rise would concern you?" — There is no single threshold, but a rise beyond roughly 30%, or any rise accompanied by worsening symptoms, oliguria, or hypotension, shifts the interpretation from haemoconcentration toward genuine injury. The clinical picture arbitrates.
  • "He is diuresing poorly after 24 hours." — Confirm adequate dosing and absorption (IV, not oral), then add a thiazide for sequential nephron blockade. Check for hypochloraemic alkalosis. Consider whether low output rather than diuretic resistance is the problem.
  • "Why not just give him inotropes?" — He is normotensive and adequately perfused. Inotropes in this profile increase arrhythmia and mortality risk without benefit — they are reserved for the "cold" hypoperfused profile.
Stage 2

He decongests well over 5 days. Creatinine settles at 150 µmol/L, potassium 4.9 on a binder. EF remains 28% on repeat echo. He is now euvolaemic and NYHA II. QRS is 158 ms with LBBB morphology. His index MI was 3 years ago.

What are his device and medication priorities before discharge?

Model answer+
  • Up-titrate GDMT intensively before discharge, not after. Current guidance gives a Class I recommendation to rapid up-titration with close follow-up through the first 6 weeks after a HF hospitalisation — that window is where the guideline wants titration to happen.
  • Consider switching ramipril to sacubitril-valsartan given persistent symptoms and reduced EF, observing the mandatory 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema.
  • CRT-D is indicated. EF 35% or below, NYHA II on GDMT, with LBBB and QRS 158 ms — this is the strongest CRT indication. He is also more than 40 days post-MI with more than 3 months of therapy, so the primary-prevention ICD criteria are met; a combined device is appropriate.
  • Complete IV iron repletion, arrange early follow-up (within 1-2 weeks), and confirm the SGLT2 inhibitor continues — it is Class I regardless of diabetes status.
Examiner probes
  • "Would CRT still be indicated with a QRS of 130 ms and RBBB?" — Much weaker. The benefit is greatest with LBBB and QRS 150 ms or more. With a narrow QRS there is no dyssynchrony to resynchronise and CRT may be harmful.
  • "His EF was 28% two weeks post-MI three years ago — does that matter now?" — It matters historically: implanting within 40 days of MI showed no mortality benefit (DINAMIT, IRIS). But he is three years out with persistent EF 28% on optimised therapy, so the waiting period is long satisfied.
  • "He is worried about the ICD firing." — A fair concern to address honestly. Discuss shock risk, the role of CRT in reducing arrhythmic burden, programming to minimise inappropriate therapy, and deactivation discussions at end of life.
What separates a strong answer
  • Refusing to withdraw prognostic therapy on the basis of numbers alone, and explaining why the creatinine rise may be benign.
  • Knowing potassium binders exist to enable rather than replace RAAS blockade.
  • Picking up the iron deficiency unprompted — it is in the stem but easy to skip past.
  • Titrating before discharge rather than deferring to the community.
Case 8 · Very high complexityProsthetic Valve Endocarditis with an Embolic Complication
+
Presentation

A 57-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve replacement 4 years ago presents with 5 weeks of fevers, night sweats, malaise and 7 kg weight loss. He had extensive dental work 2 months ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. He is on warfarin, INR 2.6.

Temp 38.4 °CBP 118/52HR 96New early diastolic murmurSplinter haemorrhages

Labs: CRP 148, Hb 9.8, WCC 13.2. Three sets of blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. TTE: suboptimal windows, no definite vegetation seen.

Stage 1

The TTE is reported as negative. A colleague suggests this makes endocarditis unlikely. What is your assessment and plan?

Model answer+
A negative TTE does not exclude prosthetic valve endocarditis — it has poor sensitivity in this setting because the prosthesis shadows the very structures you need to see.
  • Proceed to transoesophageal echocardiography, which is substantially more sensitive for prosthetic valves, perivalvular abscess and leaflet dehiscence. Repeat imaging in 5-7 days if initially negative and suspicion remains high.
  • Consider advanced imaging — 18F-FDG PET/CT and cardiac CT are now incorporated into the 2023 criteria and are particularly useful in prosthetic valve cases.
  • Applying the criteria: he already has one major criterion — persistently positive cultures with a typical organism. Minor criteria include fever, a predisposing condition (prosthetic valve), and vascular phenomena (splinter haemorrhages). Imaging evidence would supply a second major criterion.
  • Start empirical therapy after adequate cultures, covering staphylococci including MRSA, with an aminoglycoside and rifampicin per prosthetic valve regimens — do not wait for imaging in a septic patient with a prosthesis.
  • Involve the endocarditis team early — cardiology, cardiac surgery, microbiology and imaging.

Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis is a high-mortality diagnosis; the new murmur suggests valve dysfunction is already developing.

Examiner probes
  • "He had dental work without prophylaxis. Was that an error?" — Yes. He falls squarely in the high-risk category (prosthetic valve), and current guidance recommends prophylaxis for high-risk patients undergoing oral-dental procedures. Note the contrast: most native valve disease does not warrant prophylaxis, and prophylaxis is specifically not indicated to prevent device-related IE.
  • "Which criteria set would you use?" — Either the 2023 ESC version or the Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria. Both improve sensitivity over the 2000 modified Duke criteria by expanding typical organisms and incorporating PET/CT and cardiac CT. Using the 2000 criteria alone risks under-diagnosis.
Stage 2

TOE shows a 14 mm mobile vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve with a perivalvular abscess and a new paravalvular leak causing moderate-to-severe regurgitation. He develops mild pulmonary oedema.

What are the indications for surgery here, and how urgently?

Model answer+
He meets all three broad surgical indication categories simultaneously.
  • Heart failure — paravalvular leak with regurgitation and pulmonary oedema. This is the most urgent indication.
  • Uncontrolled infection — perivalvular abscess indicates local extension that antibiotics alone will not eradicate.
  • Embolism prevention — a large (over 10 mm) mobile vegetation, particularly with S. aureus.

With heart failure from valve dysfunction plus abscess, this is urgent surgery — within days, not weeks, and emergency surgery if pulmonary oedema becomes refractory. Completing a full antibiotic course before operating would be a serious error here.

Examiner probe
  • "How do you manage his warfarin peri-operatively?" — Anticoagulation is needed for the mechanical valve but complicates both haemorrhagic transformation risk and surgery. Switch to a shorter-acting agent (unfractionated heparin) that can be stopped and reversed rapidly, with close multidisciplinary coordination.
Stage 3

While awaiting theatre, he develops sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia. CT head shows an acute left middle cerebral artery ischaemic infarct, moderate size, with no haemorrhagic transformation.

Does this change the surgical plan? What about thrombolysis?

Model answer+
Thrombolysis is contraindicated. In endocarditis-related stroke the embolus is septic and often associated with mycotic aneurysm formation; thrombolysis carries a very high risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

Regarding surgery — this is genuinely nuanced, and a strong answer says so:

  • After an ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage, and where the patient is not comatose, current guidance supports proceeding with surgery without delay when the indication is strong — as here, with heart failure and abscess. The old teaching of routinely waiting weeks has shifted, because delay risks further embolism and progressive valve destruction.
  • After intracranial haemorrhage, surgery is generally deferred for around a month where possible — the opposite recommendation.
  • Image the cerebral vasculature for mycotic aneurysm, which would alter both anticoagulation and surgical timing.
  • Anticoagulation for the mechanical valve must be managed carefully given haemorrhagic transformation risk — bridge with unfractionated heparin under close monitoring.
Examiner probes
  • "He is now drowsy with a large infarct. Same answer?" — No. Extensive infarction with coma or severe neurological damage carries a poor prognosis and high perioperative risk; surgery may be deferred or, after multidisciplinary discussion, judged inappropriate. The distinction turns on infarct size and neurological status, not on the mere presence of a stroke.
  • "What is the single most important structural step in managing this case?" — Early referral to a multidisciplinary endocarditis team at a centre with cardiac surgery. Outcomes in complicated IE track closely with that.
What separates a strong answer
  • Refusing to be reassured by a negative TTE in a prosthetic valve.
  • Naming the three surgical indication categories and recognising all three are present.
  • Knowing that ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke pull surgical timing in opposite directions.
  • Ruling out thrombolysis on mechanism, not just on a memorised contraindication list.
Case 9 · Very high complexityYoung Adult with Chest Pain and Cardiogenic Shock
+
Presentation

A 26-year-old woman presents with 4 days of flu-like illness followed by 12 hours of central chest pain and progressive breathlessness. No cardiac history, no risk factors, not pregnant.

BP 86/54HR 122RR 30SpO₂ 90%Cool peripheriesJVP raised

ECG: sinus tachycardia, widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression, no reciprocal change. Troponin: markedly elevated. Echo: globally reduced LV function, EF 25%, no regional wall motion abnormality, small pericardial effusion.

Stage 1

What is your differential, and which single ECG feature most argues against acute coronary occlusion?

Model answer+
The leading diagnosis is fulminant myocarditis, likely viral, presenting with cardiogenic shock.

The discriminating ECG feature is the absence of reciprocal change. STEMI is a regional electrical event — elevation in one territory almost always produces depression opposite it. Here the elevation is diffuse with PR depression and no reciprocity, which is a global inflammatory pattern (myopericarditis), not a vascular territory.

Supporting the diagnosis: the viral prodrome, the young age without risk factors, global rather than regional hypokinesis, and an effusion.

Differential to keep open: spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD — important in young women), Takotsubo, and, if the picture were regional, genuine ACS. Peripartum cardiomyopathy would need excluding if she were peripartum.

Examiner probes
  • "Would you take her to the cath lab?" — Yes, in most protocols, precisely because the differential includes SCAD and ACS and the consequences of missing them are severe. Angiography also enables endomyocardial biopsy in the same setting. Argue the case rather than reflexively saying no.
  • "Which imaging confirms myocarditis non-invasively?" — Cardiac MRI using the updated Lake Louise criteria, assessing oedema and non-ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement in a subepicardial or mid-wall distribution — distinct from the subendocardial pattern of infarction.
Stage 2

Angiography shows normal coronaries. She deteriorates further: lactate 5.2, BP 78/48 on noradrenaline, urine output minimal, and she develops non-sustained VT.

How do you manage her now?

Model answer+
This is SCAI stage D-E cardiogenic shock from fulminant myocarditis, and the key point is that this condition is potentially fully reversible if she is supported through it.
  • Escalate to a centre with mechanical circulatory support. Fulminant myocarditis is one of the strongest indications for temporary MCS (VA-ECMO or a ventricular assist device) as a bridge to recovery — many patients recover normal ventricular function.
  • Endomyocardial biopsy is indicated here — reserved for high-risk myocarditis with haemodynamic instability or ventricular arrhythmia, which describes her exactly. It can identify giant cell myocarditis, eosinophilic myocarditis or sarcoidosis, which have specific immunosuppressive treatment.
  • Arrhythmia monitoring in a setting with immediate defibrillation capability.
  • Avoid negative inotropes acutely — beta-blockers are contraindicated during decompensation and are introduced only once she is stabilised.
  • NSAIDs are generally avoided when there is significant myocardial involvement, in contrast to their first-line role in isolated pericarditis.
Examiner probes
  • "Why biopsy if it will not change most cases?" — Because it changes management in the minority that matter most. Giant cell myocarditis carries a dismal untreated prognosis but responds to immunosuppression and often needs transplant assessment; you cannot diagnose it any other way.
  • "Would you implant an ICD now given the VT?" — No. Arrhythmia in acute fulminant myocarditis is potentially reversible, and function frequently recovers. Support acutely, reassess after recovery, and use a wearable defibrillator in the interim if risk persists.
  • "Prognosis?" — Counterintuitively, fulminant presentations that survive the acute phase often have better long-term ventricular recovery than indolent ones — which is precisely the argument for aggressive short-term support.
What separates a strong answer
  • Using absence of reciprocal change as the discriminator rather than relying on age and risk factors.
  • Still arguing for angiography — resisting the temptation to over-commit to the non-ischaemic diagnosis.
  • Framing fulminant myocarditis as reversible, which reframes the entire management goal toward support rather than palliation.
  • Knowing the specific biopsy indication rather than dismissing biopsy generically.
Case 10 · High complexityBreathless Woman with an Enlarged Right Ventricle
+
Presentation

A 48-year-old woman presents with sudden severe breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain 10 days after a long-haul flight. She takes a combined oral contraceptive. She reports a presyncopal episode on standing this morning.

BP 92/60HR 118RR 32SpO₂ 88% RAJVP raisedClear lungs

ECG: sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, T inversion V1-V4, incomplete RBBB. Echo: dilated hypokinetic RV, septal flattening, TAPSE 12 mm, no LV dysfunction.

Stage 1

Classify her risk and outline immediate management.

Model answer+
This is acute pulmonary embolism with right ventricular dysfunction. Risk stratification hinges on one question: is she haemodynamically stable?
  • BP 92/60 with presyncope, tachycardia and hypoxia places her at minimum in the intermediate-high risk category — RV dysfunction on echo plus elevated biomarkers, without frank persistent hypotension. If she had sustained SBP under 90 or required vasopressors, she would be high risk and reperfusion would be indicated immediately.
  • Start therapeutic anticoagulation immediately (LMWH or UFH) unless contraindicated — do not wait for imaging if suspicion is high and she is unstable.
  • CT pulmonary angiography to confirm, if she is stable enough to travel; bedside echo alone may justify treatment in extremis.
  • Monitor in a high-dependency setting for haemodynamic deterioration, which would trigger rescue reperfusion — systemic thrombolysis, or catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy where lysis is contraindicated.
  • Oxygen, and cautious fluid — no more than a small challenge. Aggressive fluid loading can over-distend the failing RV and worsen septal shift, reducing LV filling.
Examiner probes
  • "Why is aggressive fluid resuscitation dangerous here?" — The RV is already dilated and pressure-loaded.
