Further volume worsens RV distension and pushes the interventricular septum leftward, impairing LV filling and dropping cardiac output — the same interdependence principle behind tamponade physiology.
  • "Would you thrombolyse now?" — Not on these numbers. In intermediate-high risk PE, routine systemic thrombolysis reduced haemodynamic decompensation but increased major and intracranial bleeding (PEITHO), so the strategy is close monitoring with rescue lysis if she deteriorates.
  • "What does TAPSE 12 mm tell you?" — It quantifies longitudinal RV systolic function and is reduced (normal above roughly 17 mm), supporting genuine RV dysfunction rather than isolated dilation.
Stage 2

She is anticoagulated and improves. Six months later, despite adherent anticoagulation, she remains breathless on minimal exertion. Repeat echo shows persistent RV dilation with estimated PASP 62 mmHg.

What is the diagnosis you must not miss, and how do you confirm it?

Model answer+
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) — Group 4 pulmonary hypertension. This is the diagnosis not to miss because it is potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy.
  • The screening test is a V/Q scan, not CTPA. V/Q is more sensitive for chronic thromboembolic disease; a normal V/Q effectively excludes CTEPH. This is a commonly missed point.
  • Diagnosis requires at least 3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation before attributing persistent obstruction to chronic disease — she satisfies this.
  • Right heart catheterisation is required for confirmation, since echo estimates probability rather than establishing the diagnosis.
  • 🆕 Apply the current haemodynamic definition: mPAP above 20 mmHg, with pre-capillary disease requiring PVR above 2 Wood units and PAWP of 15 mmHg or less. If you were taught mPAP of 25 or more and PVR above 3, those thresholds were lowered in 2022.
  • Refer to a CTEPH centre for operability assessment — pulmonary endarterectomy, or balloon pulmonary angioplasty and targeted medical therapy if inoperable.
Examiner probes
  • "Why not just start a PAH drug?" — Because that would be treating Group 4 disease as Group 1 and could deny her a curative operation. Classification must precede therapy — and in Group 2 PH, pulmonary vasodilators can be actively harmful, increasing flow into a left heart that cannot accommodate it.
  • "What would you change about her long-term management?" — Lifelong anticoagulation given CTEPH, and stop the combined oral contraceptive, which was a provoking risk factor.
What separates a strong answer
  • Stratifying PE by haemodynamics rather than by clot burden on imaging.
  • Explaining why fluid can harm the failing RV, via ventricular interdependence.
  • Choosing V/Q over CTPA for CTEPH screening.
  • Citing the post-2022 PH thresholds, and insisting on catheterisation before treatment.
Case 11 · Viva styleAthlete with Exertional Syncope
+
Presentation

An 18-year-old competitive footballer collapses during a match and recovers within 30 seconds. He mentions two previous episodes of near-collapse during training that he did not report. His father died suddenly at 41; the death was attributed to "a heart attack" but no post-mortem was performed.

BP 122/74HR 62Systolic murmur at LLSBBrisk carotid upstroke

ECG: voltage criteria for LVH, deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads, T wave inversion in V4-V6. Echo: asymmetric septal hypertrophy 19 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, resting LVOT gradient 45 mmHg.

Stage 1

What is the diagnosis, and how does the murmur behave with Valsalva? Why does that matter mechanistically?

Model answer+
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (HOCM).

The murmur becomes LOUDER with Valsalva and on standing, and softer on squatting or handgrip — the opposite of most systolic murmurs. Mechanistically: reducing preload shrinks the LV cavity, which worsens systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve against the hypertrophied septum, intensifying obstruction. Increasing preload or afterload distends the cavity and relieves it.

The brisk carotid upstroke is a useful discriminator from aortic stenosis, which gives a slow-rising, late-peaking (parvus et tardus) pulse — the obstruction in HOCM is dynamic and develops during systole rather than being fixed from the outset.

The father's sudden death at 41 without post-mortem is a significant family history that should not be accepted at face value as "a heart attack."

Examiner probe
  • "He becomes hypotensive during the assessment. Which treatments would worsen him?" — Anything reducing preload or afterload, or increasing contractility: nitrates, aggressive diuresis, and inotropes all worsen dynamic obstruction. Give fluid, consider phenylephrine to raise afterload, and use beta-blockade — the reverse of instinct in most hypotensive patients.
Stage 2

How do you stratify his sudden cardiac death risk, and what do you do about an ICD?

Model answer+
Use a validated risk calculator as the first step — HCM Risk-SCD in adults — rather than a gestalt judgement or any single variable.

Inputs include age, maximal wall thickness, left atrial size, maximal LVOT gradient, family history of sudden death, non-sustained VT, and unexplained syncope.

His risk profile is concerning on several counts: unexplained exertional syncope (repeated), a first-degree relative with premature sudden death, marked hypertrophy at 19 mm, and a significant resting gradient. Cardiac MRI should assess late gadolinium enhancement as an additional modifier.

Given this combination, a primary-prevention ICD warrants serious discussion, and the decision should be shared with a clear explanation of shock risk and device complications in a young patient facing decades of therapy.

Examiner probes
  • "Why is exertional syncope weighted so heavily?" — It suggests either a haemodynamically significant arrhythmia or a marked rise in outflow obstruction during exercise. Syncope during exertion is far more ominous than syncope after stopping, which is more often vasovagal.
  • "Can he keep playing competitive football?" — No. High-intensity competitive sport should be restricted. Crucially, an ICD does not make competition safe — it may terminate an arrhythmia but does not prevent one, and repeated shocks in a young athlete carry real morbidity.
  • "What about his relatives?" — Offer family screening — clinical evaluation with ECG and echo for first-degree relatives, plus genetic testing where a causative variant is identified in the proband. Cascade screening is an explicit part of modern cardiomyopathy management.
Stage 3

He is started on a beta-blocker but remains symptomatic with exertional dyspnoea and a persistent resting gradient of 52 mmHg.

What are the next therapeutic options?

Model answer+
  • Optimise medical therapy first — maximise beta-blockade, or use a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as verapamil if beta-blockers are not tolerated. Disopyramide can be added for its negative inotropic effect.
  • 🆕 Mavacamten — a cardiac myosin inhibitor — should be considered for symptomatic obstructive HCM despite optimal medical therapy. It targets the underlying sarcomere hypercontractility, which is a genuinely new therapeutic mechanism and will not appear in older texts.
  • Septal reduction therapy for refractory symptoms: surgical myectomy (generally preferred in younger patients, with better long-term durability) or alcohol septal ablation (better suited to older or higher surgical risk patients).
  • Avoid vasodilators, high-dose diuretics and inotropes throughout — all worsen dynamic obstruction.
What separates a strong answer
  • Explaining the murmur's paradoxical behaviour mechanistically, not as a memorised fact.
  • Using the brisk carotid upstroke to separate HOCM from aortic stenosis.
  • Reaching for a validated risk calculator rather than eyeballing risk factors.
  • Stating clearly that an ICD does not license return to competitive sport.
  • Raising family screening unprompted — examiners look for this.
Case 12 · Very high complexityNSTEMI in a Patient on Anticoagulation with CKD
+
Presentation

A 78-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation on apixaban, CKD stage 3b (eGFR 34), prior peptic ulcer disease and anaemia (Hb 10.4) presents with 3 hours of chest discomfort at rest. She takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily and bisoprolol.

BP 138/78HR 74 irregularRR 18SpO₂ 96%Chest clear

ECG: AF, rate 74, 1 mm ST depression in V4-V6. Troponin: rising on serial testing. GRACE: high.

Stage 1

Outline your antithrombotic strategy and the timing of angiography. The team asks whether to load her with ticagrelor now.

Model answer+
This is NSTEMI in the high-risk tier — troponin-positive with dynamic ST changes and a high GRACE score — so early invasive angiography within 24 hours is indicated.

🆕 Do not load with ticagrelor now. Routine P2Y12 pretreatment before knowing coronary anatomy is Class III (against) in NSTE-ACS patients planned for an early invasive strategy. This is a reversal of older practice and exactly the trap in this stem. Give aspirin, proceed to angiography, and choose the P2Y12 agent once anatomy is known.

Her specific complexities:
  • She is already anticoagulated. Adding potent antiplatelets on top of a DOAC in a patient with prior peptic ulcer disease and anaemia carries substantial bleeding risk.
  • Ticagrelor and prasugrel are generally avoided in patients requiring long-term oral anticoagulation. Clopidogrel is the P2Y12 agent of choice in combination therapy.
  • Use radial access to reduce bleeding, and add a proton pump inhibitor given her ulcer history.
  • CKD: minimise contrast volume, ensure adequate pre-procedural hydration, and check whether her apixaban dose is appropriate for her renal function and age.
Examiner probes
  • "Should the apixaban be held before angiography?" — Practice varies and it is reasonable to say so. Many centres omit the morning dose before a planned radial procedure; the decision balances stroke risk against access-site bleeding. What you should not do is stop anticoagulation for a prolonged period in a patient with AF.
  • "Is her troponin rise definitely a Type 1 MI?" — A good question to interrogate. With anaemia, CKD and AF, Type 2 MI from supply-demand mismatch is a real alternative. However, rest pain with dynamic ST depression and a rising troponin favours a Type 1 event, and the invasive strategy will clarify it. Do not anchor prematurely in either direction.
Stage 2

Angiography shows a significant proximal LAD lesion treated with a drug-eluting stent, plus moderate non-obstructive disease elsewhere. She is stable post-procedure.

What antithrombotic regimen do you prescribe at discharge, and for how long?

Model answer+
The guiding principle is to minimise the duration of triple therapy.
  • Triple therapy (apixaban + aspirin + clopidogrel) for a short period — commonly limited to around the periprocedural window and up to about a week in high bleeding risk, given her ulcer history and anaemia.
  • Then dual therapy — apixaban plus clopidogrel — continued for up to 12 months, with the exact duration shortened if bleeding risk dominates.
  • Then apixaban monotherapy long term. Continuing an antiplatelet indefinitely alongside anticoagulation adds bleeding without ischaemic benefit in most patients.
  • Verify the apixaban dose: she qualifies for dose reduction if at least two of age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, or creatinine 133 µmol/L or more are met. Check rather than assume — both under- and over-dosing are common and harmful.
  • Add a PPI, high-intensity statin targeting at least 50% LDL-C reduction and under 55 mg/dL, and continue the beta-blocker.
Examiner probes
  • "Why not just keep her on aspirin plus clopidogrel and stop the anticoagulant?" — Antiplatelet therapy is markedly inferior to anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention while still carrying bleeding risk. Dropping the anticoagulant trades a small ischaemic gain for a substantial stroke risk.
  • "She bleeds from her upper GI tract at week 3. Now what?" — Resuscitate, endoscopy, hold antithrombotics briefly, and treat the lesion. Then restart as early as safely possible — prolonged interruption after recent stenting risks stent thrombosis. Usually restart the anticoagulant first with a single antiplatelet, guided by a multidisciplinary discussion.
  • "Would your answer change if she had a mechanical valve rather than AF?" — Yes, importantly. A DOAC would be contraindicated and she would require warfarin, with the same principle of minimising concurrent antiplatelet exposure.
What separates a strong answer
  • Withholding the P2Y12 load — recognising the Class III pretreatment reversal under pressure from a colleague.
  • Choosing clopidogrel over ticagrelor specifically because of concurrent anticoagulation.
  • Structuring the answer as a de-escalation ladder with defined transition points rather than a single regimen.
  • Checking the DOAC dose criteria rather than assuming the prescribed dose is right.
  • Keeping Type 2 MI alive as a differential without letting it derail appropriate management.
Case 13 · High complexityAdolescent with Fever, Arthritis and a New Murmur
+
Presentation

A 14-year-old boy presents with 10 days of migratory joint pain affecting knees then ankles, low-grade fever and fatigue. Three weeks earlier he had a sore throat that was not treated. He is from a densely populated urban area.

Temp 38.1 °CBP 104/62HR 118New apical pansystolic murmurSoft S1

Labs: ESR 68, CRP 82, ASO titre markedly raised. ECG: sinus tachycardia, PR interval 240 ms. Echo: mitral regurgitation, mild LV dilation, no vegetation.

Stage 1

What is the diagnosis, how do you establish it formally, and what is the single most important long-term intervention?

Model answer+
Acute rheumatic fever with carditis, following untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

Formal diagnosis uses the revised Jones criteria, which apply different thresholds in moderate-to-high-risk populations such as Indonesia. He has evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (raised ASO) plus:

  • Major criteria: carditis (new mitral regurgitation on echo — note subclinical carditis detected by echo now counts as a major criterion) and polyarthritis. In high-risk populations, monoarthritis or polyarthralgia also qualifies as major.
  • Minor criteria: fever, raised ESR/CRP, and prolonged PR interval.
  • Two major criteria plus evidence of preceding streptococcal infection establishes the diagnosis.
Management:
  • Penicillin to eradicate residual streptococcal carriage.
  • Anti-inflammatory therapy (aspirin or NSAIDs) for arthritis; corticosteroids are used in severe carditis with heart failure.
  • Heart failure management if required.
The single most important long-term intervention is SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS — long-acting benzathine penicillin G every 3-4 weeks, continued for years. Recurrent ARF causes cumulative valve damage, and this is what determines whether he needs valve surgery in his thirties. Candidates routinely focus on acute treatment and under-weight prophylaxis.
Examiner probes
  • "How long does prophylaxis continue?" — Duration depends on severity: longest with established carditis and residual valve disease (often to age 40 or lifelong), shorter with carditis but no residual disease, shortest with no carditis. Say that it is severity-stratified rather than quoting a single number.
  • "Which valve is most affected and why does that matter later?" — The mitral valve predominantly. Acute disease causes regurgitation from leaflet inflammation and annular dilation; chronic disease produces commissural fusion and mitral stenosis years later. That later stenosis is what decompensates in pregnancy (Case 2).
  • "Why does population risk change the criteria?" — In high-incidence populations the pre-test probability is far higher, so applying low-risk-population thresholds under-diagnoses and denies prophylaxis to those who most need it.
What separates a strong answer
  • Knowing the Jones criteria have modified thresholds for moderate-to-high-risk populations — directly relevant to Indonesian practice.
  • Recognising echo-detected subclinical carditis as a major criterion.
  • Leading with secondary prophylaxis as the intervention that alters the life course.
  • Connecting acute regurgitation to later stenosis rather than treating them as separate diseases.
Case 14 · Very high complexityAscites and Raised JVP After Treated Tuberculosis
+
Presentation

A 42-year-old man presents with 8 months of progressive abdominal distension, ankle swelling and exertional dyspnoea. He completed treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 3 years ago. He has been managed by his GP as "liver disease" with escalating diuretics and referred for hepatology assessment.

BP 98/72HR 96JVP markedly raisedTense ascitesPulsatile liver absent

Echo: normal LV size, EF 58%, biatrial enlargement, septal bounce, marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow. Tissue Doppler: lateral e′ 6 cm/s, septal e′ 12 cm/s. CT: pericardial thickening with focal calcification.

Stage 1

Why is the hepatology referral a diagnostic error, and what is the diagnosis?

Model answer+
This is constrictive pericarditis, almost certainly tuberculous, misattributed to liver disease.

The error is anchoring on ascites without examining the JVP. Ascites with a markedly raised JVP is a cardiac or pericardial problem until proven otherwise — cirrhotic ascites does not raise venous pressure. That single bedside finding redirects the entire workup, and it was available from the first consultation.

The confirmatory findings, all present:
  • Septal bounce and marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow — both reflect exaggerated ventricular interdependence within a fixed pericardial space.
  • Annulus reversus — septal e′ (12) exceeds lateral e′ (6). This is the counterintuitive finding: in constriction the myocardium is healthy, so annular motion is preserved or increased despite severe diastolic dysfunction, and lateral motion is tethered by the rigid pericardium.
  • Pericardial thickening with calcification on CT, with a fitting history — tuberculosis is a leading cause of constriction in endemic regions.

Why it matters so much: constriction is potentially curable by pericardiectomy, whereas restrictive cardiomyopathy is not. Years of diuretics for presumed liver disease represent lost curative opportunity.

Examiner probes
  • "How would restrictive cardiomyopathy differ on these tests?" — Reduced e′ (not increased), minimal respiratory variation, no septal bounce, normal pericardium, and often marked biatrial enlargement with an infiltrative cause such as amyloid. The e′ direction is the cleanest discriminator.
  • "What JVP finding would you expect?" — A sharp, deep y descent (Friedreich's sign) because early filling is rapid and unimpeded until the ventricle abruptly meets the rigid pericardium. Contrast with tamponade, where filling is impeded throughout and the y descent is blunted. Kussmaul's sign — a paradoxical inspiratory rise in JVP — is also characteristic.
  • "Is catheterisation needed?" — Often, when imaging is equivocal. It shows equalisation of end-diastolic pressures, a dip-and-plateau ("square root") ventricular waveform, and discordant RV and LV systolic pressure variation with respiration — the haemodynamic signature of interdependence.
Stage 2

He asks whether an operation will help, and whether he needs anti-tuberculous therapy again.

Model answer+
  • Pericardiectomy is the definitive treatment and can be curative. Outcomes are substantially better when performed before advanced disease develops — established myocardial atrophy, severe calcification, hepatic dysfunction or cachexia all worsen surgical mortality. His years of delay have already cost him.
  • Assess for active tuberculosis before surgery. If there is evidence of ongoing active infection, anti-tuberculous therapy should be given; corticosteroids may reduce the need for later pericardiectomy in effusive tuberculous pericarditis, though evidence is mixed. In purely chronic calcific constriction from treated disease, repeat anti-tuberculous therapy is not automatically indicated.
  • Diuretics only temporise — they relieve congestion but do not address a fixed mechanical constraint, and excessive diuresis in a preload-dependent physiology reduces cardiac output.
  • Optimise nutritional and hepatic status pre-operatively where time allows.
What separates a strong answer
  • Naming the ascites-with-raised-JVP mismatch as the point where the diagnosis was available and missed.
  • Reading annulus reversus correctly rather than assuming reduced e′ means worse disease.
  • Knowing constriction is curable and that surgical timing changes outcome.
  • Recognising tuberculosis as a leading local cause rather than reciting Western aetiologies.
Case 15 · High complexitySyncope with Bradycardia — Choosing the Right Device
+
Presentation

A 71-year-old woman has three episodes of sudden collapse without warning over 6 weeks, each with rapid full recovery and no post-ictal confusion. She sustained a facial injury in the most recent episode. She takes bisoprolol for hypertension and donepezil.

BP 142/80HR 44No murmurNormal neurological exam

ECG: sinus rhythm at 44 with 2:1 AV block, constant PR on conducted beats, QRS 138 ms with LBBB morphology. Bloods: K⁺ 4.2, TSH normal, creatinine normal.

Stage 1

The team plans to stop the bisoprolol and observe. Is that sufficient?

Model answer+
Stopping the bisoprolol is correct but not sufficient — the ECG points to infranodal disease, which will not resolve.
  • Constant PR on conducted beats with a wide LBBB QRS indicates block below the AV node (His-Purkinje disease), effectively a Mobitz II pattern. This carries a high risk of sudden progression to complete block with an unreliable, slow escape rhythm.
  • Syncope without prodrome, causing injury, is a red flag for an arrhythmic cause. This is not vasovagal syncope, which typically has a prodrome and situational trigger.
  • Permanent pacing is indicated — for symptomatic bradycardia here, and it would be indicated for infranodal second-degree block even without symptoms.
  • Do exclude reversible contributors first: rate-limiting drugs (bisoprolol — and note donepezil, a cholinesterase inhibitor, also causes bradycardia and is easily overlooked), hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism and ischaemia. All are being addressed, but none explains fixed infranodal conduction disease with LBBB.
  • Monitor on telemetry while awaiting the device; have transcutaneous pacing available.
Examiner probes
  • "How do you distinguish this from Mobitz I?" — In 2:1 block you cannot see progressive PR lengthening, so use surrogates: a wide QRS favours infranodal disease, whereas a narrow QRS favours the AV node. Block worsening with exercise or atropine also indicates infranodal disease, since improved AV nodal conduction increases the rate reaching a diseased His-Purkinje system.
  • "The donepezil — really?" — Yes, worth naming. Cholinesterase inhibitors increase vagal tone and are a recognised, frequently missed cause of bradycardia and syncope in older patients. Reviewing the whole drug list is the habit being tested.
Stage 2

Echo shows EF 34% with global hypokinesis, previously undocumented. She has no history of MI and angiography shows unobstructed coronaries.

Which device do you implant?

Model answer+
Not a standard dual-chamber pacemaker — she needs resynchronisation.
  • Conventional RV pacing worsens outcomes in patients with reduced EF, because it creates an iatrogenic LBBB-like dyssynchrony. Implanting a standard pacemaker here risks precipitating pacing-induced cardiomyopathy in a ventricle that is already impaired.
  • With EF 34%, LBBB, QRS 138 ms and an anticipated high burden of ventricular pacing, CRT is the appropriate choice. Conduction system pacing (His-bundle or left bundle branch area pacing) is an increasingly used alternative that preserves physiological activation.
  • Optimise GDMT first and reassess EF where the clinical situation allows — some of her dysfunction may be rate-related (bradycardia-induced) and improve after pacing and medical therapy, which would then inform whether a defibrillator is warranted.
  • Regarding a defibrillator: she has no documented ventricular arrhythmia, and primary-prevention ICD criteria require EF 35% or below after at least 3 months of optimised therapy. Reassess then rather than committing now.
What separates a strong answer
  • Recognising that "needs pacing" and "which pacing" are two separate decisions.
  • Knowing RV pacing can itself cause cardiomyopathy in a reduced-EF ventricle.
  • Naming donepezil — evidence of reviewing the full drug list, not just cardiac drugs.
  • Deferring the ICD decision to the appropriate reassessment window rather than bundling it in reflexively.
Case 16 · High complexityCollapse on the Ward — Drug-Induced Torsades
+
Presentation

A 68-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia and treated with intravenous levofloxacin collapses on the ward. She has been vomiting for 3 days and receiving furosemide for a history of heart failure. She was started on ondansetron and haloperidol overnight for agitation and nausea.

UnresponsiveNo palpable pulse initiallySpontaneous ROSC after 40 s

Telemetry: polymorphic VT with a twisting axis about the baseline, self-terminating after ~35 seconds. Post-event ECG: QTc 580 ms, prominent U waves. Labs: K⁺ 2.7, Mg²⁺ 0.52 mmol/L.

Stage 1

Identify the rhythm and every contributing factor, then give your immediate management. A colleague is preparing amiodarone.

Model answer+
This is Torsades de Pointes from acquired long QT — and amiodarone must not be given.

Amiodarone is a Class III agent that blocks potassium efflux and prolongs the QT further, which is the substrate for this arrhythmia. It would worsen her.

Every contributor is in the stem — name them all:
  • Levofloxacin — fluoroquinolones prolong the QT.
  • Ondansetron — QT-prolonging.
  • Haloperidol — QT-prolonging.
  • Hypokalaemia (2.7) — from vomiting and furosemide.
  • Hypomagnesaemia (0.52) — same causes.

Three QT-prolonging drugs stacked on two electrolyte deficits — this was foreseeable and preventable.

Immediate management:
  • Intravenous magnesium sulphate — first-line regardless of the measured magnesium level.
  • Aggressive potassium repletion, targeting the upper normal range.
  • Stop all QT-prolonging drugs immediately and find alternatives for the infection and agitation.
  • Defibrillate if it degenerates to sustained VT or VF with loss of output.
  • Continuous monitoring with defibrillator at the bedside; correct any bradycardia.
Examiner probes
  • "Her runs keep recurring and she has a sinus bradycardia at 46." — This is pause-dependent Torsades: a preceding pause or bradycardia sets up the triggering premature beat landing on the prolonged T wave. Increase the underlying rate — temporary overdrive pacing or an isoprenaline infusion — which shortens the QT and suppresses the arrhythmia. This is counterintuitive if you think of tachycardia as always bad.
  • "Why does hypokalaemia prolong repolarisation?" — Low extracellular potassium paradoxically reduces the repolarising potassium current, prolonging phase 3 and promoting early afterdepolarisations, which are the triggering mechanism.
  • "Does she need an ICD?" — Not if the cause is genuinely reversible and correctable, which it appears to be. Implanting before excluding a reversible cause would commit her unnecessarily to lifelong device therapy. Reassess the QTc after full correction and drug withdrawal; if it remains prolonged, consider congenital long QT and investigate accordingly.
What separates a strong answer
  • Stopping the amiodarone before anything else — refusing a colleague's plan under time pressure.
  • Listing all five contributors rather than one; the stem rewards systematic drug and electrolyte review.
  • Giving magnesium regardless of level.
  • Recognising pause-dependence and being willing to increase the heart rate.
  • Holding off on an ICD because the cause is reversible.
Case 17 · High complexityYoung Man with Resistant Hypertension
+
Presentation

A 24-year-old man is referred with hypertension resistant to three agents. He is asymptomatic apart from mild leg fatigue on prolonged walking, which he attributes to being unfit. He was told at school that he had "a heart murmur that did not matter."

BP right arm 168/94BP left arm 164/92BP leg 128/78HR 72Radio-femoral delay

Exam: systolic murmur over the left interscapular area. ECG: LVH by voltage criteria. CXR: inferior rib notching, "figure-3" contour of the aortic knuckle.

Stage 1

What is the diagnosis, which bedside finding is most specific, and what associated lesions must you exclude?

Model answer+
Coarctation of the aorta.

The most specific bedside finding is radio-femoral delay with an upper-to-lower limb BP gradient. Simply measuring leg blood pressure in any young hypertensive patient makes this diagnosis, and omitting it is why coarctation is often found late. The mild leg fatigue on walking is claudication he has rationalised away.

Rib notching reflects dilated collateral intercostal arteries eroding the inferior rib borders; the figure-3 sign is pre- and post-stenotic aortic dilation.

Associated lesions to exclude — this is what separates a complete answer:
  • Bicuspid aortic valve — present in a large proportion of coarctation patients, and it carries its own risk of stenosis, regurgitation and ascending aortopathy.
  • Berry aneurysms of the cerebral circulation — associated, with risk of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Consider intracranial imaging.
  • Turner syndrome in female patients.
  • Aortopathy — image the whole aorta with CT or MR angiography.

Note that both arms are equally hypertensive here, indicating the coarctation is distal to the left subclavian origin. A pressure difference between arms would suggest involvement at or proximal to the left subclavian.

Examiner probes
  • "He is asymptomatic. Why intervene?" — Untreated coarctation causes premature death from accelerated hypertension, stroke, aortic dissection or rupture, endocarditis and heart failure. A significant gradient with hypertension is an indication for repair regardless of symptoms.
  • "Repair options?" — Percutaneous stenting is commonly preferred in adults with suitable anatomy; surgical repair is used where anatomy is unfavourable or in association with other lesions. Either way, hypertension frequently persists or recurs and requires ongoing treatment.
  • "He is repaired. Does he need follow-up?" — Yes, lifelong. Re-coarctation, aneurysm formation at the repair site, persistent or recurrent hypertension, and progression of an associated bicuspid valve all require surveillance. Repair is not a cure.
What separates a strong answer
  • Stating that leg BP should be measured in every young hypertensive — a habit, not a reaction to this stem.
  • Reinterpreting "unfit legs" as claudication.
  • Naming the associated lesions unprompted, especially bicuspid valve and berry aneurysms.
  • Using the equal-arm pressures to localise the lesion anatomically.
  • Emphasising that repair requires lifelong follow-up.
Case 18 · Viva styleStable Angina in a Diabetic — To Revascularise or Not
+
Presentation

A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension reports 4 months of predictable chest tightness after climbing two flights of stairs, relieved within minutes by rest. No rest pain, no nocturnal symptoms, no change in threshold.

BP 146/86HR 78BMI 31No murmurNormal JVP

ECG: normal at rest. Echo: EF 58%, no regional wall motion abnormality. CT coronary angiography: moderate-to-severe stenoses in the mid-LAD and a large obtuse marginal. Stress imaging: moderate reversible ischaemia. LDL-C: 138 mg/dL. He takes metformin only.

Stage 1

He has read that stents prevent heart attacks and wants one. How do you counsel him?

Model answer+
The honest answer is that in stable coronary disease, revascularisation improves symptoms but has not been shown to reduce death or myocardial infarction compared with optimal medical therapy in patients like him.

The ISCHEMIA trial randomised patients with stable disease and moderate-to-severe ischaemia to an invasive versus conservative strategy and found no reduction in the primary composite outcome, though angina relief was better with revascularisation.

So the framing is: what is he trying to achieve?
  • If symptom relief is the goal and he remains limited despite good medical therapy, revascularisation is a reasonable option.
  • If prognosis is the goal, the evidence points to intensifying medical therapy rather than to a stent.
His medical therapy is currently inadequate, and fixing that is the priority:
  • LDL-C 138 with established coronary disease is far above target — he needs at least 50% reduction and a goal under 55 mg/dL. High-intensity statin, adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed.
  • Antiplatelet therapy — aspirin.
  • Anti-anginal therapy — beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker first-line, titrated properly before declaring medical therapy failed.
  • An SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit, given diabetes with established atherosclerotic disease — this is the intervention most likely to change his outcome.
  • BP 146/86 is above target and needs treatment; plus smoking status, weight, exercise and glycaemic control.
Examiner probes
  • "When would revascularisation improve prognosis in stable disease?" — In specific anatomical subsets: left main stenosis, and multivessel disease with reduced LV function, particularly in diabetes where CABG generally outperforms PCI (FREEDOM). ISCHEMIA specifically excluded significant left main disease, so its conclusion does not apply there.
  • "He asks whether CABG or PCI would be better if he does need revascularisation." — With diabetes and multivessel disease, CABG has shown better outcomes than PCI. The decision belongs with a Heart Team using anatomical complexity scoring.
  • "Is it paternalistic to refuse a stent he wants?" — Not if you present the evidence honestly and the choice remains his. The failure mode is agreeing to an intervention while allowing him to believe it will prevent a heart attack — that is a consent problem, not a technical one.
What separates a strong answer
  • Separating the symptom goal from the prognosis goal explicitly.
  • Auditing his medical therapy and finding it inadequate before discussing procedures.
  • Knowing which anatomical subsets ISCHEMIA excluded.
  • Naming SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 agonists in a diabetic with established atherosclerosis.
  • Handling the consent question honestly rather than deferring to the patient's request.
Case 19 · High complexityHypotension and a Large Pericardial Effusion
+
Presentation

A 59-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with 2 weeks of increasing breathlessness, now at rest. She is anxious and prefers sitting forward.

BP 88/68HR 124RR 28JVP raisedHeart sounds muffledPulsus paradoxus 22 mmHg

ECG: sinus tachycardia, low voltage, electrical alternans. Echo: large circumferential effusion, right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse, dilated IVC with minimal respiratory variation.

Stage 1

A junior doctor has prescribed intravenous furosemide for the breathlessness and raised JVP. What do you do, and explain the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus.

Model answer+
Stop the furosemide — this is cardiac tamponade, and diuresis can precipitate cardiovascular collapse.

The compressed heart has a fixed, reduced filling volume and depends critically on venous filling pressure to fill at all. Reducing preload with a diuretic (or a vasodilator, or aggressive sedation) removes the very thing sustaining cardiac output. The raised JVP here reflects obstruction to filling, not fluid overload — the same number means the opposite thing.

Pulsus paradoxus mechanism: within a fixed pericardial space, the two ventricles compete for a fixed total volume — exaggerated ventricular interdependence. On inspiration, negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right heart, so the RV fills more and the interventricular septum shifts leftward, reducing LV filling. Reduced LV stroke volume causes the inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg. It is not truly "paradoxical" — it is an exaggeration of a normal physiological variation.

Management:
  • Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis — this is the definitive treatment.
  • Cautious intravenous fluid to temporise while preparing, since she is preload-dependent.
  • Avoid positive pressure ventilation if at all possible — it further impairs venous return and can precipitate arrest at induction.
  • Send fluid for cytology and microbiology, including tuberculosis testing where locally prevalent.
Examiner probes
  • "Name a situation where tamponade occurs WITHOUT pulsus paradoxus." — Coexisting severe aortic regurgitation, an atrial septal defect, severe LV dysfunction, or markedly raised LV diastolic pressure. Its absence does not exclude tamponade.
  • "When is pericardiocentesis the WRONG first move?" — In Type A aortic dissection with haemopericardium, draining the pericardium can relieve the tamponade that is partially containing the bleed and accelerate exsanguination — the patient needs theatre. Also in traumatic haemopericardium and purulent pericarditis, where surgical drainage is usually preferred.
  • "It reaccumulates within a week." — Malignant effusions commonly recur. Options include an indwelling pericardial catheter, a surgical pericardial window, or pleuropericardial drainage, alongside systemic oncological therapy. Frame it in the context of her overall prognosis and goals of care.
What separates a strong answer
  • Recognising that raised JVP here means the opposite of what it means in heart failure.
  • Explaining pulsus paradoxus through ventricular interdependence rather than reciting the number.
  • Flagging the danger of positive pressure ventilation — a real and often fatal trap.
  • Knowing the specific situation where pericardiocentesis is contraindicated.
Case 20 · High complexitySudden Cold Painful Leg in Atrial Fibrillation
+
Presentation

A 74-year-old man with known permanent atrial fibrillation presents with 5 hours of sudden severe pain in the right leg. He stopped his anticoagulant 3 weeks ago after a dental extraction and did not restart it. He has no history of claudication.

BP 156/88HR 96 irregularRight leg pale, cold below mid-thighAbsent femoral, popliteal and distal pulses on the rightNormal pulses on the left

Exam: reduced sensation over the right forefoot; he can wiggle his toes weakly. Calf is soft and non-tender.

Stage 1

Classify the severity, decide the urgency, and explain why the contralateral pulses matter.

Model answer+
Acute limb ischaemia, almost certainly EMBOLIC from atrial fibrillation after anticoagulant interruption.

Of the six Ps, the two that grade severity are paraesthesia and paralysis. He has sensory loss with early motor weakness, which places him in the threatened limb category (Rutherford IIb — immediately threatened). This requires emergency revascularisation, within hours, not investigation-first.

Why the normal contralateral pulses matter: they argue strongly for embolism rather than in-situ thrombosis. A patient with chronic atherosclerotic disease severe enough to thrombose usually has bilateral disease, absent pulses on both sides, and a history of claudication. Normal pulses on the other leg, no claudication history, sudden onset, and a clear embolic source all point the same way — and this distinction changes the operation.

Immediate management:
  • Immediate systemic anticoagulation with an intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion, unless contraindicated. Do this before imaging.
  • Urgent vascular surgical referral — embolectomy (often with a Fogarty catheter) for embolic occlusion, versus catheter-directed thrombolysis or bypass for thrombotic disease.
  • Analgesia, keep the limb dependent and warm but do not apply direct heat.
  • Imaging (CT angiography) if it does not delay revascularisation in an immediately threatened limb.
  • Baseline bloods including creatine kinase, potassium and renal function.
Examiner probes
  • "What if the leg were mottled, insensate, with a rigid calf and no motor function?" — That is an irreversibly damaged limb (Rutherford III), where revascularisation risks fatal reperfusion injury. Primary amputation is then appropriate. Recognising the limb that should not be revascularised is as important as recognising the one that must be.
  • "What do you watch for after revascularisation?" — Reperfusion injury: hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, and compartment syndrome — which may need fasciotomy. Monitor potassium and renal function closely; sudden hyperkalaemia on reperfusion can cause cardiac arrest.
  • "He needed the dental extraction. Was stopping anticoagulation reasonable?" — Interrupting briefly may be reasonable for some procedures, though many dental extractions can be performed on continued anticoagulation with local haemostatic measures. The real failure was not restarting it — a systems and handover problem, and the direct cause of this presentation.
What separates a strong answer
  • Grading by sensory and motor findings rather than by pain and pallor.
  • Using the contralateral leg as diagnostic information.
  • Anticoagulating before imaging.
  • Knowing which limb should not be revascularised.
  • Anticipating reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome rather than treating revascularisation as the end of the problem.
Building your own cases: the pattern these follow is transferable — take a common presentation, add one feature that makes the obvious management dangerous, then evolve it over 2-3 stages so a correct early answer must be revised. These 20 plus your existing 6 case sims give you 26; at 2-3 per week across Weeks 15-16 you can work through them without repeating, and still have spares for the final taper.
